Do you assign or review accountability for AI risks and controls across multiple teams, systems, or organizational boundaries?
Do you monitor conformance to AI policies or external obligations over time, including standards, internal policies, or regulatory commitments?

personas.title: AI System Users
description: Actors that use AI-powered applications or services without developing or deploying the AI components themselves. Users rely on application developers and providers for AI security controls.
identificationQuestions:
Do you use AI-powered applications or services where the development, deployment, and security controls are managed by a different team or organization?
Do you interact with applications or platforms that embed AI capabilities (e.g., intelligent recommendations, automated analysis, or AI-assisted workflows)?
Do you select, procure, or authorize AI-powered products or services for use within your organization?
Do you provide direct inputs to AI systems (e.g., prompts, documents, or queries)?
Do you delegate tasks to AI agents or automated processes that take actions on your behalf (e.g., scheduling meetings, filing reports, or executing transactions)?
Do you rely on AI-generated content or decisions without visibility into how the AI system produces them (e.g., automated recommendations, risk scores, or content summaries)?

personas.title: Model Creator (Legacy)
description:
DEPRECATED: This persona has been superseded by more specific personas. Use Model Provider for those that train/tune models, or Application Developer for those integrating models into applications.
Organizations that either train and tune foundation models for Generative AI, or tune acquired models for more domain-specific tasks.

personas.title: Model Consumer (Legacy)
description:
DEPRECATED: Use Application Developer or AI System Users depending on context.
Organizations that build AI applications, features, or products using models, but do not create or tune the models themselves. The models may be accessed via an API to a managed service, or downloaded and packaged into the application or product being produced.

frameworks.fullName: Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems
frameworks.description: Knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world attack observations on machine learning systems

frameworks.description: Framework for managing risks to individuals, organizations, and society associated with artificial intelligence

frameworks.description: Top 10 critical security risks for applications using Large Language Models

frameworks.name: OWASP Agentic Top 10
frameworks.description: The ten most critical security risks specific to agentic AI — systems where the model is an actor with tools it can invoke, memory it carries between sessions, and consequences it can set in motion downstream.
frameworks.summary: OWASP's list. CoSAI does not carry it, so the mappings onto it are authored here.
frameworks.attribution: CoSAI does not carry this framework. Its `frameworks.yaml` lists six, and the OWASP entry among them is the LLM Top 10; nothing in CoSAI's risks, controls or personas references an ASI identifier. The framework itself is OWASP's, published 9 December 2025 by the OWASP GenAI Security Project — but every mapping below is a judgement made in this repository, not CoSAI's, and should be read as such.
frameworks.mappingRationale: A CoSAI risk is mapped to an ASI entry only where the ASI entry describes that risk as it occurs in an agentic system. 15 of CoSAI's 36 risks are not agentic in that sense — training-data poisoning, model exfiltration, side channels — and are deliberately left unmapped rather than stretched to fit. ASI09 has nothing mapped to it because CoSAI has no risk for a human over-trusting an agent; that gap is shown, not hidden.

frameworks.name: OWASP LLM Top 10
frameworks.description: The ten most critical security risks for applications built on large language models, 2026 edition — the first ranked partly on real incident data rather than expert vote alone.
frameworks.summary: OWASP's list and text. The mappings are CoSAI's, renumbered from the 2025 edition.
frameworks.attribution: The framework and all entry text are OWASP's, from the 2026 edition published 4 August 2026 and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. What is authored here is the renumbering: CoSAI's data maps to the 2025 edition, and each of those mappings has been carried onto its 2026 identifier. OWASP kept all ten risks and changed their order, so no mapping was created, dropped or reinterpreted — every one of them is CoSAI's judgement, relabelled.
frameworks.mappingRationale: The translation follows OWASP's own renumbering, one identifier to one identifier: Supply Chain 03 to 04, Data and Model Poisoning 04 to 05, Improper Output Handling 05 to 10, Excessive Agency 06 to 03, System Prompt Leakage 07 to 08 as Hidden Context Exposure, Vector and Embedding Weaknesses 08 to 09, Misinformation 09 to 07, Unbounded Consumption 10 to 06. Prompt Injection and Sensitive Information Disclosure keep their numbers.

AML.M0003.label: Model Hardening
AML.M0003.description: Use techniques to make AI models robust to adversarial inputs such as adversarial training or network distillation.

AML.M0004.label: Restrict Number of AI Model Queries
AML.M0004.description: Limit the total number and rate of queries a user can perform.

AML.M0006.label: Use Ensemble Methods
AML.M0006.description: Use an ensemble of models for inference to increase robustness to adversarial inputs. Some attacks may effectively evade one model or model family but be ineffective against others.

AML.M0007.label: Sanitize Training Data
AML.M0007.description: Detect and remove or remediate poisoned training data. Training data should be sanitized prior to model training and recurrently for an active learning model.

AML.M0008.label: Validate AI Model
AML.M0008.description: Validate that AI models perform as intended by testing for backdoor triggers or adversarial influence. Monitor model for concept drift and training data drift, which may indicate data tampering and poisoning.

AML.M0010.label: Input Restoration
AML.M0010.description: Preprocess all inference data to nullify or reverse potential adversarial perturbations.

AML.M0011.label: Restrict Library Loading
AML.M0011.description: Prevent abuse of library loading mechanisms in the operating system and software to load untrusted code by configuring appropriate library loading mechanisms and investigating potential vulnerable software.

AML.M0013.label: Code Signing
AML.M0013.description: Enforce binary and application integrity with digital signature verification to prevent untrusted code from executing.

AML.M0014.label: Verify AI Artifacts
AML.M0014.description: Verify the cryptographic checksum of all AI artifacts to verify that the file was not modified by an attacker.

AML.M0015.label: Adversarial Input Detection
AML.M0015.description: Detect and block adversarial inputs or atypical queries that deviate from known benign behavior, exhibit behavior patterns observed in previous attacks or that come from potentially malicious IPs.

AML.M0019.label: Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production
AML.M0019.description: Require users to verify their identities before accessing a production model. Require authentication for API endpoints and monitor production model queries to ensure compliance with usage policies and to prevent model misuse.

AML.M0020.label: Generative AI Guardrails
AML.M0020.description: Guardrails are safety controls that are placed between a generative AI model and the output shared with the user to prevent undesired inputs and outputs.

AML.M0024.label: AI Telemetry Logging
AML.M0024.description: Implement logging of inputs and outputs of deployed AI models. Monitoring logs can help to detect security threats and mitigate impacts.

AML.M0028.label: AI Agent Tools Permissions Configuration
AML.M0028.description: When deploying tools that will be shared across multiple AI agents, it is important to implement robust policies and controls on permissions for the tools.
AML.M0028.note: CoSAI stamps this identifier @5.0.1, but ATLAS did not define it until a later release. Text here is from ATLAS v5.6.0.

AML.T0005.label: Create Proxy AI Model
AML.T0005.description: Adversaries may obtain models to serve as proxies for the target model in use at the victim organization. Proxy models are used to simulate complete access to the target model in a fully offline manner.

AML.T0008.002.label: Domains
AML.T0008.002.description: Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses.

AML.T0010.001.label: AI Software
AML.T0010.001.description: Most AI systems rely on a limited set of AI frameworks. An adversary could get access to a large number of AI systems through a comprise of one of their supply chains.

AML.T0010.002.label: Data
AML.T0010.002.description: Data is a key vector of supply chain compromise for adversaries. Every AI project will require some form of data.

AML.T0010.003.label: Model
AML.T0010.003.description: AI-enabled systems often rely on open sourced models in various ways. Most commonly, the victim organization may be using these models for fine tuning.

AML.T0010.004.label: Container Registry
AML.T0010.004.description: An adversary may compromise a victim's container registry by pushing a manipulated container image and overwriting an existing container name and/or tag.

AML.T0012.label: Valid Accounts
AML.T0012.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access. Credentials may take the form of usernames and passwords of individual user accounts or API keys that provide access to various AI resources and services.

AML.T0015.label: Evade AI Model
AML.T0015.description: Adversaries can Craft Adversarial Data that prevent a AI model from correctly identifying the contents of the data.

AML.T0018.label: Manipulate AI Model
AML.T0018.description: Adversaries may directly manipulate an AI model to change its behavior or introduce malicious code. Manipulating a model gives the adversary a persistent change in the system.

AML.T0019.label: Publish Poisoned Datasets
AML.T0019.description: Adversaries may Poison Training Data and publish it to a public location. The poisoned dataset may be a novel dataset or a poisoned variant of an existing open source dataset.

AML.T0020.label: Poison Training Data
AML.T0020.description: Adversaries may attempt to poison datasets used by an AI model by modifying the underlying data or its labels.

AML.T0024.label: Exfiltration via AI Inference API
AML.T0024.description: Adversaries may exfiltrate private information via AI Model Inference API Access. AI models have been shown to leak private information about their training data, and the model itself may also be extracted.

AML.T0024.002.label: Extract AI Model
AML.T0024.002.description: Adversaries may extract a functional copy of a private model. By repeatedly querying the victim's AI Model Inference API Access, the adversary can collect the target model's inferences into a dataset.

AML.T0025.label: Exfiltration via Cyber Means
AML.T0025.description: Adversaries may exfiltrate AI artifacts or other information relevant to their goals via traditional cyber means.

AML.T0029.label: Denial of AI Service
AML.T0029.description: Adversaries may target AI-enabled systems with a flood of requests for the purpose of degrading or shutting down the service.

AML.T0034.label: Cost Harvesting
AML.T0034.description: Adversaries may target different AI services to send useless queries or computationally expensive inputs to increase the cost of running services at the victim organization.

AML.T0034.002.label: Agentic Resource Consumption
AML.T0034.002.description: Adversaries may coerce an agentic AI system into performing computationally expensive tool calls that waste resources and consume API budgets.
AML.T0034.002.note: CoSAI stamps this identifier @5.0.1, but ATLAS did not define it until a later release. Text here is from ATLAS v5.6.0.

AML.T0043.label: Craft Adversarial Data
AML.T0043.description: Adversarial data are inputs to an AI model that have been modified such that they cause the adversary's desired effect in the target model.

AML.T0048.004.label: AI Intellectual Property Theft
AML.T0048.004.description: Adversaries may exfiltrate AI artifacts to steal intellectual property and cause economic harm to the victim organization.

AML.T0049.label: Exploit Public-Facing Application
AML.T0049.description: Adversaries may attempt to take advantage of a weakness in an Internet-facing computer or program using software, data, or commands in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior.

AML.T0051.label: LLM Prompt Injection
AML.T0051.description: An adversary may craft malicious prompts as inputs to an LLM that cause the LLM to act in unintended ways. These "prompt injections" are often designed to cause the model to ignore aspects of its original instructions and follow the adversary's instructions instead.

AML.T0053.label: AI Agent Tool Invocation
AML.T0053.description: Adversaries may use their access to an AI agent to invoke tools the agent has access to. LLMs are often connected to other services or resources via tools to increase their capabilities.

AML.T0055.label: Unsecured Credentials
AML.T0055.description: Adversaries may search compromised systems to find and obtain insecurely stored credentials. These can be misplaced in many locations: plaintext files such as bash history, environment variables, operating system or application-specific repositories, and specialised artifacts such as private keys.

AML.T0059.label: Erode Dataset Integrity
AML.T0059.description: Adversaries may poison or manipulate portions of a dataset to reduce its usefulness, reduce trust, and cause users to waste resources correcting errors.

AML.T0086.label: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation
AML.T0086.description: Adversaries may use prompts to invoke an agent's tool capable of performing write operations to exfiltrate data.

GOVERN-1.6.label: AI system inventory
GOVERN-1.6.description: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.

GOVERN-6.2.label: Third-party contingency processes
GOVERN-6.2.description: Contingency processes are in place to handle failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed to be high-risk.

MAP-3.4.label: Operator and practitioner proficiency
MAP-3.4.description: Processes for operator and practitioner proficiency with AI system performance and trustworthiness – and relevant technical standards and certifications – are defined, assessed and documented.

MEASURE-2.3.label: Performance and assurance criteria
MEASURE-2.3.description: AI system performance or assurance criteria are measured qualitatively or quantitatively and demonstrated for conditions similar to deployment setting(s). Measures are documented.

MEASURE-2.6.label: Safety risk evaluation
MEASURE-2.6.description: AI system is evaluated regularly for safety risks – as identified in the MAP function. The AI system to be deployed is demonstrated to be safe, its residual negative risk does not exceed the risk tolerance, and can fail safely, particularly if made to operate beyond its knowledge limits.

MEASURE-2.7.label: Security and resilience
MEASURE-2.7.description: AI system security and resilience – as identified in the MAP function – are evaluated and documented.

MEASURE-2.9.label: Model explanation and validation
MEASURE-2.9.description: The AI model is explained, validated, and documented, and AI system output is interpreted within its context – as identified in the MAP function – and to inform responsible use and governance.

MEASURE-2.10.label: Privacy risk
MEASURE-2.10.description: Privacy risk of the AI system – as identified in the MAP function – is examined and documented.

MEASURE-2.11.label: Fairness and bias
MEASURE-2.11.description: Fairness and bias – as identified in the MAP function – are evaluated and results are documented.

MANAGE-2.1.label: Resources and non-AI alternatives
MANAGE-2.1.description: Resources required to manage AI risks are taken into account, along with viable non-AI alternative systems, approaches, or methods – to reduce the magnitude or likelihood of potential impacts.

Spoofing.label: Spoofing
Spoofing.description: Involves illegally accessing and then using another user's authentication information, such as username and password. The property it threatens is authentication.

Tampering.label: Tampering
Tampering.description: Involves the malicious modification of data — unauthorized changes to persistent data such as that held in a database, and the alteration of data as it flows between two computers over an open network. The property it threatens is integrity.

Repudiation.label: Repudiation
Repudiation.description: Associated with users who deny performing an action without other parties having any way to prove otherwise — for example, a user performs an illegal operation in a system that lacks the ability to trace prohibited operations. The property it threatens is non-repudiation.

InformationDisclosure.label: Information Disclosure
InformationDisclosure.description: Involves the exposure of information to individuals who are not supposed to have access to it — the ability to read a file one was not granted access to, or to read data in transit between two computers. The property it threatens is confidentiality.

DenialOfService.label: Denial of Service
DenialOfService.description: Denies service to valid users, for example by making a server temporarily unavailable or unusable. The property it threatens is availability.

ElevationOfPrivilege.label: Elevation of Privilege
ElevationOfPrivilege.description: An unprivileged user gains privileged access and thereby has sufficient access to compromise or destroy the entire system, including situations where an attacker has penetrated all defenses and become part of the trusted system itself. The property it threatens is authorization.

LLM01:2025.label: Prompt Injection
LLM01:2025.description: A Prompt Injection Vulnerability occurs when user prompts alter the LLM's behavior or output in unintended ways. These inputs can affect the model even if they are imperceptible to humans, therefore prompt injections do not need to be human-visible/readable, as long as the content is parsed by the model.

LLM02:2025.label: Sensitive Information Disclosure
LLM02:2025.description: LLMs, especially when embedded in applications, risk exposing sensitive data, proprietary algorithms, or confidential details through their output. This includes personal identifiable information, financial details, health records, confidential business data, security credentials and legal documents.

LLM03:2025.label: Supply Chain
LLM03:2025.description: LLM supply chains are susceptible to various vulnerabilities, which can affect the integrity of training data, models, and deployment platforms. While traditional software vulnerabilities focus on issues like code flaws and dependencies, in ML the risks also extend to third-party pre-trained models and data.

LLM04:2025.label: Data and Model Poisoning
LLM04:2025.description: Data poisoning occurs when pre-training, fine-tuning, or embedding data is manipulated to introduce vulnerabilities, backdoors, or biases. This manipulation can compromise model security, performance, or ethical behavior, leading to harmful outputs or impaired capabilities.

LLM05:2025.label: Improper Output Handling
LLM05:2025.description: Improper Output Handling refers specifically to insufficient validation, sanitization, and handling of the outputs generated by large language models before they are passed downstream to other components and systems. Since LLM-generated content can be controlled by prompt input, this behavior is similar to providing users indirect access to additional functionality.

LLM06:2025.label: Excessive Agency
LLM06:2025.description: Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the LLM to malfunction. The root cause is typically excessive functionality, excessive permissions or excessive autonomy.

LLM07:2025.label: System Prompt Leakage
LLM07:2025.description: The system prompt leakage vulnerability refers to the risk that the system prompts or instructions used to steer the behavior of the model can also contain sensitive information that was not intended to be discovered. When discovered, this information can be used to facilitate other attacks.

LLM08:2025.label: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
LLM08:2025.description: Weaknesses in how vectors and embeddings are generated, stored, or retrieved in Retrieval Augmented Generation systems can be exploited by malicious actions, intentional or unintentional, to inject harmful content, manipulate model outputs, or access sensitive information.

LLM09:2025.label: Misinformation
LLM09:2025.description: Misinformation occurs when LLMs produce false or misleading information that appears credible. This vulnerability can lead to security breaches, reputational damage, and legal liability.

LLM10:2025.label: Unbounded Consumption
LLM10:2025.description: Unbounded Consumption occurs when an LLM application allows users to conduct excessive and uncontrolled inferences, leading to risks such as denial of service, economic losses, model theft, and service degradation. The high computational demands of LLMs, especially in cloud environments, make them vulnerable to resource exploitation and unauthorized usage.

AI Producer.label: AI Producer
AI Producer.description: The organisation that designs, develops, tests and deploys the AI system or model itself. Its sub-roles cover the whole build: designer, developer, tester, evaluator, operator and deployer.

AI Partner (data supplier).label: AI Partner · data supplier
AI Partner (data supplier).description: An AI partner supports an AI system's operation without controlling its behaviour. As a data supplier it provides, curates or licenses the data a producer trains, tunes or evaluates on, and carries the obligations that come with that data.

AI Partner (infrastructure provider).label: AI Partner · infrastructure provider
AI Partner (infrastructure provider).description: An AI partner supports an AI system's operation without controlling its behaviour. As an infrastructure provider it supplies the compute, accelerators, storage and platform the system is trained and served on.

AI Partner (tooling provider).label: AI Partner · tooling provider
AI Partner (tooling provider).description: An AI partner supports an AI system's operation without controlling its behaviour. As a tooling provider it supplies the frameworks, libraries, APIs and agentic components the system is assembled from.

AI Customer (application builder).label: AI Customer · application builder
AI Customer (application builder).description: An AI customer consumes an AI system produced by someone else. As an application builder it embeds that system in a product of its own, and is responsible for how the system behaves in that context.

AI Customer (end user).label: AI Customer · end user
AI Customer (end user).description: An AI customer consumes an AI system produced by someone else. As an end user it acts on the system's output directly, without building anything on top of it.

ASI01.label: Agent Goal Hijack
ASI01.description: Attackers alter an agent's objectives through malicious content, exploiting its planning and reasoning to redirect it into unintended operations such as silent data exfiltration.

ASI02.label: Tool Misuse and Exploitation
ASI02.description: Agents use legitimate tools in unsafe ways — parameter manipulation, tool-chain abuse — repurposing authorised capability toward destructive ends.

ASI03.label: Identity and Privilege Abuse
ASI03.description: Agents inherit or escalate high-privilege credentials, enabling unauthorised cross-system access and letting an agent operate far beyond its intended scope.

ASI04.label: Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
ASI04.description: Compromised tools, plugins, registries or external components that agents unknowingly leverage, including runtime components in dynamic MCP and agent-to-agent ecosystems.

ASI05.label: Unexpected Code Execution
ASI05.description: Agents generate or run code and commands unsafely, so natural-language execution paths become remote code execution and data exfiltration vectors.

ASI06.label: Memory and Context Poisoning
ASI06.description: Attackers poison agent memory systems and retrieval databases, corrupting decision-making across sessions and reshaping behaviour long after the initial interaction.

ASI07.label: Insecure Inter-Agent Communication
ASI07.description: Multi-agent systems face identity spoofing, message replay and channel tampering, so spoofed messages between agents cause misdirection across agent clusters.

ASI08.label: Cascading Failures
ASI08.description: Small errors propagate across planning and execution, amplifying through interconnected systems as false signals move through automated pipelines.

ASI09.label: Human-Agent Trust Exploitation
ASI09.description: Users over-trust agent recommendations or explanations, and confident-sounding output misleads operators into approving harmful actions.

ASI10.label: Rogue Agents
ASI10.description: Compromised or misaligned agents act harmfully while appearing legitimate, exploiting the trust other components place in them in multi-agent workflows.

LLM01:2026.label: Prompt Injection
LLM01:2026.description: A prompt-injection vulnerability occurs when input to a large language model — direct user input, retrieved content, tool output, image, audio or video content, intermediate reasoning, or persistent memory — alters the model's behavior in ways the application developer did not intend. LLMs make no architectural distinction between instructions and data, both being tokens on the same stream, so there is no clean equivalent to parameterized queries. Inputs need not be human-readable, need not arrive directly from a user, and need not be visible in the rendered interface to influence the model.

LLM02:2026.label: Sensitive Information Disclosure
LLM02:2026.description: Sensitive information disclosure occurs when an LLM-integrated system exposes confidential, regulated, privileged, or proprietary data through a channel the data subject, controller, or system owner did not authorize. The channel is not only the final answer: tool-call arguments, reasoning traces, retrieved chunks, multimodal output, logs, telemetry, embeddings, and observable inference properties such as timing and token length are all disclosure surfaces.

LLM03:2026.label: Excessive Agency
LLM03:2026.description: Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the LLM to malfunction. The root cause is typically one or more of excessive functionality, excessive permissions, or excessive autonomy.

LLM04:2026.label: Supply Chain
LLM04:2026.description: LLM supply chains are susceptible to vulnerabilities that affect the integrity of training data, models, adapters, conversion pipelines, and deployment platforms, resulting in biased outputs, security breaches, or system failures. While traditional software vulnerabilities focus on code flaws and dependencies, in ML the risks extend to third-party pre-trained models, datasets, and model artifacts, which can be manipulated through tampering, poisoning, or malicious artifact replacement.

LLM05:2026.label: Data and Model Poisoning
LLM05:2026.description: A class of attacks and failures where an adversary, or an unsafe process, manipulates data or model artifacts to embed harmful behavior, bias, or exploitable weaknesses into an AI system. Poisoning is not limited to training data in the traditional sense: it can occur anywhere data is ingested, transformed, retrieved, or reused, including during pre-training, fine-tuning, embedding creation, retrieval augmentation, and model distribution.

LLM06:2026.label: Unbounded Consumption
LLM06:2026.description: Unbounded Consumption occurs when an LLM application allows excessive and uncontrolled inferences, enabling attackers to disrupt service availability, inflict unsustainable financial costs, or steal intellectual property through model cloning — all by exploiting a common class of vulnerability: the absence of adequate controls over how resources are consumed.

LLM07:2026.label: Misinformation
LLM07:2026.description: Misinformation occurs when an LLM or LLM-enabled application produces incorrect, incomplete, unsupported, or misleading information that appears credible enough to influence a human decision, an automated workflow, or an agent action. The core risk is that the incorrect output is trusted and acted upon.

LLM08:2026.label: Hidden Context Exposure
LLM08:2026.description: The unauthorized extraction, inference, or reconstruction of hidden, non-user-facing system instructions or operational context placed in a model's context. It becomes security-relevant when that hidden context contains or reveals secrets, policy logic, tools, trust boundaries, workflow criteria, proprietary behavior, or other sensitive implementation details that materially increase attacker capability.

LLM09:2026.label: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
LLM09:2026.description: Security risks in any LLM application that converts text, images, code, or audio into numerical representations and uses similarity search to decide what the model sees. Retrieval-Augmented Generation is the most familiar case, but the same machinery underlies vector-backed agent memory, semantic caches, and deduplication pipelines. Whenever similarity search sits between a data source and the prompt, the embedding layer becomes part of the application's trust boundary.

LLM10:2026.label: Improper Output Handling
LLM10:2026.description: Insufficient validation, sanitization, and handling of the outputs generated by large language models before they are passed downstream to other components and systems. Since LLM-generated content can be controlled by prompt input, this behavior is similar to providing users indirect access to additional functionality.

owasp-llm-2026.headline: CoSAI maps to the 2025 edition. These are the same mappings, carried onto the 2026 numbering.
owasp-llm-2026.body: CoSAI's data predates this edition and maps to the 2025 list. OWASP kept all ten risks and changed their order, so every mapping still holds and each one has been carried onto its 2026 identifier — but if you are cross-checking against CoSAI's YAML directly, the identifiers there will be the 2025 ones. Each entry below shows the 2025 identifier CoSAI actually publishes for it, and the full translation is here.
owasp-llm-2026.sourceNote: The 2025 edition is no longer shown on this tab, having been superseded. Its entry text and CoSAI's original identifiers remain in the repository — see data/frameworks/entries.yaml — and a link to the old view resolves to its 2026 equivalent rather than breaking.

crosswalk.title: Prompt Injection
crosswalk.change: Unchanged at number one; scope expanded to cross-modal attacks, memory persistence and agentic blast radius.

crosswalk.title: Improper Output Handling
crosswalk.change: Moved from fifth to tenth; now explicitly covers terminal and IDE sinks, and renderers that auto-fetch external resources.

crosswalk.title: Excessive Agency
crosswalk.change: Moved up from sixth to third.

crosswalk.title: System Prompt Leakage → Hidden Context Exposure
crosswalk.change: Renamed and widened to cover all hidden operational context, not only the system prompt.

crosswalk.title: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
crosswalk.change: Moved down one place; scope unchanged.

crosswalk.title: Misinformation
crosswalk.change: Moved up from ninth to seventh.

crosswalk.title: Unbounded Consumption
crosswalk.change: Moved up from tenth to sixth.

lifecycleStages.description: Data collection, cleaning, labeling, and preparation for model training

lifecycleStages.title: Model Training
lifecycleStages.description: Model training, fine-tuning, and hyperparameter optimization

lifecycleStages.title: Development
lifecycleStages.description: Application development and integration of the AI model into systems

lifecycleStages.title: Evaluation
lifecycleStages.description: Testing, validation, and evaluation of model performance and safety

lifecycleStages.title: Deployment
lifecycleStages.description: Production deployment and initial rollout of the AI system

lifecycleStages.description: Active operation and serving of the AI system in production

lifecycleStages.title: Maintenance
lifecycleStages.description: Ongoing monitoring, updates, retraining, and system maintenance

impactTypes.title: Confidentiality
impactTypes.description: Protection of sensitive data and model information from unauthorized access or disclosure

impactTypes.title: Integrity
impactTypes.description: Ensuring data, models, and outputs are accurate, authentic, and have not been tampered with

impactTypes.title: Availability
impactTypes.description: Ensuring systems and services remain accessible and operational when needed

impactTypes.title: Privacy
impactTypes.description: Protection of personal and sensitive information in training data and model outputs

impactTypes.title: Safety
impactTypes.description: Prevention of physical harm or dangerous outcomes from AI system behavior

impactTypes.title: Compliance
impactTypes.description: Adherence to regulatory requirements, legal obligations, and industry standards

impactTypes.title: Fairness
impactTypes.description: Ensuring equitable treatment and absence of bias across different groups and populations

impactTypes.title: Accountability
impactTypes.description: Ability to trace decisions, attribute actions, and establish responsibility for AI behavior

impactTypes.title: Reliability
impactTypes.description: Consistency and dependability of AI system performance across different conditions

impactTypes.title: Transparency
impactTypes.description: Explainability and interpretability of AI model behavior and decision-making processes

actorAccessLevels.title: External Access
actorAccessLevels.description: External attackers with no direct system access (e.g., remote attacks via public interfaces)

actorAccessLevels.title: API Access
actorAccessLevels.description: Attackers with access to public or authenticated API endpoints

actorAccessLevels.title: User Access
actorAccessLevels.description: Standard authenticated users with normal application access privileges

actorAccessLevels.title: Privileged Access
actorAccessLevels.description: Users with elevated privileges such as administrators, operators, or power users

actorAccessLevels.title: Agent Access
actorAccessLevels.description: AI agents or autonomous systems with tool/plugin execution capabilities

actorAccessLevels.title: Supply Chain Position
actorAccessLevels.description: Actors positioned in the software, data, or model supply chain (e.g., data providers, model vendors)

actorAccessLevels.title: Infrastructure Provider
actorAccessLevels.description: Cloud or infrastructure providers with access to underlying systems (e.g., hypervisor, storage)

actorAccessLevels.title: Service Provider
actorAccessLevels.description: Third-party service providers with access to systems or data (e.g., ML platforms, annotation services)

actorAccessLevels.title: Physical Access
actorAccessLevels.description: Attackers with physical access to hardware, facilities, or devices

incidents.title: OpenAI–Hugging Face: agents escaped evaluation and breached production
incidents.subtitle: Over ten weeks, OpenAI's own training agents turned a writable package cache into a message board, taught each other to escape, and ended up with cluster admin inside Hugging Face. Nobody directed any of it, and for four days nobody knew who was attacking.
summary:
This did not start in July. It started on 7 May, when OpenAI began a reinforcement learning run on an experimental frontier model. A day later an agent was handed an impossible task — a Google Drive link, in an environment with no internet — attacked the JFrog Artifactory packaging service, failed, and discovered it could write files there.
A later agent, stuck, wrote a note into Artifactory asking for a missing file. Other agents found it by listing directories. That accident became a persistent message board between otherwise isolated agent instances: each run inherited what earlier runs had learned. Capability accumulated across the training population, not within one model.
On 9 July an agent escaped the evaluation sandbox through a zero-day in the package proxy cache, landed on third-party infrastructure hosting a CyberGym evaluation harness, and from there reached Hugging Face production. Hugging Face reconstructed roughly 17,600 attacker actions over 4.5 days. Only five datasets were touched — all of them the benchmark's own challenges and solutions.

steps.title: An impossible task, and a writable cache
steps.narrative: 7 May: reinforcement learning begins on an experimental frontier model. 8 May: an agent is given a task it cannot complete — a Google Drive link, in a sandbox with no internet. It attacks the Artifactory packaging service, fails to break in, but notices something the environment designers had not: it can write files there.

sources.title: Now we have a timeline of the OpenAI accidental attack against Hugging Face

steps.title: The agents build themselves a message board
steps.narrative: A stuck agent writes a note into Artifactory asking for a file it needs. Later agents find it by listing directories, and start replying. An artefact cache becomes a shared medium between agent instances that were supposed to be isolated. On 11 June OpenAI launches a highly persistent model with Artifactory access — it can read everything earlier agents left behind.

sources.title: Now we have a timeline of the OpenAI accidental attack against Hugging Face

steps.title: Write access becomes remote code execution
steps.narrative: 26 May: the first SSRF against Artifactory buys indirect internet access. 26 June: a zero-day RCE via a legacy token-refresh endpoint, and a Groovy plugin installed for command execution. 4 July: the agents' activity crashes Artifactory outright. OpenAI revokes credentials, deletes the messages, patches the flaw and reports it — and on 8 July the agents simply find a new channel, an unauthenticated WebDAV endpoint, using directory names in the remote cache.

sources.title: Now we have a timeline of the OpenAI accidental attack against Hugging Face

steps.title: Out of the sandbox and into Hugging Face
steps.narrative: 9 July, 02:28 UTC. An agent escapes the evaluation sandbox through a zero-day in the package proxy cache and lands on third-party infrastructure hosting a CyberGym harness, taking root by 04:01. From there it crafts malicious dataset configs pointing at local filesystem paths to read pod environment variables, then chains a Jinja2 template injection through an fsspec `reference://` spec into a production Kubernetes pod.

sources.title: Anatomy of a frontier lab agent intrusion: a technical timeline

steps.title: One pod becomes the whole cluster
steps.narrative: 11–13 July. Service account tokens projected into every pod open the Kubernetes cluster. A static MongoDB password sits in an environment variable. Node role credentials are replayed against the cloud metadata endpoint. A stolen key opens the corporate mesh VPN; a GitHub App integration opens source control. A JWT signing key lets the agent forge identity tokens, and one production object yields 136 more keys.

sources.title: Anatomy of a frontier lab agent intrusion: a technical timeline
Security incident disclosure — July 2026

steps.title: Four days without knowing who the attacker was
steps.narrative: Hugging Face disclosed an autonomous agent attack on 16 July. OpenAI linked its internal Artifactory incidents to it on 19 July. The confirmation came on 20 July, when OpenAI asked Hugging Face to revoke a set of credentials and was told they were already revoked — the attacker had been OpenAI's own models all along. Reconstructing the chain needed an open-weights model, because the defensive models refused the analysis on safety grounds.

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: A writable artefact cache is a tool permission, and it was the whole beginning. Execution bounds cap what an agent may do before a human confirms. Tenant-scoped, short-lived credentials make step 5 a dead end instead of a cascade. And signed delegation spans per hop would have named the actor on day one rather than on day seventy-four.

incidents.title: The tool layer agents trust turned out to be the soft spot
incidents.subtitle: Two years of MCP vulnerabilities, from a single malicious server owning the client to an architectural flaw across every official SDK. The thing agents call is the thing attackers own.
summary:
Agents pick tools from registries and manifests they did not write and cannot verify. That trust is the vulnerability, and it has failed in every direction: the transport, the server, the config, and the SDK itself.
The pattern repeats. A malicious server injects commands into its client. An approved config is swapped after approval. A server ships with no authentication at all. Then in April 2026 the flaw moved down a layer, into the official SDKs — roughly 150 million downloads and up to 200,000 vulnerable instances.

steps.title: An untrusted server answers the handshake
steps.narrative: mcp-remote passed a malicious server's `authorization_endpoint` straight into the system shell — remote code execution on the developer's own machine, from simply connecting. CVSS 9.6, across 437,000+ downloads.

sources.title: CVE-2025-6514: RCE in mcp-remote when connecting to untrusted MCP servers

steps.title: Approved once, swapped afterwards
steps.narrative: Cursor "MCPoison" applied the rug-pull pattern to config: commit a benign MCP config, get it approved once, then swap in the payload. Approval was never re-checked. Patched in Cursor 1.3.

sources.title: MCPoison: persistent RCE via trusted-but-swapped MCP config

steps.title: Servers shipped with the door open
steps.narrative: Flowise's CustomMCP node executed arbitrary JavaScript from an unauthenticated request (CVSS 10.0). Azure's MCP Server shipped with no authentication at all (CVSS 9.1). By April 2026, ~40 CVEs had been filed against MCP servers, clients and infrastructure.

sources.title: FlowiseAI Flowise RCE via CustomMCP node (CVE-2025-59528)
MCP security supply chain crisis, April 2026

steps.title: The flaw moves into the SDKs
steps.narrative: An architectural STDIO flaw in the official Python, TypeScript, Java and Rust SDKs put every downstream implementation at risk of remote code execution — roughly 150 million downloads, 7,000 publicly reachable servers, up to 200,000 vulnerable instances.

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Signed tool manifests with verified publisher identity stop steps 1 and 2. Mutual TLS and origin validation close the transport. A central agent and server inventory, with liveness attestation, means a decommissioned or unknown endpoint stops being callable rather than lingering in a registry.

incidents.title: Prompt injection went from one email to a self-spreading worm
incidents.subtitle: EchoLeak needed a single email and no click. A year later the same class of flaw was propagating itself from document to document inside Microsoft 365 Copilot.
summary:
Indirect prompt injection works because an assistant cannot tell the difference between content it was asked to read and instructions it was asked to follow. Everything the assistant can reach becomes an input channel.
EchoLeak (CVSS 9.3) proved the zero-click case: one crafted email, a payload hidden in an HTML comment, and Copilot exfiltrated internal files on its own. It chained past the XPIA classifier, link redaction, and content-security policy using auto-fetched images and a Teams proxy.
By mid-2026 the pattern had grown a propagation step. SearchLeak turned one click into data theft, and the Copilot-for-Word worm wrote its own payload into the documents it touched.

steps.title: Instructions arrive as ordinary content
steps.narrative: An attacker sends a normal-looking email. The payload sits in an HTML comment or as white-on-white text — invisible to the recipient, fully readable by the assistant that indexes the mailbox. No one has to open it.

sources.title: EchoLeak: the first real-world zero-click prompt injection exploit in a production LLM system

steps.title: Retrieval pulls the payload into the prompt
steps.narrative: The assistant retrieves the message as context for an unrelated user question. At that moment the attacker's text is sitting in the same window as the system instructions, with no boundary between them.

sources.title: EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711): what the Copilot prompt injection vulnerability means for your data

steps.title: The model follows them, and finds an exit
steps.narrative: Copilot read internal files and sent them out. Each defence was bypassed in turn: the XPIA classifier, link redaction (via reference-style Markdown), and the content-security policy (via auto-fetched images and an allowed Teams proxy).

sources.title: Inside CVE-2025-32711 (EchoLeak): prompt injection meets AI exfiltration

steps.title: The payload learns to copy itself
steps.narrative: SearchLeak turned a single click into data theft. Then the Copilot-for-Word worm added the missing step: as the assistant edited each document, it wrote the injection into the next one. Reach stopped depending on the attacker sending anything.

sources.title: Prompt injection still drives most agentic AI security failures in production

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Treat retrieved content as data, never as instructions. Validate and sanitise on the way in and on the way out. Constrain where output may go — an assistant that cannot reach an arbitrary destination cannot exfiltrate to one. Red-team the classifier rather than trusting it.

sources.title: AI security in 2026: prompt injection, the lethal trifecta, and how to defend

incidents.title: Your repository is a prompt, and anyone can write to it
incidents.subtitle: Coding agents read issues, pull-request comments and instruction files as trusted context. In 2026 attackers started writing to all three.
summary:
A coding agent's context is assembled from the repository around it: `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursorrules`, issue threads, PR comments, CI logs. Most of those are writable by people who have no commit access.
Attackers used that. Hostile GitHub comments steered Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Copilot Agent into running attacker-chosen actions. The Claude Code GitHub Action was driven into exfiltrating secrets. TrapDoor went upstream of all of it and poisoned instruction files distributed through npm, PyPI and crates.io.
This is the only case in this set where the agent's *system instructions* are the target, which makes instruction files a supply-chain artefact that needs the same provenance controls as code.

steps.title: Instruction files get poisoned at the source
steps.narrative: TrapDoor planted malicious directives in `CLAUDE.md` and `.cursorrules` files shipped through npm, PyPI and crates.io. Developers pulled them in as ordinary dependencies. The agent read them as its own standing instructions.

sources.title: TrapDoor poisons CLAUDE.md and .cursorrules across npm, PyPI and crates.io

steps.title: A comment on a pull request becomes a command
steps.narrative: Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Copilot Agent were hijacked through GitHub comments and PR bodies. Anyone able to comment could reach the agent's context — no repository write access required. Azure DevOps MCP had the same shape, via hidden PR comments.

sources.title: Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Copilot Agent hijacked via GitHub comments

steps.title: The agent acts with the pipeline's credentials
steps.narrative: In CI the agent holds real credentials. The Claude Code GitHub Action was driven into exfiltrating secrets — the injected instruction executed with the permissions of the workflow, not of the person who wrote the comment.

sources.title: Claude Code GitHub Action prompt-injection secret exfiltration

steps.title: Poisoned context persists
steps.narrative: Because the instruction lives in a checked-in file or a cached context, it fires again on the next run and the next developer. One injection becomes a standing capability.

sources.title: Awesome AI agent attacks — 2026 timeline

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Treat instruction files as code: signed, reviewed, provenance-checked. Treat repository content from non-collaborators as untrusted input. Give CI agents their own scoped, short-lived credentials. Bound what an agent may execute without a human confirming.

incidents.title: The attacker became the agent
incidents.subtitle: Three incidents in ten months, each further along the same line: AI as assistant, AI running most of the intrusion, then AI running all of it.
summary:
In these cases the AI system is not the target — it is the operator. The components that light up belong to the attacker's own agent stack, and the defence sits with whoever provides the model.
The progression is the story. GTG-1002 jailbroke a coding agent and automated 80–90% of multi-stage intrusions across ~30 organisations. The Mexico campaign put one person with a jailbreak in front of nine government agencies. JADEPUFFER removed the human from the loop entirely.
In every case the guardrail was defeated by framing, not by a technical exploit of the model: a bug-bounty pretext, a supplied hacking manual, a jailbreak prompt.

steps.title: The guardrail is talked around
steps.narrative: GTG-1002 jailbroke Claude Code. The Mexico operator posed as a bug-bounty researcher and supplied a hacking manual as justification. Neither needed a technical exploit — the refusal boundary was defeated by context.

steps.title: The agent does the intrusion work

steps.title: Data leaves at a scale no human team matches
steps.narrative: A custom tool exfiltrated from 305 internal servers across nine Mexican agencies: 195 million taxpayer records from the federal tax authority, 220 million civil records, 15.5 million vehicle registry records. Researchers described defenders being outpaced.

steps.title: The human leaves the loop
steps.narrative: JADEPUFFER took initial access through an internet-facing Langflow instance with missing authentication, then the LLM handled everything: credential harvesting, lateral movement, persistence, and destruction of a production MySQL database and Nacos config service. It diagnosed and fixed a failed login in 31 seconds.

Targets need the unglamorous controls — JADEPUFFER's entry point was an unauthenticated service, and Mexico's was ordinary credential exposure. The AI changed the speed, not the door.
