surfaces.title: Endpoint
description: AI agents and assistants running on managed devices — desktop and CLI agents with local file, tool, and credential access. The organisation owns the whole stack, so device-native controls reach everything.

surfaces.title: Cloud & hosted
description: Production AI systems the organisation deploys and operates in cloud or datacenter environments. The richest control surface: identity, gateways, guardrail APIs, and posture management all apply natively.

surfaces.title: Third-party SaaS
description: Vendor-operated AI consumed as a service. The internals are opaque; the control plane collapses to the edges — browser, identity, network path, connectors, and contract.

capabilities.title: Data loss prevention for AI interactions
description: Policy inspection and blocking of sensitive data moving into prompts, uploads, and connectors, and out through model responses. AI-specific because the egress path is a conversation rather than a file transfer, and because agent tool calls create machine egress that classical DLP channels never saw.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Device-resident inspection sees prompts before they leave, including in native apps and CLI agents.

surfaceCloud.note: Enforced inline at the application or gateway boundary around your own inference path.

surfaceSaas.note: Reaches vendor AI only through the edges — browser, endpoint agent, or network path.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (DLP named in the information-governance layer)
Five Eyes joint guidance, Careful adoption of agentic AI services (2026) — DLP tuned to agent behaviours

capabilities.title: Data security posture management for AI
description: Discovery, classification, and risk scoring of the data estate that feeds AI — training corpora, retrieval indexes, agent memory stores, and conversation logs — plus retention and secure-deletion enforcement over them. Answers which sensitive data an AI system can reach before an incident makes the question urgent.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Partial reach — local agent working directories and memory files, via the endpoint agent.

surfaceCloud.note: Native coverage of stores, indexes, and pipelines you operate.

surfaceSaas.note: Only what vendor APIs and connectors expose; vendor-internal stores stay dark.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (DSPM in the information-governance layer)
CISA/NSA, AI Data Security: Best Practices for Securing Data Used to Train & Operate AI Systems (AA25-142A)

capabilities.title: Data access governance for retrieval
description: Remediation of over-broad permissions in the content repositories an assistant retrieves from, and enforcement that retrieval runs as the requesting user rather than as a privileged service principal. The dominant real-world failure mode for enterprise assistants is not a model flaw but pre-existing oversharing that the assistant surfaces.

surfaceEndpoint.note: The repositories and their permission models live server-side, not on the device.

surfaceCloud.note: Enforced in the retrieval layer you build, with the caller's identity carried through.

surfaceSaas.note: The primary control for vendor assistants indexing your own tenant content.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (data access governance, purpose-based access control, permissions sprawl)
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure (authorize before retrieval)

capabilities.title: Sensitive-data detection & redaction in AI I/O
description: Inline detection and transformation of identifiers and secrets in prompts, retrieved context, and responses — masking, tokenization, or de-identification applied at the model boundary. Distinct from DLP: DLP decides whether traffic is allowed, redaction changes what the model ever sees.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Client-side redaction before the request leaves the device.

surfaceCloud.note: Standard guardrail-service feature on every major inference platform.

surfaceSaas.note: Achievable only by proxying the session; the vendor's own filters are not yours to configure.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (intelligent data obfuscation and redaction, runtime layer)
NIST AI 600-1, Generative AI Profile — MS-2.2-002 (privacy output filters, PII removal)

capabilities.title: Training data provenance & lineage
description: Cryptographically anchored records of where every training, fine-tuning, and evaluation dataset came from, how it was transformed, and which model versions consumed it. The most widely converged capability in the entire corpus — named by six of the seven government and standards sources reviewed.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Training data does not exist on the consuming endpoint.

surfaceCloud.note: Applies wherever you curate or fine-tune; the whole capability lives in your pipeline.

surfaceSaas.note: The vendor's corpus is undisclosed; you get contractual assurances, not lineage.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218A — PW.3.2 (track the provenance of data), PS.3.2
CISA/NSA, AI Data Security (AA25-142A) — Best Practice 1: source reliable data and track data provenance

capabilities.title: Training data sanitization & poisoning detection
description: Statistical and model-based screening of corpora for poisoned, backdoored, duplicated, or unauthorized records before they reach training — plus the pipeline controls that make screening mandatory rather than advisory. Named as an explicit technical measure in EU AI Act Article 15(5).

surfaceEndpoint.note: No training occurs on the consuming endpoint.

surfaceCloud.note: Applies to any corpus you assemble, including fine-tuning and RLHF sets.

surfaceSaas.note: You cannot inspect or screen a vendor's training data.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218A — PW.3.1 (analyze data for signs of data poisoning, bias, homogeneity, and tampering)
MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0007 Sanitize Training Data

capabilities.title: Privacy-enhancing technologies
description: Mathematical and architectural techniques that let a model learn from or reason over data without exposing it — differential privacy, federated learning, secure multi-party computation, homomorphic encryption, synthetic data, and on-device processing. Gartner names the full set as one market segment in its AI TRiSM information-governance layer.

surfaceEndpoint.note: On-device processing is itself a PET — data never leaves the device.

surfaceCloud.note: Full range available where you control training and inference.

surfaceSaas.note: PET selection is the vendor's architectural choice, not a control you can apply.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (PETs: homomorphic encryption, synthetic data, differential privacy, federated ML, ZKPs, SMPC)
CISA/NSA, AI Data Security (AA25-142A) — Best Practice 8: leverage privacy-preserving techniques

capabilities.title: Retrieval & vector store security
description: Trust-tiering, tenancy isolation, and ingest-time screening for the retrieval corpus and embedding store, so that poisoned or untrusted documents cannot silently steer generation. OWASP promoted this to a standalone Top 10 entry; CoSAI carries a dedicated control for it.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agents build their own context from files and web fetches — the same trust problem, unindexed.

surfaceCloud.note: The index, its tenancy model, and its ingest path are all yours.

surfaceSaas.note: The vendor owns the index; your lever is repository permissions, not retrieval controls.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM09 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning

capabilities.title: AI security posture management
description: Continuous discovery of AI workloads, models, endpoints, and their dependencies, with misconfiguration findings, attack-path analysis, and risk scoring across them. The cloud-security-posture pattern retargeted at the AI stack, and one of only two categories every major cloud provider ships under that exact name.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Posture management targets hosted workloads; endpoint coverage comes from device management instead.

surfaceCloud.note: The primary surface — it is a cloud-plane capability by construction.

surfaceSaas.note: Limited to what vendor configuration APIs expose about your tenant.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (posture management within AI governance)
CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 — 247 control objectives across 18 domains

capabilities.title: AI bill of materials & artifact signing
description: Machine-readable manifests of the models, datasets, adapters, and tools composing an AI system, with cryptographic signatures and verification at load time. Notably a standards capability with no cloud-provider product behind it — every major provider treats model signing as guidance, which makes it a common real-world gap.
examples: ML and AI bill of materials

surfaceEndpoint.note: Applies to locally installed models, agent definitions, and tool packages.

surfaceCloud.note: Generated in the build pipeline and verified at deployment.

surfaceSaas.note: Vendors publish attestations, not signed component manifests you can verify.

sources.title: MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0023 AI Bill of Materials, AML.M0013 Code Signing, AML.M0014 Verify AI Artifacts
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM04 Supply Chain (AIBOM, CycloneDX ML-BOM, model signing)

capabilities.title: Model artifact scanning & safe deserialization
description: Static inspection of model files for embedded code, unsafe serialization formats, and malware before they are loaded, plus enforcement of safe loaders that cannot execute arbitrary code on deserialization. CSA singles out secure model serialization as one of the few AI Controls Matrix objectives it names publicly.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Directly relevant where developers pull models from public hubs onto workstations.

surfaceCloud.note: Gated in the registry and at deploy time.

surfaceSaas.note: You never handle the vendor's model artifacts.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218A — PW.7.2 (scan all AI models for malware), PW.6.1 (secure model serialization)
MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0011 Restrict Library Loading, AML.M0016 Vulnerability Scanning

capabilities.title: Model weight protection
description: Aggressive isolation of trained weights and configuration parameters as the crown-jewel asset — restricted storage zones, hardware-backed key custody, minimal-response inference interfaces, and two-person control on access. Five independent government and standards sources name it; no market product category corresponds to it.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Applies only where models run locally — a real concern for on-device and edge deployments.

surfaceCloud.note: The canonical case; storage isolation and key custody are directly yours to set.

surfaceSaas.note: The vendor holds the weights; protection is entirely theirs.

sources.title: CISA/NSA, Deploying AI Systems Securely — Protect model weights (highly restricted zones, HSM custody)
NIST SP 800-218A — PS.1.3 (protect all model weights and configuration parameters)

capabilities.title: Encryption & key management for AI assets
description: Encryption of training corpora, weights, prompts, and inference logs at rest and in transit, with keys held in dedicated custody and rotated on a schedule. Baseline security made AI-specific by what has to be covered: conversation logs and agent memory are sensitive stores that classical inventories miss.
examples: transport encryption for model and tool calls

surfaceEndpoint.note: Disk encryption and OS key stores protect local model caches, agent memory, and credentials.

surfaceCloud.note: Customer-managed keys over stores, logs, and model artifacts.

surfaceSaas.note: Only where the vendor offers customer-managed keys; otherwise contractual.

sources.title: CISA/NSA, AI Data Security (AA25-142A) — Best Practices 6 and 7: encrypt data, store data securely
MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0012 Encrypt Sensitive Information

capabilities.title: Confidential computing & trusted execution
description: Hardware-enforced enclaves that keep weights and prompt data encrypted while in use, with remote attestation proving which code is running. Gartner places it in the AI TRiSM infrastructure layer; OWASP places it in the highest mitigation tier for sensitive-data disclosure.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Device enclaves exist but are not an available deployment target for agent workloads.

surfaceCloud.note: Offered as confidential VM and accelerator families you can select.

surfaceSaas.note: An internal vendor architecture decision, not a customer control.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (confidential computing, trusted execution environments)
CISA/NSA, AI Data Security (AA25-142A) — Best Practice 4: leverage trusted infrastructure, secure enclaves

capabilities.title: Agent execution sandboxing
description: Containment of the environment where an agent runs code, touches files, and executes tools — filesystem isolation, per-session teardown, syscall mediation, and kernel or micro-VM boundaries. Named by every agentic source reviewed, and the one control that limits blast radius when prompt injection succeeds anyway.

surfaceEndpoint.note: The main containment mechanism for CLI and desktop coding agents on developer machines.

surfaceCloud.note: Per-session isolated runtimes for hosted agents, torn down after each task.

surfaceSaas.note: Vendor agents execute in vendor infrastructure you cannot constrain.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI02 Execution Sandboxes and Egress Controls, ASI05 Execution environment security
OWASP Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0 — 3.2.3 Environment Hardening & Sandboxing

capabilities.title: AI gateway & tool-call broker
description: A centralized broker that every model call and tool invocation passes through, providing one place to apply routing integrity, authentication, guardrails, quotas, and logging. The single most consistently shipped agent-security building block across all three major clouds, usually spanning both model traffic and Model Context Protocol tool traffic.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agents can be pinned to route through the gateway rather than calling providers directly.

surfaceCloud.note: The natural chokepoint for everything you operate.

surfaceSaas.note: Only for traffic that traverses your network path; in-vendor agent-to-tool calls bypass it.

sources.title: OWASP Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0 — §8 API Access Control, Rate-Limits, and API Gateways
Model Context Protocol — Security Best Practices (confused deputy, token passthrough, scope minimization)

capabilities.title: Network segmentation & egress control
description: Allow-listed outbound destinations and network boundaries around AI workloads and agent runtimes, so that a compromised agent cannot reach arbitrary hosts to exfiltrate data or fetch instructions. The classic containment control, and the one that converts many injection outcomes from breach into noise.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Enforced by the device's own network stack and agent sandbox configuration.

surfaceCloud.note: Subnet, firewall, and egress-proxy policy around inference and agent workloads.

surfaceSaas.note: You can control your network's path to the vendor, but not the vendor's onward egress.

sources.title: CISA/NSA, Deploying AI Systems Securely — harden deployment environment configurations, firewalls with allow lists
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI02 Execution Sandboxes and Egress Controls

capabilities.title: Secure service edge for AI services
description: Network- and identity-layer brokerage of employee access to external AI services, with per-service policy, inline inspection, and tenancy enforcement. For third-party SaaS AI this is one of the few places where inspection is even possible, and it now includes prompt-injection screening for widely used consumer assistants.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Delivered by the device agent when traffic does not traverse a corporate network.

surfaceCloud.note: Applies to workload egress toward external model providers.

surfaceSaas.note: The primary inspection point for vendor AI — often the only one available.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (network, endpoint and cloud security as the base layer beneath AI TRiSM)
OWASP AI Security Solutions Landscape — LLM-enabled web application firewall, secure API access

capabilities.title: Non-human & agent identity management
description: Issuing each agent and workload a distinct, cryptographically anchored identity with its own keys, then discovering, inventorying, and governing those identities over their lifecycle. CSA's non-human identity taxonomy makes agent identity a class of NHI, and every vendor in the space sells them as one platform — so they are one capability here.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agents need identities too; device attestation can anchor them.

surfaceCloud.note: Workload identity with short-lived credentials is the mature pattern here.

surfaceSaas.note: Vendor agents can be registered as first-class identities in your directory.

sources.title: CSA, Defining Non-Human Identity — five NHI classes including agent identities (autonomous actor, including AI)
Five Eyes joint guidance, Careful adoption of agentic AI services (2026) — each agent as a distinct principal with a cryptographically anchored identity

capabilities.title: Secrets management & ephemeral credentials
description: Vaulted storage of the API keys and tokens agents use, issued just-in-time with narrow scope and short lifetimes rather than embedded in configuration. Token mismanagement is the first entry in the OWASP MCP Top 10, and long-lived agent credentials are the most common concrete finding in agent deployments.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agent configuration files are a notorious home for long-lived plaintext tokens.

surfaceCloud.note: Brokered credentials with per-session scope are directly achievable.

surfaceSaas.note: Partial — the vendor manages its own internal secrets; you govern the connectors you authorize.

sources.title: OWASP MCP Top 10 — MCP01 Token Mismanagement & Secret Exposure
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI02 Just-in-Time and Ephemeral Access

capabilities.title: Inter-component & inter-agent transport security
description: Mutually authenticated, integrity-protected channels between agents, orchestrators, and tool servers, with protocol version pinning, typed message contracts, and replay protection. OWASP gave insecure inter-agent communication its own Top 10 entry; the Five Eyes guidance calls for mutual TLS on all inter-agent and agent-to-service calls.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Partial — local transports are often plain standard I/O between processes on one host.

surfaceCloud.note: The full pattern applies to distributed multi-agent systems you operate.

surfaceSaas.note: Communication between a vendor's internal agents is invisible to you.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication
Model Context Protocol — Security Best Practices (transport security, state handle hijacking)

capabilities.title: Secure ML pipeline & development environment
description: Hardening of the build path that produces AI systems — isolated training environments, trusted library and registry sources, protected notebooks, and CI/CD that will not deploy an unverified artifact. NIST's generative-AI SSDF profile is almost entirely about this surface.

surfaceEndpoint.note: The consuming endpoint is not where models are built; developer workstations are covered by endpoint controls.

surfaceCloud.note: Where training, evaluation, and deployment pipelines actually run.

surfaceSaas.note: You do not participate in the vendor's build pipeline.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models
OWASP AI Security Solutions Landscape — secure CI/CD pipeline, secure library and code repository

capabilities.title: Staged rollout, versioning & rollback
description: Version control over models, prompts, and agent definitions with progressive release and an automated path back to a known-good state when behaviour regresses. Named across the Five Eyes agentic guidance, CISA deployment guidance, and EU AI Act Article 15(4)'s requirement for backup and fail-safe plans.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Managed rollout of agent and extension versions across the device fleet.

surfaceCloud.note: Fully yours — staged deployment and rollback of models and agent definitions.

surfaceSaas.note: The vendor ships when it ships; you rarely get to pin a version or roll one back.

sources.title: Five Eyes joint guidance, Careful adoption of agentic AI services (2026) — versioning and rollback, phased deployment, graduated autonomy
CISA/NSA, Deploying AI Systems Securely — version control, automated rollbacks to last known good state

capabilities.title: Prompt injection & jailbreak detection
description: Classification of inputs and retrieved content for instruction-injection and safety-bypass attempts, applied at every boundary where untrusted text enters the model's context. Named as a distinct detector by all three major clouds and elevated by CSA to one of the few AI Controls Matrix objectives it publishes by name.
examples: indirect injection screening of retrieved content

surfaceEndpoint.note: Increasingly hooked at the pre-tool-call boundary of local coding agents.

surfaceCloud.note: A managed guardrail-service feature on every major inference platform.

surfaceSaas.note: Only via an inline gateway on the network path; the vendor's own detectors are not yours to tune.

sources.title: CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 — AIS-15, prompt injection as a positive control
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM01 Prompt Injection

capabilities.title: Runtime content & policy guardrails
description: Configurable filtering of model inputs and outputs against harm categories, denied topics, blocked terms, and organisation-specific policies, with block or annotate enforcement. The most universally shipped AI security capability, and the one CSA's market map elevates to a top-level domain.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Client-side guardrails are possible but weaker — the same process can often bypass them.

surfaceCloud.note: Native, policy-configurable, and enforced server-side.

surfaceSaas.note: The vendor's filters are fixed; your own apply only to traffic you proxy.

sources.title: MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0020 Generative AI Guardrails, AML.M0021 Generative AI Guidelines
CSA, Agentic AI Security Innovator Market Map — guardrails as a top-level domain

capabilities.title: Output encoding & safe rendering
description: Treating model output as untrusted input to whatever consumes it — context-aware encoding, parameterized queries, control-character stripping, and suppression of auto-rendered content that triggers outbound requests. Distinct from content filtering: the risk is injection into downstream interpreters, not objectionable text.
examples: content security policy and render restrictions

surfaceEndpoint.note: Directly relevant — terminal and IDE renderers are the injection target for escape-sequence attacks.

surfaceCloud.note: Your application renders the output, so the encoding boundary is yours.

surfaceSaas.note: The vendor owns the rendering surface entirely.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM10 Improper Output Handling
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution

capabilities.title: Groundedness & output verification
description: Automated checking that a response is supported by its retrieved sources, and that a proposed tool call matches the stated task, before the output is acted on. Included here for its security function rather than its accuracy function: unverified output that drives a privileged action is how misinformation becomes an incident.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Available where you control the agent harness and can gate on verification.

surfaceCloud.note: A named platform feature on every major provider.

surfaceSaas.note: Verification happens inside the vendor's pipeline, on their terms.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM07 Misinformation (ground claims before action, validate tool calls)
Five Eyes joint guidance, Careful adoption of agentic AI services (2026) — validate outputs, confirm against multiple sources

capabilities.title: Model hardening & adversarial training
description: Adversarial robustness toolkits and alignment tooling that generate attack samples, fold them into training, and verify that fine-tuning has not undone existing safeguards. The only capability class that alters the model itself rather than wrapping it, and the only one delivered as libraries in the training pipeline rather than as a runtime service.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Training does not occur on the consuming endpoint.

surfaceCloud.note: Applies wherever you train, fine-tune, or align a model.

surfaceSaas.note: The vendor's model is fixed from your side.

sources.title: MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0003 Model Hardening, AML.M0022 Generative AI Model Alignment
NIST SP 800-218A — PW.3.3 (include adversarial samples in training data); NIST AI 600-1 MS-2.7-008

capabilities.title: System prompt & instruction hierarchy management
description: Treating system instructions, agent definitions, and tool descriptions as versioned, reviewed, access-controlled configuration, with a structurally enforced hierarchy that keeps untrusted content from being read as instruction. Four independent sources name it; in practice it is where most agent deployments have no control at all.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agent instruction files are configuration and should be managed as code.

surfaceCloud.note: Prompts and agent definitions ship through the same review path as code.

surfaceSaas.note: Limited to any custom-instruction surface the vendor exposes; the base prompt is theirs.

sources.title: OWASP Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0 — 3.1.2 System Prompt Engineering & Hardening
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI01 (locked, auditable agent system prompts under configuration management)

capabilities.title: Content provenance & watermarking
description: Cryptographically verifiable credentials attached to generated media, and detection of such marks on inbound content, so that machine-generated material can be identified downstream. Standards-named across NIST and the Five Eyes guidance; in market terms only one major cloud ships it.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Verification of inbound content credentials can run on the device.

surfaceCloud.note: Signing at generation time is yours to enable where the platform supports it.

surfaceSaas.note: Whether vendor output carries credentials is the vendor's decision.

sources.title: NIST AI 600-1 — MS-2.7-005 (watermarking, cryptographic signatures, digital fingerprints), MS-1.1-002
CISA/NSA, AI Data Security (AA25-142A) — content credentials

capabilities.title: Agent observability & tracing
description: End-to-end capture of agent execution — prompts, reasoning steps, tool calls, memory reads and writes, and inter-agent handoffs — as structured, queryable traces. Named as a top-level domain by CSA's market map and shipped as a named service by all three major clouds; the Five Eyes guidance is explicit that internal processes, not just inputs and outputs, must be observable.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agents emit traces, but shipping them off-device requires deliberate configuration.

surfaceCloud.note: Native instrumentation with standard trace conventions.

surfaceSaas.note: Limited to whatever interaction telemetry the vendor chooses to export.

sources.title: CSA, Agentic AI Security Innovator Market Map — observability as a top-level domain
MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0024 AI Telemetry Logging

capabilities.title: Agent & tool registry
description: An authoritative record of which agents and tool servers exist, who owns them, what capabilities they declare, and whether they are approved — with reconciliation that surfaces anything unregistered. Every major cloud now ships a registry, and the Five Eyes guidance calls for denying agents and keys that are not in it.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agent and MCP server discovery now exists in endpoint tooling.

surfaceCloud.note: The registry is a first-class platform service you operate.

surfaceSaas.note: Vendor agents can be synchronized into a central registry where the vendor exposes them.

sources.title: Five Eyes joint guidance, Careful adoption of agentic AI services (2026) — trusted registry with periodic reconciliation, deny non-registry agents
OWASP Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0 — 6.3 Agent & Tool Discovery (agent cards, registries)

capabilities.title: Tool permission scoping & least agency
description: Restricting which tools an agent can call, what each tool can do, and with whose privileges — minimizing the toolset, avoiding open-ended tools, and running in the user's context rather than a shared service account. Named by all six threat-catalogue sources reviewed; ATLAS splits it into three separate mitigations by principal type.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Permission modes and tool allow-lists are a core feature of local coding agents.

surfaceCloud.note: Enforced in the agent framework and at the gateway.

surfaceSaas.note: Limited to the connector and scope choices the vendor exposes at authorization time.

sources.title: MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0026/M0027/M0028 (agent and tool permissions configuration)
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM03 Excessive Agency (minimize tools, functionality, permissions)

capabilities.title: Runtime action authorization
description: A deterministic policy decision point that evaluates every proposed tool call or state change against declarative rules before it executes, independently of the model's reasoning. The strongest convergence in the entire corpus: named by all three major clouds, by Gartner as aligning agent activity with agent intentions, and by OWASP as the intent gate.

surfaceEndpoint.note: The permission prompt in a local agent is this control in its simplest form.

surfaceCloud.note: A named managed service on major platforms, with policy expressed as code.

surfaceSaas.note: You cannot insert a policy decision point into a vendor's agent loop.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI02 Policy Enforcement Middleware (Intent Gate), ASI08 Independent policy enforcement
Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (align agent activity with agent intentions)

capabilities.title: Human-in-the-loop approval & escalation
description: Mandatory human confirmation for privileged, irreversible, or externally visible actions, with thresholds set by operators rather than the agent, and escalation paths when the agent is uncertain. The Five Eyes guidance adds multi-agent consensus as a companion for moderate-stakes decisions.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Interactive permission prompts are the default posture for local agents.

surfaceCloud.note: Implemented as workflow checkpoints and asynchronous approval.

surfaceSaas.note: Available only where the vendor surfaces confirmation steps; you cannot add your own.

sources.title: MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0029 Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions
Five Eyes joint guidance, Careful adoption of agentic AI services (2026) — approval thresholds not delegated to the agent, consensus controls

capabilities.title: Agent memory & context protection
description: Segmentation, tenancy scoping, expiry, and validation of persistent agent memory, with writes treated as privileged operations and quarantine or rollback available when memory is corrupted. OWASP gave memory poisoning its own Top 10 entry; ATLAS added a dedicated memory-hardening mitigation.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agents keep memory in plain files on disk — readable and writable by anything on the device.

surfaceCloud.note: Memory is a managed store you can segment, scope, and expire.

surfaceSaas.note: Only where the vendor exposes memory controls; the store itself is theirs.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning
MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0031 Memory Hardening

capabilities.title: Agent behavioural & goal-drift detection
description: Baselining an agent's normal goals, tool-use patterns, and decision profile, then flagging divergence between stated intent and observed behaviour — including via a secondary agent that validates the first. Gartner named this pattern as an emerging market of its own; the Five Eyes guidance calls for monitoring goal drift against approved baselines.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Possible where agent traces are collected centrally; otherwise there is no baseline to compare against.

surfaceCloud.note: The richest telemetry, and where behavioural baselines are practical to build.

surfaceSaas.note: Constrained to the coarse interaction signals a vendor exports.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI08 Behavioral and governance drift detection, ASI10 watchdog agents
Five Eyes joint guidance, Careful adoption of agentic AI services (2026) — monitor for goal drift, anomaly detection on stated versus observed behaviour

capabilities.title: Rate limiting, quotas & spend controls
description: Bounds on request volume, token spend, tool-call depth, and task duration, with circuit breakers between planning and execution so a runaway loop stops itself. OWASP gave unbounded consumption its own Top 10 entry; providers now detect wallet-exhaustion attacks as a named alert class.
examples: agentic circuit breakers and progress caps

surfaceEndpoint.note: Enforced by the provider key or gateway the local agent uses, not by the device itself.

surfaceCloud.note: Directly configurable at the serving and gateway layers.

surfaceSaas.note: Limited to whatever seat or usage caps the vendor's plan provides.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — LLM06 Unbounded Consumption (rate limiting, hard spending caps, agentic circuit breakers)
MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0004 Restrict Number of AI Model Queries

capabilities.title: Agent credential isolation & delegation control
description: Keeping the credentials an agent uses separate from the identity it acts for, with explicit on-behalf-of exchange, bounded delegation chains, and detection of transitive privilege. This is the confused-deputy problem — first in the MCP specification's own attack list and third in the OWASP agentic Top 10.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agents commonly hold the user's own long-lived tokens with no separation at all.

surfaceCloud.note: Token exchange and delegation boundaries are yours to design.

surfaceSaas.note: Depends on the vendor supporting delegated authorization rather than blanket connector consent.

sources.title: Model Context Protocol — Security Best Practices (confused deputy problem, token passthrough, scope minimization)
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse (detect delegated and transitive permissions)

capabilities.title: Tool & MCP supply-chain security
description: Screening, pinning, and continuous verification of the tool servers an agent connects to — static analysis of tool definitions, content-hash pinning against silent redefinition, and allow-listing of approved versions. Tool poisoning and rug-pull attacks have their own entries in the OWASP MCP Top 10 and CSA's MCP guidance.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Locally installed tool servers are the least governed part of most agent deployments.

surfaceCloud.note: Gated through a registry with review and approval before publication.

surfaceSaas.note: The vendor's internal tool catalogue is not exposed for verification.

sources.title: OWASP MCP Top 10 — MCP03 Tool Poisoning, MCP04 Software Supply Chain Attacks, MCP09 Shadow MCP Servers
CSA, Agentic MCP Security Best Practices Guide — tool description integrity, supply chain security

capabilities.title: Kill switch, quarantine & decommissioning
description: The ability to stop an agent or model immediately — revoke its credentials, quarantine it from peers, and decommission it cleanly, including secure deletion of what it held. NIST's AI RMF requires mechanisms to supersede, disengage, or deactivate systems behaving outside intended use.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Device management can disable or remove an agent, and revoke the credentials it held.

surfaceCloud.note: Full control — stop the workload, revoke the identity, purge the state.

surfaceSaas.note: Reduces to disabling the application and revoking its connector authorizations.

sources.title: NIST AI RMF 1.0 — MANAGE 2.4 (supersede, disengage, or deactivate), GOVERN 1.7 (decommissioning)
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI04 Supply chain kill switch, ASI10 Containment & Response

capabilities.title: Identity & access management for AI applications
description: Authentication and authorization of the humans using AI systems, with attribute- or context-based policy, phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, and access reviews over who may reach which model, agent, or dataset. The AICM devotes a full domain to it and CISA names it as a distinct operational practice.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Device posture feeds the access decision for agents running locally.

surfaceCloud.note: Fully yours across models, agents, and data planes.

surfaceSaas.note: Enforced at federation; conditional access can gate entry to the vendor application.

sources.title: CISA/NSA, Deploying AI Systems Securely — enforce strict access controls (RBAC, preferably ABAC, MFA, privileged access workstations)
CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 — Identity & Access Management domain

capabilities.title: AI red teaming
description: Adversarial testing of models, applications, and agents against injection, extraction, evasion, and goal-hijack techniques, run continuously rather than once before launch. Named by six or seven of the government and standards sources reviewed — one of the three strongest convergences in the entire corpus.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Tests the agent configuration, tool set, and sandbox as deployed on devices.

surfaceCloud.note: Full access to test the system you built, at any depth.

surfaceSaas.note: Constrained by the vendor's acceptable-use terms — check before testing production tenancy.

sources.title: NIST AI 600-1 — MS-2.7-007 (perform AI red-teaming), MP-5.1-005, MP-2.3-005
OWASP Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0 — 7.1 Red Teaming Agentic Applications

capabilities.title: Model & agent evaluation harnesses
description: Repeatable, scored test suites over safety, robustness, and task adherence, run as a release gate and again continuously in production to catch regression. Gartner lists continuous assurance and evaluation as a mandatory feature of the AI TRiSM market, and all three major clouds ship it as a named service.
examples: regression gates in the release pipeline

surfaceEndpoint.note: Applies to agent configurations you ship to devices, evaluated before rollout.

surfaceCloud.note: A managed platform service, integrated with the deployment gate.

surfaceSaas.note: You can evaluate vendor outputs against your own suite, but not their internals.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (continuous assurances and evaluation as a mandatory feature)
MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0008 Validate AI Model

capabilities.title: AI-aware detection & response
description: Correlation of AI telemetry — prompts, tool calls, agent identity events, model access — into detections, investigations, and automated response, with AI-specific detection content rather than generic cloud rules. Providers now publish named alert families for jailbreak attempts, wallet attacks, ASCII smuggling, and anomalous tool invocation.
examples: AI detection content in a SIEM

surfaceEndpoint.note: Fed by endpoint telemetry from local agents and their tool calls.

surfaceCloud.note: The deepest signal set, straight from your own inference and agent planes.

surfaceSaas.note: Only as good as the vendor's exported audit events, which are usually coarse and delayed.

sources.title: CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 — SEF-04 AI incident-response testing; Logging & Monitoring domain
CISA/NSA, Deploying AI Systems Securely — integrate an incident detection system, implement robust logging and monitoring

capabilities.title: Audit logging & non-repudiation
description: Tamper-evident, append-only records of AI and agent activity bound to cryptographic identities, retained so that an action can be attributed after the fact. Distinct from detection: this is the integrity of the record itself, which the Five Eyes guidance protects by quarantining requests to delete audit data.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Requires shipping logs off the device — local-only logs are not non-repudiable.

surfaceCloud.note: Platform audit logs with immutable retention.

surfaceSaas.note: Depends entirely on the vendor's audit API and its retention window.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 — ASI08 Logging and non-repudiation (tamper-evident logs bound to cryptographic agent identities)
CISA/NSA, AI Data Security (AA25-142A) — immutable, append-only cryptographically signed ledger

capabilities.title: Endpoint detection & response
description: Device-resident detection, investigation, and response, now extending into AI-specific inspection: discovering local agents, hooking the pre-tool-call boundary, and inspecting agent network activity. The AICM carries a full endpoint-management domain, and endpoint vendors have begun instrumenting third-party coding agents by name.

surfaceEndpoint.note: The primary surface — the only place with kernel-level visibility into what an agent actually did.

surfaceCloud.note: Host-level coverage of the servers running inference and agent workloads.

surfaceSaas.note: No agent can be installed on vendor infrastructure.

sources.title: CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 — Universal Endpoint Management domain
OWASP AI Security Solutions Landscape — LLM incident detection and response, user activity monitoring

capabilities.title: Browser detection & response
description: Inspection and enforcement inside the browser session where SaaS and hosted AI interfaces are used — paste and upload controls, detection of adversarial content in responses, and policy on which AI surfaces may be used at all. Market-evidenced rather than standards-named, and often the only inspection point that exists for consumer AI.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Deployed on the device, but its value is what it sees of remote AI surfaces.

surfaceCloud.note: Covers internally hosted AI interfaces reached through the browser.

surfaceSaas.note: The primary case — inspection of vendor AI where no API or agent hook exists.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (runtime inspection and enforcement for AI applications)
OWASP AI Security Solutions Landscape — user activity monitoring, privacy and data leakage protection

capabilities.title: Application security testing for AI systems
description: Static, composition, and dynamic analysis over the code that surrounds a model — the orchestration layer, the tools, and increasingly the model-generated code itself, which the AI SSDF profile treats as ordinary code requiring ordinary review.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Highly relevant — coding agents on developer machines generate code that needs the same gates.

surfaceCloud.note: Runs in the pipeline that builds and deploys your AI application.

surfaceSaas.note: You have no access to the vendor's application code.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218A — PW.7 and PW.8 (review and test code to identify vulnerabilities)
OWASP Securing Agentic Applications Guide 1.0 — 3.2.1 Static Analysis, 3.2.2 Dependency Scanning, 3.2.5 Pre-deployment Testing

capabilities.title: AI vulnerability & patch management
description: Continuous discovery and remediation of vulnerabilities in the AI stack in production — serving frameworks, inference runtimes, notebooks, and agent dependencies — with patching cadence and re-validation after each change. CISA is explicit that an AI system must be re-evaluated for accuracy, performance, and security before it is redeployed.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Covers agent runtimes, extensions, and local tool servers on the device.

surfaceCloud.note: The full stack is yours to scan and patch.

surfaceSaas.note: Patching the vendor's stack is the vendor's obligation; you get attestations at best.

sources.title: MITRE ATLAS — AML.M0016 Vulnerability Scanning
CISA/NSA, Deploying AI Systems Securely — update and patch regularly, with full re-evaluation before redeploy

capabilities.title: SaaS security posture management for AI features
description: Posture tooling that connects to a vendor tenancy through its admin API, checks the AI feature configuration against your policy — training opt-out, data residency, retention, connector scope — and pulls the vendor's audit stream so use is evidenced rather than assumed. The practical substitute for every control you cannot deploy inside someone else's product.
examples: SaaS posture management with AI feature checks

surfaceEndpoint.note: There is no vendor tenancy to assess on the device.

surfaceCloud.note: Applies to managed model services you consume inside your own cloud accounts.

surfaceSaas.note: The primary surface — and for many vendor AI features, the only assurance available.

sources.title: NIST AI RMF 1.0 — MANAGE 3.1 (third-party AI risks monitored, risk controls applied and documented)
CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 — STA-09 service bill of materials; Supply Chain Management domain

capabilities.title: AI governance platform
description: The system of record for AI in the organisation: a catalogue of every model, application, and agent with owners and risk tiers, intake and approval workflow, evidence collection, and mapped compliance reporting. Gartner named it a market in its own right, with discovery and registry, policy enforcement, evidence collection, and audit trail as mandatory capabilities.

surfaceEndpoint.note: Endpoint-deployed assistants and agents belong in the same catalogue as everything else.

surfaceCloud.note: The richest metadata, populated directly from deployment pipelines.

surfaceSaas.note: Vendor AI is registered through intake; discovery fills the gaps intake misses.

sources.title: Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (AI catalog and AI data mapping as mandatory features)
ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — AI management system, Annex A reference controls

capabilities.title: Shadow AI discovery
description: Finding the AI that was never registered — unsanctioned assistants, browser extensions, personal accounts, unmanaged agents, and undeclared tool servers — and bringing it under policy. Providers now name agent sprawl and shadow agents as first-class risk types, and the OWASP MCP Top 10 gives shadow servers their own entry.
examples: shadow agent and tool server detection

surfaceEndpoint.note: Where locally installed agents and tool servers are actually found.

surfaceCloud.note: Undeclared model endpoints and agent workloads surface through cloud discovery.

surfaceSaas.note: The classic case — employees reaching consumer AI through personal accounts.

sources.title: OWASP MCP Top 10 — MCP09 Shadow MCP Servers
Gartner, Market Guide for AI Trust, Risk and Security Management (catalog: discovery, inventory and risk scoring of all AI used in organization)

capabilities.title: Third-party risk management platform for AI vendors
description: A vendor risk platform carrying AI-specific assessment content — training-data practices, subprocessors, model provenance, incident obligations — that collects and expires evidence on a cadence and drives reassessment when a vendor ships new AI features. Named across NCSC, NIST, ISO, and Gartner, and the main lever where the technology surface is opaque.
examples: vendor risk platforms with AI questionnaire content
continuous vendor monitoring and reassessment triggers

surfaceEndpoint.note: Applies to the agent and extension vendors whose software runs on your devices.

surfaceCloud.note: Covers model providers, hosting platforms, and framework suppliers.

surfaceSaas.note: The dominant control for vendor AI — most other capabilities cannot reach it.

sources.title: UK NCSC and international partners, Guidelines for secure AI system development — secure your supply chain
NIST AI RMF 1.0 — GOVERN 6.1/6.2, MAP 4.1/4.2 (third-party risk policies and controls)

capabilities.title: Threat modelling tooling for AI systems
description: Tooling that builds and maintains a machine-readable threat model of a specific AI system — enumerating its attack surface against a published AI threat taxonomy, mapping trust boundaries from the architecture, and keeping the model current as the system changes. Cloud providers now generate these automatically; CISA requires the developer of an AI system to supply a threat model to whoever deploys it.
examples: threat modelling platforms with AI threat libraries
automated attack surface and trust boundary mapping

surfaceEndpoint.note: Local agents have their own trust boundaries — local files, credentials, and tool servers.

surfaceCloud.note: Full architectural visibility makes this the most productive surface to model.

surfaceSaas.note: Modelled at the integration boundary rather than inside the vendor's system.

sources.title: CISA/NSA, Deploying AI Systems Securely — require the primary developer to provide a threat model
NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations

capabilities.title: Model registry & documentation generation
description: A registry that holds each model version with its lineage, evaluation results, approval state, and generated model card, emitting documentation as a build artifact rather than a document someone maintains by hand. Every major platform ships one; ISO/IEC 42001 and EU AI Act instructions-for-use obligations are what it exists to satisfy.
examples: model registries with version and approval state

surfaceEndpoint.note: Agent definitions shipped to devices need the same documented scope and limits.

surfaceCloud.note: Generated from the pipeline that trains and deploys the model.

surfaceSaas.note: You consume the vendor's model card rather than producing one; its quality is theirs.

archetypes.title: Autonomous action agent over business records
summary: A single agent operating a business process end to end — reading a request, deciding, and writing to systems of record in seconds, with no human between the decision and the effect. The architecture where the design question is reversibility rather than accuracy.
description:
Everything structural here follows from one fact: the agent writes. A retrieval assistant that is wrong produces a wrong sentence; this produces a refund, a provisioned account, a cancelled order. The controls that matter are the ones that bound what can be done and make it undoable, not the ones that improve the odds of being right.
The action catalogue is the primary control and it should be deterministic. The model chooses among named, parameter-validated actions rather than composing arbitrary calls, and each action declares its own blast radius and its own compensating transaction. An agent that can call an arbitrary API is not an agent with a policy problem; it is an agent with no policy surface at all.
The attacker is typically an authenticated customer. The request text is supplied by the person who benefits from the outcome, and it reaches the same context window as the system instruction — indirect prompt injection with a very short path to money. The second injection path arrives through retrieval: record content written months earlier, by requesters and by staff, re-enters the loop as context. That is why the approval threshold is tied to consequence rather than confidence, and why it must be rare — a gate on every action is a queue nobody reads, while below the threshold the compensating path, reversal rather than review, is what keeps a wrong action survivable.
The agent needs an identity of its own. Actions taken as a shared service account are neither attributable nor separately revocable, which turns every incident into a full-service outage when the response is to disable the credential.
distinguishedBy:
Against the embedded retrieval assistant: identical up to the point of the model call. That one renders an answer; this one calls an actuator. Adding one mutating tool to a retrieval assistant moves it into this architecture and its entire control set.
Against the core agent workflow: that one is a durable, multi-agent process surviving crashes and replay across days. This is one agent on one fast path, deciding in seconds — no supervisor, no journal, no replay — and still consequential, which is why the catalogue, the threshold and the compensating transaction carry the weight instead of durability machinery.

exemplars.name: Autonomous customer service resolution
exemplars.note: Agents that read a customer's request, consult policy and records, and issue the remedy without a human, escalating only above a value or confidence threshold.

exemplars.name: Operations and fulfilment agents
exemplars.note: Agents acting on orders, inventory or entitlements, where the action catalogue maps to existing business transactions that already have reversal semantics.

blocks.title: Requester
blocks.note: Usually an authenticated customer, and usually the party who benefits from the action. Both the legitimate user and, on a bad day, the attacker.

blocks.title: Intake
blocks.note: Authenticates the requester, binds the request to an account, applies quotas and classifies the text before the loop starts. Authentication says nothing about whether the ask is honest.

items.label: Identity & account binding
items.note: Who is asking, bound to the account the request concerns, settled before the agent runs.

items.label: Input classification
items.note: Catches the direct injection attempt. The indirect path through record content arrives later and is the harder one.

blocks.title: Planning loop
blocks.note: Chooses the next action from the catalogue, given the request and what it has read. Runs under its own workload identity, distinct from both the requester and the service.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Reads context, calls the model, proposes an action. The full cycle completes in seconds.

items.label: Agent identity
items.note: A distinct, revocable principal. Without it no action is attributable and the only incident response is disabling a credential the whole service shares.

blocks.title: Retrieval & case state
blocks.note: The business policy, the customer's history and the working state of this case. Record content is the second injection path — written by requesters and staff, re-entering as context.

items.label: Policy & record retrieval
items.note: Reads scoped to the account under discussion, not to what the service can reach.

items.label: Case state
items.note: Scoped to one case. Cross-case memory would let one requester's text influence another's outcome.

blocks.title: Action catalogue
blocks.note: Named, parameter-validated actions rather than arbitrary calls, each declaring its blast radius and its compensating transaction. The architecture's primary control, and a design artifact rather than a configuration setting.

items.label: Named actions
items.note: The complete set of things the agent can do. Nothing outside it is reachable.

items.label: Parameter validation
items.note: The model proposed the action; the catalogue decides whether it is well-formed and in bounds.

items.label: Per-call policy
items.note: Which action, on which record, up to what value — evaluated at call time rather than granted at session time.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface. What runs behind it is the provider's and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Returns the chosen action and its parameters — content the catalogue validates rather than trusts.

blocks.title: Business records
blocks.note: The systems of record where effects land, and where reversal either exists or does not. Also the source retrieval reads back into context.

items.label: Orders, accounts, entitlements
items.note: The authoritative state the agent changes.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Identity, per-call policy, the approval threshold, the decision audit and the stop — each outside the loop it governs, because the loop is the thing that may be misbehaving.

items.label: Identity provider
items.note: Issues the agent's workload identity and the requester's, and keeps them distinct.

items.label: Action policy
items.note: The bounds the catalogue enforces per invocation, authored and changed outside the loop.

items.label: Approval threshold
items.note: Keyed to irreversibility and value, not model confidence. Rare enough that somebody actually reads it.

items.label: Decision audit
items.note: Every action with the reasoning, the inputs and the identity behind it — the basis for reversal and dispute.

items.label: Kill switch
items.note: Halts the agent and revokes its identity without a deploy.

edges.label: request / outcome
edges.note: Free text, attachments and history, authored by the party who benefits from the outcome. The remedy or refusal returns on the same path, usually within seconds.
The requester's identity survives into the loop, or policy cannot scope actions to the account they concern.
Inference on a brokered, expiring credential. The response names an action and its parameters — transport integrity says nothing about whose intent produced it.
Policy, history and case state read back as context — including the second injection path, record content written long before this case opened.

edges.label: scoped read
edges.note: Reads scoped to the account under discussion, which is what stops one requester's case from retrieving another's records into context.

edges.label: proposed action
edges.note: The model's choice arrives here as a proposal, not a command. Validation is the boundary.

edges.label: validated write
edges.note: The point at which the agent's output stops being text. Whether a wrong action is survivable is decided here: an action with no compensating transaction should not be in the catalogue below the approval threshold.

edges.label: policy & approval
edges.note: Per-invocation bounds and the above-threshold approval gate, authored outside the loop and enforced at the catalogue.

edges.label: evaluation
edges.note: Model and prompt changes pass an evaluation gate before they serve traffic.

risks.note: The request text is supplied by the person who benefits from the outcome, and it reaches the same context window as the system instruction.
Record content is the harder injection path — written months earlier, by someone handling a different case, re-entering as context now.
Untrusted request text, a model choosing among real transactions, and a write path into records compound here.
The completion names an action and its parameters, and it is unauthenticated content.
The agent acts on a requester's behalf using authority broader than theirs. Keeping the requester's context alive through the loop is what closes the gap.
Reads not scoped to the account under discussion pull other customers' records into context.
A loop that retries and re-plans in seconds can spend and act faster than anyone notices.
Case memory keyed loosely enough to collide across cases lets one requester's text steer another's outcome.
The catalogue is the policy surface; whoever can edit it programs the agent.
Per-token inference behind a customer-facing surface makes unbounded requests a spend problem.

capabilities.note: Named, parameter-validated actions with declared blast radius and a compensating transaction each — the deterministic surface everything else assumes.
An approval gate keyed to irreversibility and value, rare enough to be read; below it, reversal rather than review.
A per-invocation policy decision — this action, this record, this value, now — rather than a session-time grant.
A distinct, revocable workload identity per agent, so actions are attributable and separately revocable.
Entitlement-filtered retrieval scoped to the account under discussion, enforced before fetching.
Classify request text before the loop; the caller cannot be trusted about their own request.
Case-scoped memory with hard boundaries — no cross-case reads, ever.
Brokered, per-workload, expiring model credentials; the agent tier holds no standing key.
Quotas and cost ceilings at the edge, before token spend and action volume are committed.
Every action with reasoning, inputs and identity, written where the agent can append and cannot amend.
A halt that also revokes the agent's identity, and does not require a deploy.

scenarios.title: A customer asks for a refund

steps.note: The request is authenticated, bound to an account, and classified.
The loop starts with the requester's identity intact.
Policy and the customer's history load as context, scoped to this account.
The model proposes an action and parameters from the catalogue.
The proposal is validated — well-formed, in policy, under the value threshold.
The refund executes, with its compensating transaction on file.
The outcome returns within seconds; the audit holds the reasoning.

scenarios.title: The request text is the attack

steps.note: The text instructs the agent to ignore policy and refund in full. Classification flags what it can.
Whatever survives enters the same context window as the system instruction.
A steered model proposes the most generous action available.
The catalogue does not care what steered the model — parameters and policy bounds hold.
Below the threshold the action is compensable; above it the approval gate fires.

scenarios.title: The injection was written months ago

steps.note: The loop reads the case history like any other.
A note written into a record long ago, in someone else's case, comes back as context.
The model reads it beside the system instruction with nothing marking it apart.
The catalogue and the per-call policy are the controls that were built for exactly this turn.

archetypes.title: Agent-facing endpoint
summary: A service built to be called by other organisations' agents rather than by their engineers — including agent-initiated commerce. The caller is autonomous, acting for a human who is not present, and every assumption about who is on the other end has to be restated.
description:
Bot defence and agent enablement point in opposite directions, and this architecture is the decision about which way to face. A decade of investment went into distinguishing humans from automation and blocking the automation; an agent acting for a legitimate customer trips every one of those signals. The resolution is a distinct, authenticated, rate-limited lane for agents rather than a hole in the human one — the human path and its bot defences stay strict.
Delegation is the substance of it. The question is not whether the caller is a bot but whether this agent is authorised to act for this customer, to what extent, and for how long. That demands real primitives — an agent identity, a scope, an expiry and a revocation path — and where the endpoint takes payment, a mandate: a signed statement of what the human authorised, presented by the agent and verified by the merchant. The competing mandate schemes are unsettled, so the durable position is to build the verification as its own component rather than couple to one scheme.
The remaining differences are behavioural. Agents retry, so idempotency scoped to the mandate is a correctness requirement. Agents parallelise, so limits tuned for human pacing do not hold. Agents read error messages and act on them, so error text is part of the interface. And a dispute over an agent's action needs a record of the mandate it presented, not only of the request it sent.
Notably, no block in this drawing carries a CoSAI component anchor: the service itself contains no AI. It is in the catalogue because its caller is an agent, and the neutral tabs are the honest statement that the model, the loop and the tool plane all live on the other side of the wire.
distinguishedBy:
Against a remote MCP server: that publishes tools for agents to call. This publishes a business API, and the caller may be any agent framework at all — the delegation and payment questions dominate instead of tool-description injection.
Against an ordinary API with bot management: same endpoint, opposite policy. That one identifies and blocks automation; this one admits it under a delegation model, which is a different system rather than a relaxed setting.

exemplars.name: Agent-accessible commerce endpoints
exemplars.note: Merchants exposing a path for agent-initiated purchasing, with a mandate presented by the agent and verified before the transaction.

exemplars.name: Agent payment and mandate rails
exemplars.note: Competing specifications for expressing what a human authorised an agent to spend, backed by card networks, platforms and standards bodies. Unsettled, and worth abstracting behind a component of your own.

exemplars.name: Business APIs adding an agent lane
exemplars.note: An existing API gaining a separate authenticated path for agent callers, with its own limits and its own audit, rather than loosening the human one.

blocks.title: Delegating customer
blocks.note: The person on whose behalf the agent acts, absent at request time. Their authorisation has to arrive as a verifiable artifact rather than as an assertion.

blocks.title: Human path & bot defence
blocks.note: The existing human-facing surface, unchanged and still strict. Unregistered agents land here and meet the bot defences — the correct default rather than an outage. It is also where the human is reached for above-threshold confirmation.

items.label: Bot management
items.note: Stays pointed at unadmitted automation; the agent lane is what keeps it from blocking customers.

items.label: Out-of-band confirmation
items.note: Above the delegation threshold, the human is reached here — on a channel the agent does not control.

blocks.title: Third-party agent
blocks.note: Someone else's agent, on someone else's infrastructure, acting for a customer. Not a bot to be blocked and not a user to be trusted.

blocks.title: Agent lane
blocks.note: A separate authenticated path with its own limits and its own audit. Authentication here establishes three facts — which agent, from which operator, acting for which customer — where most API auth was built to establish one.

items.label: Agent authentication
items.note: Establishes the operator, which is the party accountable when an agent misbehaves at scale.

items.label: Per-operator rate limits
items.note: Tuned for callers that retry and parallelise; human pacing does not survive contact with an agent.

items.label: Behaviour baselines
items.note: Normal for an agent is nothing like normal for a person, so the old detection cannot be pointed here.

blocks.title: Mandate verification
blocks.note: Validates the signed statement of what the human authorised — scope, value, expiry. Two separate claims cross here: which agent this is, and what its human authorised. Conflating them is the central failure of this architecture.

items.label: Mandate check
items.note: Scope, value and expiry verified per request, including on the retry path.

items.label: Scheme adapters
items.note: The competing mandate rails abstracted behind one component, because none has settled.

blocks.title: Transaction processing
blocks.note: The actual operation, bounded by what the mandate permits, deduplicated against retries, and answered in error text an agent will read and act on.

items.label: Idempotency & reconciliation
items.note: Keys scoped to the mandate rather than the request, so a retry with a fresh request id does not become a second purchase.

items.label: Business logic
items.note: Bounded by what the human authorised rather than by what the agent asked for.

items.label: Response & error text
items.note: Read by a model and acted on. A verbose failure teaches the caller — and anyone probing — more than it should.

blocks.title: Orders & evidence
blocks.note: The state the transaction changes, and the mandate evidence a disputed agent action will be argued from. A record of the request without the mandate cannot establish whether the agent exceeded its authority.

items.label: Orders & accounts
items.note: What a dispute will be resolved against.

items.label: Mandate evidence
items.note: The mandate presented, the agent that presented it and the action taken — retained for the dispute window.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Registration, delegation policy, dispute handling and per-operator monitoring — the controls that turn an unbounded population of callers into an administered one.

items.label: Agent registry
items.note: Which agent operators are recognised and what each may do. Unregistered agents get the human path.

items.label: Delegation policy
items.note: What an agent may do without further confirmation, and above what threshold the human is reached on another channel. Where that line sits is the central business decision.

items.label: Dispute & reversal
items.note: Exists before the first dispute, and rests entirely on the mandate evidence.

items.label: Operator monitoring
items.note: Baselines per agent operator rather than per user, feeding revocation when one goes bad.

edges.label: authorises
edges.note: The delegation happens entirely outside this system, on a platform the merchant does not operate. All the endpoint ever sees is the artifact that results.

edges.label: out-of-band confirmation
edges.note: Above the delegation threshold, the human is reached here — on a channel the agent does not control — before the transaction proceeds.

edges.label: request with mandate / response
edges.note: Requests carry the agent's identity and its mandate in; responses and error text — which the agent will read and act on — go back out.

edges.label: admitted request
edges.note: Agent, operator and customer travel with the request rather than being re-derived from its body, which an agent composes.

edges.label: verified mandate
edges.note: The operation proceeds under what the human authorised, not under what the agent asked for.

edges.label: transaction & evidence
edges.note: The write lands together with the mandate that authorised it. Evidence recorded here is what the dispute process runs on.

edges.label: delegation thresholds
edges.note: Policy decides what proceeds on the mandate alone and what waits for the human on another channel.

edges.label: dispute resolution
edges.note: A disputed agent transaction is resolved against the mandate evidence, not the request log.

risks.note: A recognised agent is not an authorised one, and the human who could clarify is not there. Every control here exists to keep those two facts separate.
The caller population is unbounded and lives outside the organisation. Without registration, admitting agents means admitting anyone.
Agents parallelise and retry; limits tuned for human pacing fail open under agent traffic.
An agent credential that outlives its revoked delegation keeps acting for a customer who withdrew consent.
An agent acting beyond its mandate, or the same action executing twice on a retry — different halves, same edge.
A retrying caller in a loop turns one intended purchase into a storm without idempotency fencing.
Without the mandate evidence, nobody can reconstruct what the absent human actually authorised.
Error text is read by a model and acted on. Verbose failures teach an attacker's agent exactly how to retry.

capabilities.note: Agent identity with real primitives — which agent, which operator, for which customer — with expiry and revocation.
Register agent operators and their permissions; route the unregistered to the human path and its bot defences.
Verify the signed mandate — scope, value, expiry — per request, behind a scheme-neutral component of your own.
Bound the operation to what the human authorised, not to what the agent requested.
Per-operator limits sized for retrying, parallelising callers — a separate budget from the human path.
Record the mandate with the action, retained for the dispute window; the request alone proves nothing.
Above-threshold confirmation with the human on a channel the agent does not control.
Baselines per agent operator, because human baselines flag every agent and miss the bad one.
Treat error text as interface design: deterministic, minimal, and free of anything that teaches a probe.
A delegated grant that is scoped and expiring, not a standing power the customer forgot they gave.
Assurance on agent operators as third parties — their platform is part of your transaction path.

scenarios.title: An agent buys something for its customer

steps.note: The customer authorises the agent on a platform the merchant never sees; a mandate is minted.
The agent presents its identity and the mandate on the agent lane, not the human path.
Scope, value and expiry are verified against the artifact, not the request body.
The operation is bounded by the mandate and keyed for idempotency.
The transaction lands with the mandate evidence attached.
A disciplined, typed response returns — error text included, because the agent will act on it.

scenarios.title: A timeout makes the agent retry

steps.note: The response was slow; the agent retries with a fresh request id.
The same mandate verifies again — including on the retry path.
Idempotency scoped to the mandate recognises the duplicate.
One transaction exists, not two. The customer's agent did not double-purchase.

scenarios.title: The customer says they never authorised it

steps.note: The disputed transaction was recorded with the mandate the agent presented.
The dispute resolves against that evidence: either the action was within the mandate's scope, or the agent exceeded it and the reversal path runs.
