archetypes.title: Core agent workflow
summary: A hosted agent system doing real work over business records: a front end takes requests, a durable orchestration layer plans and delegates across subagents, and every tool call leaves through one governed gateway. This is the target shape most cloud agent deployments should converge on, whatever they orchestrate.
description:
The spine is a request path: application front end, agent orchestration, agentic gateway, tool services, downstream systems. The architecture's security posture lives almost entirely in one decision — that agents do not hold credentials or reach tools directly. Every tool call, model call and connector call leaves through the gateway, which brokers short-lived credentials, enforces policy per call, applies rate and budget limits, and writes the audit trail as a tap rather than a favour asked of the agent.
Orchestration is durable: a supervisor decomposes work for subagents and an engine journals every step so the process survives crashes. Durability has two consequences nobody expects from reliability machinery. Everything a step returns is written down, so a step that returns a credential has persisted it. And the engine replays steps to recover, so a side effect that is not idempotent can execute more than once — including a payment.
Delegation is the other axis. A subagent should inherit a narrowed slice of the supervisor's authority, not all of it; delegation that does not narrow is privilege distribution. And inter-agent messages are model output becoming model input — one confused agent propagates through the graph, which is what distinguishes multi-agent failure from a single agent with more tools.
The governance plane is drawn as its own column because it is what the personal-agent archetype lacks: workload identities for every agent, a registry deciding what may run and which tools are admitted, evaluation gates in front of change, an append-only audit sink, and a stop that works while a process is mid-flight.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint personal agent: the loop is nearly identical; the governance is not. Hosting buys an identity per agent, a policy boundary on every tool call, an audit trail and an administrator — none of which the endpoint pattern supplies.
Against a RAG assistant: that architecture retrieves and answers. This one acts — its outputs are writes to business systems, which is why the gateway, the approval gate and replay safety carry the weight here.

exemplars.name: Durable execution engines running agent steps
exemplars.note: Workflow platforms that journal step results and replay to recover, with agent invocations as steps alongside conventional ones.

exemplars.name: Supervisor and subagent orchestration
exemplars.note: A coordinating agent decomposing work across specialists, each with its own context and tool set, over a process too long to hold in one conversation.

exemplars.name: Managed agent runtimes
exemplars.note: Cloud agent services package this same shape — runtime, gateway, registry, observability — as discrete products behind one control plane.

blocks.title: Initiator
blocks.note: Starts the process and is absent for the rest of it. The approval they gave at the start is the only human decision until something escalates.

blocks.title: Schedules & events
blocks.note: Timers, webhooks and queue messages that start work with no human in the room.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: The only place a request is still a request, before it becomes a plan.

items.label: App & API endpoint
items.note: The published surface users and systems call.

items.label: Identity & input checks
items.note: Who is asking, and whether the request is well-formed — settled before any agent runs.

blocks.title: Agent orchestration
blocks.note: The supervisor plans and delegates; the durable engine journals every step and replays to recover. Delegation should narrow authority at every hop.

items.label: Supervisor agent
items.note: Decomposes the goal and routes work to specialists.

items.label: Subagents
items.note: Specialists with their own contexts and tools. Their messages to each other are model output becoming model input.

items.label: Durable engine
items.note: Journals results and replays to recover. Replay without re-authorisation re-executes side effects.

items.label: Delegation scopes
items.note: Each hop carries less authority than its parent, and the chain is reconstructable.

blocks.title: State & knowledge
blocks.note: What the workflow knows and what it has done. The journal is a reliability feature and a secrets sink in the same breath.

items.label: Step journal
items.note: Everything a step returns is persisted here. A returned credential is a stored one.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: Retrieval context for the agents.

items.label: Shared memory
items.note: Cross-step working state the agents read back as context.

blocks.title: Agentic gateway
blocks.note: The one door. Agents hold no credentials and reach nothing directly; every model and tool call is brokered, policy-checked, rate-limited and logged here.

items.label: Credential broker
items.note: Short-lived, scoped credentials fetched at step time — never held for the process's life.

items.label: Policy enforcement
items.note: A per-call decision about this agent, this tool, this argument — not a standing grant.

items.label: Rate & budget limits
items.note: The brake on loops and runaway spend, enforced outside the loop it limits.

items.label: Audit taps
items.note: The trail is recorded by the gateway, not volunteered by the agent.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface, called many times across the process. Everything behind it is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Reached only through the gateway, on brokered credentials.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The action surface: MCP servers, connectors and peer agents. Everything here is admitted by the registry and reached only through the gateway.

items.label: MCP servers
items.note: Tool providers with declared scopes, admitted against the registry.

items.label: SaaS connectors
items.note: Vendor-side capabilities the workflow drives on scoped grants.

items.label: Peer agents
items.note: Cross-org delegation. A peer's output enters this graph as input.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: The systems the workflow actually changes — where a wrong action becomes a real one.

items.label: Business records
items.note: The systems of record the agents write to.

items.label: Email & SaaS
items.note: Messages sent and tickets moved on the organisation's behalf.

items.label: External APIs
items.note: Third-party services, and the untrusted content they return.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: The column the personal-agent archetype is missing. Identity, admission, evaluation, audit and the ability to stop a running process — each its own service, none of them inside the loop they govern.

items.label: Identity provider
items.note: A workload identity per agent, distinct from any user.

items.label: Agent & tool registry
items.note: What may run, and which tools it may be offered. Admission, not discovery.

items.label: Evaluation gates
items.note: Behavioural checks in front of every model, prompt or tool change.

items.label: Audit sink
items.note: Append-only, off the agents' write path, able to reconstruct the delegation chain.

items.label: Kill switch
items.note: Stops a mid-flight process without waiting for it to finish misbehaving.

edges.label: request / result
edges.note: The human's request in, and the outcome back — often days later.

edges.label: trigger
edges.note: Unattended starts. Most of this architecture's runs begin here, not with a person.
An authenticated request becomes a goal; results and escalations flow back.
Steps journal their results and read shared state back as context — the replay and persistence surface.
Every model and tool call the agents make leaves through here. There is no side door.
Inference on brokered credentials, with limits and logging applied per call.
Tool calls carry the narrowed, per-step grant — not the supervisor's authority.
Actions land on real systems; whatever comes back — records, pages, API responses — is untrusted content entering agent context.

edges.label: admission
edges.note: Tools and servers exist here only if the registry admitted them.

edges.label: evaluation
edges.note: Model and prompt changes pass an evaluation gate before they serve traffic.

risks.note: Records, documents and API responses read over the process's lifetime are chances to steer an agent whose output another agent will trust.
Inter-agent messages are model output landing in another agent's context as instruction.
A subagent that inherits its parent's full authority is privilege distribution, not delegation.
The journal records everything a step returns. A returned secret is a persisted one.
Consequential writes with no human present — and replay can execute a non-idempotent one twice.
An unbounded loop between agents burns budget for as long as nobody notices.
Inference called many times across days of process is a spend surface worth a brake.
The admission list is the tool supply chain; whoever writes it programs the agents.

capabilities.note: The user's identity and a delegated grant scoped to this request, not a standing power.
A workload identity per agent and subagent, so the chain is attributable.
Credentials brokered at step time, short-lived and scoped; agents hold none.
A policy decision on every tool call — agent, tool, arguments — outside the loop.
Each delegation hop carries a narrower grant than its parent.
Rate and budget ceilings that end loops the agents cannot end themselves.
Returned content is classified before it re-enters any agent's context.
Redaction on what steps may journal, because the journal outlives the process.
An approval gate on consequential writes, sized to the blast radius.
Admission for agents and tools — nothing runs or is offered by default.
An append-only trail that can reconstruct who delegated what to whom.
A stop that works mid-flight, because these processes run for days.

scenarios.title: A user asks the agent to act

steps.note: The request is authenticated and a scoped grant is minted for it.
The supervisor decomposes the goal across subagents.
Every call the agents make funnels through the one door.
Inference on brokered credentials, limits applied.
Tool calls carry the narrowed per-step grant.
The write lands — behind an approval gate when it is consequential.
The result returns, possibly days after the request.

scenarios.title: A step replays after a crash

steps.note: The engine rebuilds state from the journal — including anything a step persisted.
Replayed steps re-request credentials; nothing survives from the first run.
Idempotency fencing decides whether the side effect may run again.
Without fencing, the payment executes twice. The journal replays; the world does not.

scenarios.title: An event fires days into the process

steps.note: A timer or webhook resumes work with nobody watching.
The waiting step wakes with its narrowed grant, not the initiator's.
Credentials are fetched now — the ones from day one would be stale authority.
The action proceeds under the same per-call policy as an attended run.

deviations.subject: Subagents are drawn as one item
deviations.reason: There are several, with different contexts and tools. They are drawn as one because the risks — inherited authority, message propagation, chain opacity — are properties of the delegation pattern rather than of any particular specialist.

deviations.subject: Two of this architecture's risks have no CoSAI equivalent
deviations.reason: OWASP's agentic taxonomy names memory poisoning and cascading hallucination as distinct threats; CoSAI's risk set has neither. They are pinned here as prompt injection and insecure model output, the nearest true statements, which lose the compounding that makes both dangerous in a multi-agent system. Recorded rather than papered over.

archetypes.title: AI-augmented API backend
summary: A conventional API with a model somewhere in the middle — classifying, extracting, summarising or routing — behind a contract that promises a typed response. The most widespread AI architecture and the least often recognised as one.
description:
There is no chat interface here and frequently no user-visible AI at all. A support ticket gets categorised, an invoice gets extracted, a message gets routed, and the caller receives a normal API response. The AI is an implementation detail of an endpoint, which is exactly why this architecture tends to skip the controls the chat-shaped ones get.
The defining property is that model output re-enters a deterministic system. Downstream code branches on a classification, writes an extracted value to a record, or passes a generated string into a query. The schema is the output contract: model output is validated against it before anything downstream sees it, and a response that does not conform is rejected — routed to a deterministic fallback — rather than coerced. Free-text fields inside a structured response are where this goes wrong: a schema that validates shape but leaves a string unconstrained has validated nothing about the content of the field most likely to reach a template, a query or another prompt.
Two operational properties differ from a normal backend. Latency and availability now depend on an external inference call, so timeouts, retries and the fallback path are functional requirements rather than resilience niceties. And cost is per-token on a path called at request volume, which makes an unbounded input a financial exposure as well as a performance one.
distinguishedBy:
Against the embedded retrieval assistant: no conversation, no retrieval, no human reading the output. The consumer of the model's output is code, which changes the control set from grounding and rendering to schema validation and fallback.
Against an autonomous action agent: this has no loop and no discretion. It performs one transformation per request within a fixed contract; where the extracted value drives a write, the write is the calling system's decision, not the model's.

exemplars.name: Classification and routing endpoints
exemplars.note: Ticket triage, content moderation, intent routing. A typed response consumed by code, with the model replacing a rules engine that used to be maintained by hand.

exemplars.name: Document extraction services
exemplars.note: Invoices, forms and contracts turned into structured records. The extracted values are written to systems of record, which is where the validation question becomes concrete.

blocks.title: Calling system
blocks.note: Another service or a customer integration, submitting content authored by someone else entirely. Expects a typed response and will not tolerate a prose apology when the model misbehaves.

blocks.title: API contract
blocks.note: The published contract and the checks in front of it. Its promise of a typed response is what the whole validation discipline downstream exists to keep.

items.label: Published endpoint
items.note: Conventional API authentication — it authenticates the caller and nothing about the content.

items.label: Input validation & bounds
items.note: Size, type and content limits before anything reaches a model. On a per-token dependency, bounding input length is a cost control as much as a safety one.

items.label: Quotas
items.note: Enforced at the edge, because by the service tier the token spend is already committed.

blocks.title: Transformation
blocks.note: Builds the prompt, calls the model, and is the only place in the service that knows an AI is involved at all. Everything after the edge treats the payload as adversarial regardless.

items.label: Prompt construction
items.note: Submitted content becomes model input here, without ever having looked like a prompt.

items.label: Timeouts & retries
items.note: An external inference call now sits inside the endpoint's latency and availability budget.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface. What runs behind it is the provider's and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Authenticated transport carrying unauthenticated content back into a deterministic system.

blocks.title: Output validation
blocks.note: Schema conformance with rejection rather than coercion, then constraints on the fields themselves. This is the boundary between model text and the typed object the contract promised.

items.label: Schema conformance
items.note: A response that does not conform is rejected, never coerced into shape.

items.label: Field constraints
items.note: Enumerations wherever the domain allows. Validating shape alone says nothing about the contents of a string.

items.label: Output encoding
items.note: Free-text values encoded for wherever they land — markup, a query, another prompt.

items.label: Deterministic fallback
items.note: What the endpoint returns when the model is slow, unavailable or non-conforming. A functional requirement, because the contract promised a response.

blocks.title: Systems of record
blocks.note: Where extracted values and classifications become state. The model influenced the value; it did not authorise the write.

items.label: Records & downstream code
items.note: Code that branches on the value was written expecting a value, not an adversary.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Credentials, cost ceilings, evaluation and the record of what the model was asked and answered — all easy to skip here, precisely because the endpoint does not look like an AI feature.

items.label: Credential broker
items.note: Short-lived provider credentials issued per workload, not a key in the service's configuration.

items.label: Quota & cost ceiling
items.note: A per-token dependency called at request volume; without a ceiling, traffic and cost are the same variable.

items.label: Accuracy & adversarial evaluation
items.note: Behaviour on a labelled set and on inputs designed to break the schema. Where a chat product degrades noticeably, this one silently miscategorises.

items.label: Prompt & response log
items.note: The only way to reconstruct why a record holds the value it does.

edges.label: request / typed response
edges.note: Submitted content in — ticket text, documents, message bodies, written by whoever submitted them — and the contract's typed response back out.

edges.label: bounded input
edges.note: The edge has bounded size and stripped what it can; the payload is treated as adversarial anyway.
Inference on a brokered, per-workload credential. The response returns over authenticated transport as unauthenticated content.

edges.label: model response
edges.note: Model output enters the validation boundary. Every control from here to the write path exists because of this crossing.

edges.label: typed or fallback response
edges.note: What crosses back out is a validated, constrained object — or the deterministic fallback, which honours the same contract. A caller cannot tell the difference.

edges.label: extracted value
edges.note: The value becomes state in someone else's system. Keeping the model's influence separate from write authorisation is what stops this architecture quietly becoming an action agent.

edges.label: evaluation & credentials
edges.note: Model, prompt and schema changes pass evaluation before serving traffic, and the provider credential is brokered rather than stored.

risks.note: The central risk: model output flows into branching logic, record writes and sometimes queries, and every consumer was written expecting a value rather than an adversary.
Injection arrives inside ordinary business content, on an endpoint nobody thinks of as an AI feature — which is why the controls get skipped here more than anywhere else.
An external inference call sits inside a synchronous request path; its availability is now yours.
Whatever the caller submitted leaves your tier inside the prompt, and again into the logs.
Per-token cost at request volume makes an unbounded input a financial exposure.
Inputs crafted to break the schema or skew the classification fail silently — a miscategorisation, not an error.
An extracted value that drives a write turns a wrong answer into a wrong record.

capabilities.note: Schema validation with a deterministic failure path — reject non-conforming responses, never coerce them.
Constrain fields to enumerations where the domain allows, and encode free-text values for wherever they land.
Classify submitted content before it becomes a prompt, because it never looks like one.
Bound input size and enforce quotas and cost ceilings at the edge, before spend is committed.
Make the fallback the default answer to every model failure mode — slow, unavailable, non-conforming — so the contract holds without the model.
Brokered, short-lived provider credentials; no key at rest in the service tier.
Evaluate conformance under adversarial input, not only accuracy on the happy path, before any model or prompt change ships.
Log the prompt and the response per request — the only record of why a field holds its value.
A review gate where extracted values drive consequential or irreversible writes.
Workload identity for callers — non-human clients with their own credentials and retry behaviour.

steps.note: The request is authenticated and its content bounded.
The ticket text becomes a prompt in the only component that knows a model is involved.
Inference on a brokered credential, inside the endpoint's latency budget.
The response is validated against the schema; the category must be one of the enumeration.
A typed object crosses back out — the contract kept.
The caller consumes a normal API response, unaware of the machinery.
The call times out, or returns something that is not the schema.
Conformance fails; the response is rejected rather than coerced.
The deterministic fallback honours the same contract. The caller cannot tell.

scenarios.title: The injection is inside an invoice

steps.note: A document authored by a third party arrives as ordinary business content.
Its text reaches a prompt without ever having looked like one.
The model follows the strongest instruction in its context.
The payload rides out in the free-text field the schema left unconstrained.
Field constraints and encoding decide what actually lands in the record.

archetypes.title: AI gateway, router and guardrail plane
summary: A shared platform service every AI workload calls through: one endpoint across many providers, with redaction, guardrails, model routing, a response cache and credentialed egress on the data path, and enforcement, credentials, budgets, the catalogue and the aggregate log in the control plane. Built once so twenty teams do not each solve the same problems differently.
description:
This architecture exists because of a counting argument. Twenty teams calling model providers directly produce twenty credential stores, twenty logging conventions, twenty quota decisions and no aggregate view. One gateway produces one of each. Nothing about it is novel infrastructure — it is an egress proxy specialised for a metered, non-deterministic dependency — and its value is entirely in being the only path.
Which makes network enforcement the load-bearing control, and it belongs to the control plane rather than the drawing's data path: default-deny egress to model endpoints with the gateway as the sole exception is what converts a convention into an architecture. Everything else on this diagram assumes that enforcement holds. The drawing keeps the two planes honest — requests flow left to right through the gateway tiers; the governance column supplies credentials, budgets, the catalogue and collects the log, and touches the data path only at those points.
The gateway is also the highest-value target in the organisation's AI estate and its single point of failure. Every prompt and response passes through it, so it sees more sensitive data than any single application; it holds the provider credentials for all of them; and when it degrades, every AI workload degrades with it. Its own access control, log retention and blast radius deserve the treatment given to a secrets manager, not a proxy.
Two design cautions. Guardrails at the gateway see text without application context, so they catch policy violations and generic injection patterns and cannot judge whether a particular retrieval was appropriate — they are a floor beneath application controls, not a replacement. And a semantic cache keyed loosely enough to cross callers returns one tenant's response to another: a disclosure path wearing a performance feature's clothes.
distinguishedBy:
Against managed model API consumption: that architecture is about the relationship with one provider. This is about operating the crossing as a platform for many teams and several providers, with the failover, cost attribution and policy uniformity that implies.
Against the internal AI platform: that is the whole paved road, including agent runtimes and data plumbing. This is one component of it, and usually the first one built because it pays for itself immediately.

exemplars.name: Managed AI gateways
exemplars.note: Cloud and CDN-operated gateways offering routing, caching, quotas and observability across multiple model providers behind one endpoint.

exemplars.name: Self-operated proxy layers
exemplars.note: An open-source or in-house proxy standardising on one API shape across providers, with per-team keys, budgets and logging.

blocks.title: Content inside prompts
blocks.note: Whatever the workloads put in context. The gateway sees the text and not the application logic that assembled it, which bounds what its guardrails can conclude.

items.label: Untrusted context
items.note: Documents, records and tool output already mixed into the prompt upstream.

blocks.title: AI workloads
blocks.note: Every AI application, agent and pipeline in the organisation. Whether they can reach a provider without passing through the gateway decides whether this architecture is real.

blocks.title: Gateway endpoint
blocks.note: One API shape across providers, plus the policy pipeline on both legs — redaction on the way out, guardrails on the way out and the way back. The uniform floor beneath every application's own controls.

items.label: Unified API
items.note: One shape across providers, which is what makes routing and failover possible without changing any caller.

items.label: Prompt redaction
items.note: The last chance to stop a secret or an identifier reaching a provider, applied uniformly rather than per team.

items.label: Guardrails, both legs
items.note: Inbound and outbound classification. The return leg is the half most often left unimplemented.

blocks.title: Routing & failover
blocks.note: Selects a provider by capability, cost or availability, fails over when one degrades, and enforces budgets inline. Turns a hard provider dependency into a soft one — and whoever alters the routing steers every application at once.

items.label: Model router
items.note: Provider and version selection against the approved catalogue.

items.label: Budget enforcement
items.note: Inline, per caller — a monthly cost report is not a control on an agent that can loop.

blocks.title: Semantic cache
blocks.note: Reuses responses across similar requests to cut cost and latency. Keyed loosely enough to cross callers, it returns one tenant's data to another — and it will look like a cache hit rather than an incident.

items.label: Cached responses
items.note: Other callers' completions, one loose key away from being yours.

blocks.title: Provider egress
blocks.note: The actual crossing, holding the provider credentials so no workload has to. The reason this tier is the organisation's highest-value AI target: a compromise here is a compromise of every provider relationship at once.

items.label: Credential injection
items.note: The provider credential is attached here and never leaves this tier.

items.label: Egress proxy
items.note: The one place model traffic actually crosses out.

blocks.title: Model providers
blocks.note: Several, deliberately. Multi-provider routing is a resilience property and a negotiating position, and it is only practical because the gateway normalises them.

items.label: Inference APIs
items.note: Published interfaces with versions that deprecate on each provider's own schedule.

blocks.title: Gateway control plane
blocks.note: What makes the data path govern anything: the egress enforcement that makes the gateway the only path, the credential store, budgets, the model catalogue, and the aggregate log — the most sensitive record in the estate, because it is the only complete one.

items.label: Egress enforcement
items.note: Default-deny to model endpoints, gateway excepted. Every other control on this diagram rests on it.

items.label: Provider credentials
items.note: All of them, in one place, rotatable in one operation — concentration as benefit and exposure at once.

items.label: Budgets & quotas
items.note: Per team, per workload, per model — and the cost attribution that usually funds the gateway in the first place.

items.label: Model catalogue
items.note: Which models are approved, pinned and deprecated; one place to roll a provider version change.

items.label: Aggregate telemetry
items.note: Every prompt, response, caller and cost. It needs the access control and retention of a secrets store, not a proxy log.

edges.label: text in prompts
edges.note: Uniform classification for every workload, applied to text without application context — a floor beneath each application's own defences, not a replacement for them.

edges.label: model call / response
edges.note: Per-caller workload identity rather than a shared gateway key, because quota, attribution and the log all key off it. A shared key makes the aggregate view anonymous.
Redacted, admitted requests forward; completions return through the guardrail's output leg.

edges.label: cache lookup
edges.note: The scoping is the control. A key that ignores the caller returns one tenant's response to another, and it will look like a cache hit rather than an incident.
The routed request moves to the crossing; nothing upstream of this point ever saw a provider credential.

edges.label: provider call
edges.note: The credential is injected here and never leaves this tier. One rotation point for the organisation — and one blast radius covering every provider relationship.

edges.label: credentials
edges.note: Provider credentials issued from one store to one tier, with no key in any application's configuration.

edges.label: catalogue & terms
edges.note: The catalogue decides which providers and versions are approved and pinned, so a provider change is a gateway event rather than a migration across every caller.

risks.note: The gateway's entire value is being the only path, and that is a network property; every control here is conditional on egress enforcement holding.
The gateway sees text without the application logic that assembled it, so injection detection here is generic by construction.
A shared gateway key collapses caller identity, making quotas collective and the aggregate log anonymous.
The return leg through the guardrail is the half most often omitted, and the half that catches a model that has been successfully steered.
Budgets enforced inline here are the only brake between a looping agent and per-token billing across every provider.
Whoever alters the routing configuration steers every application's traffic to a model of their choosing.
A poisoned or mis-keyed cache entry serves every later request that matches it, across teams.
A cache key that ignores the caller returns one tenant's response to another, disguised as a performance win.
This tier sees every prompt in the organisation and holds every provider credential — the highest-value AI target in the estate.
One choke point means one outage takes every AI workload with it; failover across providers is the mitigation the gateway itself must supply.
Provider versions change on the provider's schedule; the catalogue's pinning and staged rollout are the one-place answer.

capabilities.note: The platform itself — one API shape, one policy pipeline, one place every model call crosses.
Default-deny egress to model endpoints with the gateway as the sole exception. Deploy this or the rest is a suggestion.
All provider credentials brokered from one store to one tier, rotatable in one operation.
A workload identity per caller, so quota, attribution and the log survive the crossing.
Per-team, per-workload, per-model budgets enforced inline, not reported after the fact.
Uniform detection and masking of secrets and identifiers before anything reaches a provider.
Classification on both legs of the pipeline — and verify the return leg exists, because it usually does not.
Generic injection screening as a uniform floor, with the application-context half of the defence left where the context lives.
Caller-scoped cache keys, so a semantic hit can never cross a tenant boundary.
The aggregate record of every prompt, caller and cost — protected like a secrets store, because it is the most sensitive log in the estate.
The catalogue of approved, pinned and deprecating models, maintained where a version roll is one change.
Provider credentials confined to this tier, unreachable from any workload or any prompt.

steps.note: The call arrives on the caller's own workload identity — the fact everything downstream keys off.
Redacted and admitted, the request is routed against the approved catalogue within budget.
A cache lookup, scoped to the caller — a hit is free, and the scoping is what keeps it legal.
On a miss, the request moves to the crossing.
The provider credential is injected here, for the first and only time.
The completion returns and heads back through the pipeline.
The response passes the output-leg guardrail before the caller ever sees it.
Latency and error rates climb on the primary provider.
Failover reroutes to an approved alternate without changing a single caller — the payoff of one API shape.
The catalogue decides which alternates were approved and pinned in advance; failover is a selection, not a scramble.

scenarios.title: The gateway itself is the prize

steps.note: Every prompt in the organisation passes through this tier — it sees more sensitive data than any single application.
Every provider credential lives behind it; compromise here is compromise of every provider relationship at once.
And a loosely keyed cache quietly hands one tenant's responses to another. The tier deserves a secrets manager's controls, and its outage plan deserves a single-point-of-failure review.

archetypes.title: Text-to-SQL analytics agent
summary: A natural-language interface over a data warehouse that generates and runs queries against live records. The semantic layer is the security control, the query runs as the asking user, and treating either as a convenience is the characteristic mistake.
description:
This is the one archetype where the model composes executable code against production data as its normal mode of operation. Retrieval assistants read a pre-built index; this one writes a query and runs it. That makes the question not "what was indexed" but "what can be expressed" — and filtering generated SQL is not a viable control, because a language rich enough to be useful is rich enough to evade a filter. The semantic layer is the constraint instead: a curated set of tables, columns, joins and metrics the generator may reference, with row-level policy attached. What cannot be named cannot be queried.
The second control is the execution identity. The query runs as the asking user, not as a service account with warehouse-wide read, so the platform's row-level security and column masking apply automatically and the access-control question becomes one the data platform already answers. A service account anywhere on the path turns every generated query into a potential entitlement bypass, and voids every other control on this page. The execution role is read-only, and the cost ceiling is per query, because a generated query can scan the warehouse and the person who asked did not know they were asking for that.
Two quieter surfaces round out the archetype. Result rows re-enter the model for summarisation — which sends live records to the provider and carries customer-entered free text back into the model as context, making the warehouse itself an injection path. And aggregation has no clean preventive answer: a user entitled to aggregates can reconstruct individuals by asking enough narrow questions, each individually legitimate, so the realistic control is detective — query logging and pattern detection over a session.
distinguishedBy:
Against the embedded retrieval assistant: that one retrieves from an index built earlier; this one composes a query against live data. The control moves from index-time permissions to the semantic layer and the execution identity.
Against an AI-augmented API backend: both produce structured output consumed by code, but here the output is executed rather than validated and stored. Schema validation does not help when the schema is "a valid query".

exemplars.name: Warehouse-native analytics agents
exemplars.note: Natural-language querying built into a data platform, executing against a curated semantic model with the platform's own row-level security applied.

exemplars.name: BI assistant layers
exemplars.note: Conversational front ends over an existing BI semantic model, which is the best case: the constraint layer already exists and was built for a different reason.

blocks.title: Analyst
blocks.note: Asks in natural language. Their entitlements should be the whole of what the answer can contain, which is only true if the query runs as them.

blocks.title: Question interface
blocks.note: The conversational surface, and the session every query is attributed to. The identity established here has to reach the execution engine intact.

items.label: Conversation UI
items.note: Where a question becomes a request, and the answer returns as prose.

items.label: Session attribution
items.note: Binds every generated query to the asking user — the identity the warehouse will enforce.

blocks.title: Query generation
blocks.note: Turns the question into a query, given the semantic layer's description of what exists, and turns result rows back into prose. Composes executable code against production data as its normal operation.

items.label: SQL generator
items.note: Prompted with the curated schema and the question — never the full warehouse.

items.label: Constraint check
items.note: Confirms the query references only the semantic layer, is read-only, and is bounded. A safety net over the constraint, not a filter — filtering a query language is a game the filter loses.

items.label: Result summarisation
items.note: Rows become prose here. Row content re-enters the model, which is the injection path that starts in a customer-entered field.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface. It receives the schema description and the question, and later the result rows for summarisation — both directions carry data worth accounting for.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The generated query it returns is executable code from an unauthenticated content channel.

blocks.title: Semantic layer
blocks.note: The curated tables, joins, metrics and row policies the generator may reference — the security control of the archetype. What cannot be named cannot be queried, and adding a table here is granting access to it.

items.label: Curated tables & metrics
items.note: The whole of what the generator is told exists. Curation is authorisation in disguise.

items.label: Row policies & masking
items.note: Attached here, enforced by the platform when the query runs as the user.

items.label: Read-only views
items.note: A generated write would be unrecoverable; the execution role cannot express one.

blocks.title: Warehouse & engine
blocks.note: The execution engine and the live records, including everything outside the semantic layer that should stay unnameable. Most of this archetype's security is the data platform's existing machinery, used properly.

items.label: Query execution as the user
items.note: Runs the query under the analyst's own identity, so row-level security and column masking apply without the application re-implementing them.

items.label: Live records
items.note: Production data, including free-text columns holding customer and partner input.

items.label: Scan & runtime limits
items.note: Per query, enforced by the platform — by the time the query runs, the cost is committed.

blocks.title: Upstream authors
blocks.note: Customers and partners whose free text lands in warehouse columns. Their content is returned in results and summarised back into the model — the injection arrives through data collection, not through the assistant.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Curation, identity propagation, aggregation monitoring and cost ceilings — the decisions that happen away from any single query.

items.label: Semantic-layer curation
items.note: Deciding what is exposed and what stays out. A security review disguised as a data-modelling task, and usually staffed as the latter.

items.label: Identity & entitlements
items.note: Carries the analyst's identity through to execution. One substitution for a service account anywhere on the path voids the entire model.

items.label: Aggregation monitoring
items.note: Watching sequences of individually legitimate queries that together reconstruct individuals. Detective, because there is no preventive answer at query granularity.

items.label: Query cost ceiling
items.note: Per-query scan and runtime limits. A generated query can scan the warehouse, and the person who asked did not know they were asking for that.

edges.label: question / answer
edges.note: The identity established here has to reach the execution engine intact. Everything about this archetype's access control depends on that one property.

edges.label: question / summary
edges.note: The question goes forward with its session identity; the summarised answer comes back.

edges.label: schema & question / generated SQL
edges.note: The curated schema and question go out; executable code comes back from an unauthenticated content channel. Later, result rows make the same trip for summarisation — the leg most often left out of disclosure accounting.

edges.label: schema out / constrained query in
edges.note: The layer describes only what the generator may use, and the generated query is checked against it before execution. Describing the full warehouse and hoping the model behaves is the failure this boundary exists to prevent.

edges.label: query as the asking user
edges.note: Executed under the analyst's identity, so the platform's row-level security and column masking apply. A service account here turns every query into an entitlement bypass. The rows that return are exactly what the analyst was entitled to see.

edges.label: free-text content
edges.note: Customer-entered text lands in columns that will be returned and summarised. The injection arrives through data collection, long before any question is asked.

edges.label: identity, audit & cost limits
edges.note: Identity propagation, the per-session query log and the per-query cost ceiling are all enforced at the platform, where the query actually runs.

risks.note: The model composes executable code against production data as its normal operation. The constraint check, not a SQL filter, is what stands between output and execution.
The analyst's identity has to survive from the question to the engine. One substitution for a service account voids every other control on the page.
The injection path starts in a customer-entered field and ends in an analyst's answer, via rows returned and summarised.
Result rows re-enter the model at summarisation, carrying whatever free text the warehouse collected.
Three disclosures ride this edge: what the schema reveals about the business, the question, and the live result rows sent for summarisation. Only the first is usually accounted for.
Adding a table to the semantic model is granting access to it. Treating curation as data modelling rather than authorisation is the characteristic mistake.
A sequence of legitimate aggregate queries can reconstruct individuals. No single query is wrong, so the control is detective and operates over the session.
A generated query can scan the warehouse. The cost ceiling is per query, because by the time it is running the spend is committed.
A generated write would be unrecoverable. The execution role is read-only so the model cannot express one, whatever it generates.

capabilities.note: Curate the semantic layer as an authorisation surface: what the generator may reference, with row policies attached. What cannot be named cannot be queried.
Propagate the analyst's identity to execution so row-level security and column masking apply — the single most important control on the diagram.
A constraint check on every generated query: references only the semantic layer, read-only, bounded. A verification of the boundary, not a SQL filter.
Per-query scan and runtime ceilings enforced by the platform, sized so one generated query cannot become a financial event.
Classify returned row content before it re-enters the model for summarisation — the rows carry customer-entered text.
Redact result rows before they leave for summarisation; this leg sends live records to the provider and is frequently overlooked.
Log every generated query per session, attributed to the asking user — the record the aggregation analysis runs over.
Detect aggregation patterns across a session — sequences of legitimate queries that together reconstruct individuals.
Know where the sensitive columns are and whether masking covers them — the semantic layer's exclusions are only as good as the classification behind them.
Check the summarised answer against the returned rows before it ships — the summary is the one artifact the analyst will actually read.

steps.note: The question arrives; the session binds it to the analyst's identity.
The question goes to the generator with that identity attached.
The generator is shown only the curated schema — the full warehouse stays unnameable.
Schema and question out; a generated query back, from an unauthenticated channel.
The constraint check confirms the query stays inside the layer, read-only and bounded.
The query runs as the analyst; row-level security and masking apply automatically.
The rows that return are exactly what the analyst was entitled to see.
Those rows make a second trip to the provider for summarisation.
The answer lands as prose, grounded in the returned rows.

scenarios.title: An injection rides a customer record

steps.note: Hostile free text was collected months ago, through an ordinary application.
A legitimate query returns the row among thousands of others.
The row content heads for summarisation as untrusted context.
The hostile text enters the model alongside the instruction to summarise.
A steered summary is the payoff — unless row content was classified before the trip.
A sequence of narrow, individually legitimate questions begins.
Each query passes every check — the entitlements genuinely allow it.
Session-level monitoring is the only control that can see the pattern.

archetypes.title: Batch and offline AI pipeline
summary: Scheduled, high-volume model inference over stored data — enriching records, classifying a backlog, generating embeddings, summarising a corpus. Nobody is watching at runtime, and the output becomes durable state that downstream systems treat as fact.
description:
The distinguishing property is that the output persists and loses its provenance. A synchronous endpoint's mistake affects one response; a batch job's mistake is written into a million records that downstream systems, analysts and other models will read as ground truth for years. By the time anyone notices, the derived data has been copied into three other places.
That makes provenance the primary control rather than a compliance nicety. Every generated field carries which model version produced it, when, from what source and at what confidence — because the only realistic response to a discovered defect is to find and regenerate the affected subset, and that is impossible without the stamp. Poisoning also scales here in a way it does not elsewhere: content that reaches a batch job influences everything the job produces, and each individual bad record looks fine. Sampling and distribution comparison against the previous run are the controls that see it; per-record validation cannot.
Operationally the risks are the mundane ones with unusual severity. Volume plus per-token pricing makes an unbounded job a financial event, retries without idempotency duplicate both cost and output, and there is no user watching to abandon a runaway run — so the budget ceiling is a hard stop enforced from the governance plane, and the pipeline identity is deliberately asymmetric: read on the source, write on the derived store, and nothing else, so a bad run stays recoverable.
distinguishedBy:
Against an AI-augmented API backend: the same transformation on a schedule instead of in a request. Latency stops mattering and durability starts — nobody is waiting, and the output will outlive the job by years.
Against the fine-tuning pipeline: they share the build-system trust properties, but that one produces a model and this one produces data. The data can be corrected in place; the model cannot.

exemplars.name: Bulk enrichment and classification
exemplars.note: Scheduled jobs adding derived fields to a warehouse — sentiment, category, extracted entities — consumed thereafter by analysts and other systems as though they were collected data.

exemplars.name: Embedding generation at corpus scale
exemplars.note: Re-embedding a corpus on a schedule or after a model change. The output is an index, and the job's failure modes are the index's failure modes.

exemplars.name: Provider batch inference tiers
exemplars.note: Discounted asynchronous inference for large volumes, which makes this archetype cheap enough to run over everything and therefore common.

blocks.title: Source authors
blocks.note: Whoever wrote the records being processed — customers, partners, staff, other systems. One hostile input is amplified across everything the run produces.

blocks.title: Schedule
blocks.note: Starts the run with nobody watching. There is no user to notice that the output looks wrong, which is why sampling replaces observation in this archetype.

blocks.title: Source corpus
blocks.note: The records being processed, and the permissions the derived output should inherit. The job reads broader than any individual user ever could.

items.label: Stored records
items.note: Authored long before the pipeline existed, by parties it never authenticates.

items.label: Source permissions
items.note: The access rules the derived output should inherit — and often does not.

blocks.title: Job orchestration
blocks.note: Batching, checkpointing, retries and prompt construction, running under a service identity with no human in the loop. Retry without idempotency duplicates both the output and the bill.

items.label: Batching & checkpoints
items.note: A pipeline that fails halfway leaves the corpus half-treated, which is worse than either outcome alone.

items.label: Prompt construction
items.note: Source content and instruction are concatenated here, at volume, with no review of any result.

items.label: Retry & idempotency
items.note: The mechanism that decides whether a transient failure costs one record or the whole run twice.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published batch inference interface, holding a large volume of the corpus for the duration of the job. Everything behind it is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Batch inference API
items.note: Asynchronous and discounted. Retention terms matter more here than on a per-request path.

blocks.title: Validation & stamping
blocks.note: Per-record checks and the provenance stamp, applied inside the write path where they are true. A stamp added later is a guess.

items.label: Output validation
items.note: Schema conformance and range checks per record. Catches malformed output, not systematic drift — each bad record looks individually plausible.

items.label: Provenance stamp
items.note: Model version, run identifier, timestamp, source record and confidence on every generated field. Without it, regeneration is a full re-run of everything.

blocks.title: Derived data
blocks.note: Generated fields, embeddings and summaries. Nothing about their shape says a model produced them, which is why the stamp travels with the record.

items.label: Generated fields
items.note: Read as facts by every consumer that never sees the pipeline.

items.label: Embeddings & indexes
items.note: Where a poisoned input becomes a durable influence on retrieval.

blocks.title: Downstream consumers
blocks.note: The systems and people that read derived data as collected data — and copy it onward before anyone checks.

items.label: Warehouse & BI
items.note: Analysts querying generated fields alongside measured ones.

items.label: Retrieval indexes
items.note: Derived output feeding another system's context.

items.label: Training sets
items.note: Where unstamped model output quietly becomes training data.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Provenance, sampling, budget and the ability to find and undo what a bad run produced — each enforced outside the pipeline it governs.

items.label: Pipeline identity
items.note: A workload identity with read on the source and write on the derived store, and nothing else. The asymmetry keeps a bad run recoverable.

items.label: Run budget & kill
items.note: A hard token and spend ceiling per run — a stop, not an alert, because nobody is watching.

items.label: Run & lineage registry
items.note: Which run produced which records with which model version. The artifact that makes a targeted rollback possible instead of a full regeneration.

items.label: Sampling & drift review
items.note: Human and automated review of a sample per run, plus distribution comparison against the previous one. The only control that catches systematic error at this volume.

edges.label: authored records
edges.note: Nothing AI-specific gates this, and it happened long before the pipeline existed. One poisoned record becomes an influence on everything the run produces.

edges.label: scheduled run
edges.note: The unattended start. Every run of this architecture begins with a timer, not a person.

edges.label: batched records
edges.note: A read broader than any individual's access, because the job processes everything. Whether the derived output inherits the source's permissions is decided downstream — often not at all.

edges.label: batch submission
edges.note: Carries a large share of the corpus to the provider in one submission, which makes the retention terms on the batch tier a material question rather than boilerplate.

edges.label: results
edges.note: Unauthenticated content arriving at volume, with nobody reading it. Every downstream consumer will treat what survives validation as collected data.

edges.label: stamped output
edges.note: Write access limited to the derived store rather than the source. A pipeline that can overwrite its own inputs makes a defect unrecoverable.

edges.label: read as fact
edges.note: Derived data is indistinguishable from collected data once written, so it flows into dashboards, indexes and training sets that never see the pipeline.

edges.label: sampling & lineage
edges.note: Per-run sampling, drift comparison and the lineage that maps runs to records. The version recorded has to be the version the provider actually served.

edges.label: vendor assurance
edges.note: Retention, training-use and residency terms on the batch tier, assessed before a large share of the corpus is handed over per run.

risks.note: One hostile input is amplified across everything the run produces, then made durable. The pipeline never authenticates who authored its inputs.
Record content and instruction are concatenated at volume, and no human reviews any individual result.
The pipeline identity reads broader than any user, unattended. What the job can see, a misconfigured run can propagate.
Volume, per-token pricing, retries and no human watching. Together they are the most common way this archetype produces an incident that is purely financial.
A single submission carries a large share of the corpus to the provider, and holds it there for the duration of the job.
Unauthenticated content at volume, with nobody reading it. Per-record validation passes records that are individually plausible and systematically wrong.
Amplified and durable. A defect here is read as fact by systems and people who never see the pipeline, and has been copied onward by the time it is found.
Derived data flows into training sets and indexes indistinguishable from collected data. Without the stamp nobody can tell what a model generated.

capabilities.note: Stamp every generated field with model version, run, source and confidence, inside the write path. This is the control everything else depends on.
A hard token and spend ceiling per run, enforced by the platform — there is no user watching to abandon a runaway job.
Compare each run's output distribution against the last. This is what catches a model change or a poisoning campaign that per-record checks cannot see.
A workload identity for the pipeline: read on the source, write on the derived store, nothing else, and rotated rather than pasted.
Scope what the job may read to the dataset approved for the run, and decide explicitly whether derived output inherits the source's permissions.
Filter and sanitise inbound records before they can be batched — the only point where a poisoned example is one record rather than a run's worth of influence.
Classify record content before prompt construction; every record is untrusted input that will be concatenated with instructions.
Schema, range and content checks on every returned record before it can be written — automated, because no human reads batch output.
Human review of a sample per run, before consumers read the batch. The single human touchpoint in this architecture is deliberate and after the fact.
A lineage record per run — dataset, model version, prompt version — so a defect found months later can be scoped to affected records.
Assess the batch tier's retention and training-use terms; the submission holds a large share of the corpus at the vendor for hours.
A stop that halts a mid-flight run and marks its partial output, because half-treated is worse for consumers than untreated.

scenarios.title: A nightly run processes the backlog

steps.note: The timer fires. Nobody is present for anything that follows.
The job reads everything — broader than any user's own access.
A large share of the corpus leaves in one submission, under the run's budget ceiling.
Results return at volume; validation and the provenance stamp are the only checks.
Stamped records land in the derived store — write-scoped, so the source is untouched.
From here on, generated data is read as collected data.

scenarios.title: One poisoned record enters the corpus

steps.note: A hostile input lands among millions of legitimate ones, unauthenticated.
It is batched with everything else and concatenated into a prompt.
Each affected output record is individually plausible; per-record validation passes it.
The influence is now durable, and stamped — which is what will save the cleanup.
Distribution comparison against the previous run is the control that notices.

scenarios.title: A defect is discovered months later

steps.note: The lineage registry maps the defective run and model version to the affected records.
A targeted regeneration run is scheduled over just that subset.
Regenerated records overwrite the defective ones, with a new stamp. Without lineage, this is a full re-run of everything.

archetypes.title: Internal multi-tenant AI platform
summary: The paved road: a shared platform on which internal product teams build AI features, with the gateway, the agent runtime, the data plane and the templates supplied centrally so every tenant inherits controls it did not have to build. The architecture whose unit of concern is the population of workloads rather than any one of them.
description:
Every organisation that gets past its third AI workload builds some version of this, usually after discovering it has three different credential arrangements and no aggregate view. The platform's purpose is to make the governed path the easy path, so that a team choosing the quickest route also chooses the controlled one. That framing produces the design rule: adoption is a security control. A platform teams route around produces worse outcomes than no platform, because it also produces the belief that AI use is governed — so the adoption rate is monitored as carefully as any control on this page.
Tenancy is the hard technical part. Product teams share a gateway, an agent runtime, a vector store and node pools, and the isolation between them is a platform property no tenant can verify. Namespace, network and data isolation each fail differently, and a shared vector store with per-tenant filtering rather than per-tenant separation is a disclosure waiting for a query bug. The drawing keeps the planes honest: the data path is tenants calling shared services; everything in the governance column — tenancy policy, the catalogue, the inventory, evaluations, operator access — is control plane, and it governs only the workloads that actually run here.
The platform's own access is the concentration risk. Platform operators can typically read across tenants by construction, the central log holds every product's prompts, and the shared credential store holds every provider relationship. The platform team's privileges deserve the scrutiny normally reserved for a domain administrator, and they rarely get it. In exchange, this is where organisation-wide controls become possible at all: model approval, evaluation gates, inventory and cost attribution work here and nowhere else, because nowhere else sees all of it.
distinguishedBy:
Against the AI gateway: that is one component of this, and usually the first built. This is the whole paved road — runtime, data plane, templates and standards — with the population problem as its subject.
Against any single application architecture: those describe one workload. This describes the substrate several of them share, and its risks are aggregation, isolation and adoption rather than anything in a request path.

exemplars.name: Internal AI platform teams
exemplars.note: A central team offering gateway, runtime, vector store and templates as a product to internal product teams, with an onboarding path and a support rota.

exemplars.name: Multi-tenant generative AI platform reference designs
exemplars.note: Cloud providers publish this as a named architecture, which is a reasonable indicator that most large organisations converge on it.

blocks.title: Product teams
blocks.note: The tenants. Each builds its own workload, and each can leave the platform if leaving is easier — which is why friction anywhere on this page is a security parameter.

blocks.title: Onboarding & templates
blocks.note: How a team gets started, and the reference implementations it starts from. Slow onboarding produces workloads built somewhere else; the templates are the most effective security artifact the platform ships, and a supply chain into every workload at once.

items.label: Registration
items.note: Entry into the inventory. A team that starts without it is invisible to every governance control here.

items.label: Paved-road templates
items.note: Controls arriving pre-wired — and one reviewed artifact propagating into every tenant's codebase.

blocks.title: Tenant workloads
blocks.note: Whatever each team is building — an assistant, an agent, a pipeline. Each is one of the other architectures in this catalogue, running here and inheriting the platform's controls.

items.label: Assistants & agents
items.note: Per-team products with per-team data, sharing one substrate.

items.label: Batch pipelines
items.note: Unattended tenants of the same shared services.

blocks.title: Shared AI gateway
blocks.note: One crossing to model providers for every tenant, with per-tenant quotas, tenant-tagged telemetry and cost attribution. Described in full as its own architecture; here it is the component every tenant inherits first.

items.label: Provider crossing
items.note: One relationship per provider, used on behalf of every tenant.

items.label: Per-tenant quotas
items.note: One tenant's loop must not be everyone's budget.

items.label: Tenant-tagged telemetry
items.note: Tagged so a team can see its own traffic without seeing everyone's.

blocks.title: Shared agent runtime
blocks.note: A common place to run agents, with sandboxing, workload identity and observability supplied. Tenants inherit controls they did not build — and an isolation guarantee they cannot verify.

items.label: Tenant execution
items.note: Every tenant's agents on shared infrastructure, separated by platform-asserted isolation.

items.label: Sandboxed execution
items.note: Isolation supplied by the platform rather than rebuilt per team.

blocks.title: Shared data plane
blocks.note: Vector stores, memory and state for several tenants in one system. Per-tenant separation means a bug returns nothing; per-tenant filtering means a bug returns another tenant's data — and the difference only shows up when something goes wrong.

items.label: Shared vector store
items.note: Several tenants' embeddings, one query bug from crossing.

items.label: Memory & state
items.note: Keying is the whole of the isolation; a key that omits the tenant collapses it silently.

blocks.title: Model providers
blocks.note: Several, consumed on behalf of every tenant through one relationship each. Everything behind the published interfaces is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference APIs
items.note: Reached only through the shared gateway, on the platform's credentials.

blocks.title: Platform governance
blocks.note: The organisation-wide controls that are only possible because one place sees everything: tenancy policy, the model catalogue, the workload inventory and adoption signal, shared evaluation, and the central log with the operator access that reads across every tenant.

items.label: Tenancy & isolation policy
items.note: Stated and tested by the platform team, because no tenant can verify it — a guarantee, not a wiki claim.

items.label: Model catalogue
items.note: Which models any tenant may use, at which versions, with which terms — enforceable only because there is one gateway.

items.label: Inventory & adoption
items.note: Every workload, its owner, its data and its risk class — plus what fraction of AI workloads actually run here, tracked as a security metric.

items.label: Shared evaluation service
items.note: Adversarial and safety testing offered as a service, which is why teams actually do it.

items.label: Central log & operator access
items.note: Every tenant's prompts in one place, readable by a platform team whose privileges deserve domain-administrator scrutiny.

edges.label: build & operate
edges.note: Each team ships and runs its own product on the shared substrate.

edges.label: paved-road start
edges.note: Registration puts the workload in the inventory and the template wires the controls in before the first line of product code.

edges.label: model calls
edges.note: Per-tenant workload identity on every call, because quota, cost attribution and the log all key off it. A shared platform credential makes every downstream record anonymous.

edges.label: agent execution
edges.note: Agents run on shared infrastructure under isolation the tenant cannot test — which is why the tenancy policy has to be stated and verified by the platform.
Runtime-hosted agents make their model calls through the same crossing as everything else, attributed per tenant.

edges.label: retrieval & state
edges.note: Separation versus filtering is decided on this edge. Separation means a bug returns nothing; filtering means a bug returns another tenant's data.

edges.label: provider call
edges.note: One relationship per provider used on behalf of every tenant — concentration as the benefit and the exposure at once.

edges.label: catalogue & quotas
edges.note: The approved-model catalogue and per-tenant ceilings are enforced at the one crossing, which is the only reason an organisation-wide model policy can exist at all.

edges.label: tenancy & entitlements
edges.note: Isolation guarantees and data entitlements applied to the shared stores — tested and published by the platform team, because the tenants cannot test them.

risks.note: A slow or restrictive onboarding produces workloads built somewhere else, with none of these controls and full confidence that AI use is governed.
Templates are a supply chain into every tenant's codebase; a flaw here propagates platform-wide.
Gateway, runtime, vector store and memory all share tenants, and each isolates differently — tenancy is a claim about four systems at once.
Shared node pools put every tenant on common physical substrate, below every namespace boundary.
Per-tenant filtering in a shared store is one query bug away from returning another tenant's records.
A poisoned embedding in a shared index steers retrieval for whichever tenant matches it.
One tenant's runaway loop spends against the organisation's provider relationships unless per-tenant ceilings hold.
Every tenant's prompts cross to providers through one relationship, under terms the platform negotiated once for all of them.
The catalogue is the organisation-wide model supply chain; whoever writes it decides what every tenant serves.
Platform operators can read across tenants by construction, and the central log holds every product's prompts — domain-administrator privileges without the name.

capabilities.note: The shared crossing, built once — the first platform component because it pays for itself immediately.
Per-tenant workload identity on every call, so attribution, quotas and the log never collapse into one anonymous principal.
Registration at onboarding is the inventory entry; nothing the platform governs exists outside it.
Sandboxed execution supplied by the platform, so tenant isolation is engineered once instead of assumed twenty times.
Per-tenant separation over per-tenant filtering wherever the data warrants it, decided as policy rather than left to schema convenience.
Tenant-scoped retrieval with entitlement checks at query time, because the vector store serves everyone.
Per-tenant token and spend ceilings, plus the cost attribution that keeps the platform funded.
Templates with the controls pre-wired, so the quickest start is also the governed one.
Posture across the whole estate — every workload, its models, its data and its drift — possible only where everything is visible.
Evaluation as a shared service; a policy requiring testing without supplying a harness produces evidence rather than testing.
Domain-administrator scrutiny on platform operator access, because the team that runs the platform can read every tenant by construction.
Monitor adoption and drift — which teams left and why — because a workload that left has none of these controls.

scenarios.title: A team onboards onto the paved road

steps.note: A product team starts building. The platform's job is to be the quickest way to do this.
Registration enters the workload in the inventory; the template arrives with controls pre-wired.
The first model call goes out attributed, quota'd and logged per tenant, with nothing extra built.
The provider is reached through the organisation's one governed relationship.
Tenant A's agent executes on infrastructure tenant B also uses.
Retrieval hits the shared store — separation returns nothing on a bug, filtering returns tenant B's data.
The tenancy policy is the platform's answer, tested and published, because neither tenant can verify it.
Both tenants' model calls stay individually attributed through the same crossing.
Friction at onboarding sends the next team elsewhere — the leak starts here, not at the firewall.
The catalogue, the quotas and the aggregate view now cover a shrinking fraction of the organisation's AI use.
The teams that left still ship — ungoverned, uninventoried, and officially believed to be covered. Adoption is the multiplier on every control on this page.
