archetypes.title: Managed agent runtime
summary: A cloud provider's hosted agent service: the loop, the memory, the sandbox and the tool gateway supplied as published, separately billed products, with the customer owning the front end, the agent definitions, the tools admitted, the identities and the audit export. The governance plane arrives built in, and the trade is that it is configured rather than designed.
description:
Every provider converged on the same decomposition: a runtime, a memory service, a tool gateway, an identity service, a code interpreter and browser, observability, evaluation and policy. That convergence is itself the finding — the governance plane most self-built agent architectures never get is exactly what these services sell. The provider blocks on this diagram are drawn because they are documented, separately addressable products, not inferred internals; the loop's execution behind them remains genuinely uninspectable.
The consequential choice is between the managed harness and the code escape hatch. Every provider offers both: a declarative agent whose loop they run, and a bring-your-own-code runtime where they supply the sandbox and the identity but the loop is the customer's. The first inherits the platform's guardrails automatically; the second inherits only what it explicitly calls. Teams routinely start with the first, hit a limitation, move to the second, and do not notice which controls stopped applying.
Managed memory is the component most likely to be switched on without a decision. Its scope — per session, per user, or shared across users — is a configuration flag with a data-protection consequence, and cross-user scope means one user's content can shape another's turn.
The genuine advantage is agent identity: first-class, revocable principals distinct from the service and from the user, supplied as a service. Using them properly — rather than collapsing everything onto one service principal — is most of what separates a well-governed deployment from a poorly governed one on the same platform. The costs are portability and opacity: the policy language moves to no other provider, and debugging a misbehaviour means reading traces rather than code.
distinguishedBy:
Against building the agent tier: the same components with the provider supplying them. The work moves from designing an identity model, a policy engine and a sandbox to configuring three, and from having to build observability to having to export it.
Against a vendor in-app action agent: that agent belongs to a SaaS product and acts on its records. This is a platform for building the customer's own agents on the customer's own data, with the loop hosted rather than the application.

exemplars.name: Hyperscaler agent runtimes
exemplars.note: Managed agent services decomposed into runtime, memory, gateway, identity, sandbox, observability, evaluation and policy, billed per component.

exemplars.name: Managed harness with a code escape hatch
exemplars.note: A declarative agent the provider runs, alongside a bring-your-own-code runtime for cases the declarative form cannot express. The pair is now standard across providers.

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: Whose identity should reach the tool call, rather than being replaced by the agent's along the way.

blocks.title: Agent definition & code
blocks.note: The deployable artifact that decides what the agent may do — instructions, tool configuration, or the customer's own loop code. Treating it with less rigour than application code is common and unwarranted.

items.label: Declarative definition
items.note: Instructions and tool bindings the provider's harness runs, inheriting platform guardrails automatically.

items.label: Custom loop code
items.note: The escape hatch. It inherits only the controls it explicitly calls.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: The customer's surface, where the user's identity is established — and where output handling still belongs, because only the application knows where the text will land.

items.label: App & API surface
items.note: The published entry point users and systems call.

items.label: User identity
items.note: Established here and carried into the runtime, or the agent acts as itself for everyone.

blocks.title: Managed runtime
blocks.note: The hosted loop, invoked and configured through published interfaces; the execution itself is not inspectable. Provider code in the path, released on the provider's schedule, with the customer's agent inside it.

items.label: Runtime API
items.note: Where agents are invoked and sessions managed — the published surface over an unreadable loop.

items.label: Declarative harness
items.note: The provider runs the loop and applies guardrails automatically.

items.label: Custom-code runtime
items.note: The customer's loop in the provider's container — sandbox and identity supplied, guardrails only on request.

blocks.title: Managed memory
blocks.note: A documented, separately billed memory service whose scope — session, user or cross-user — is selected by configuration. Cross-user scope means one user's content reaches another's turn, and it is a flag rather than a design review.

items.label: Memory store
items.note: What the agent keeps between turns and reads back as context.

items.label: Scope configuration
items.note: The whole control, in one flag.

blocks.title: Managed sandbox
blocks.note: Code interpreter and hosted browser, isolated by the provider. Among the strongest reasons to choose a managed runtime over building the tier — and the isolation guarantee is a vendor claim the customer cannot test.

items.label: Code interpreter
items.note: Generated code runs here, not in the application's process.

items.label: Hosted browser
items.note: Web content is fetched and rendered inside the provider's isolation.

blocks.title: Managed tool gateway
blocks.note: The provider's brokered path to tools and MCP servers, with scoping and logging supplied. Reached automatically by a declarative agent and only on request by custom code — the asymmetry deployments most often lose coverage to.

items.label: Scoped tool brokering
items.note: Per-tool grants under the agent's own identity, not a service-wide credential.

items.label: MCP & connectors
items.note: The tool population the customer admits — the part of the tool plane the customer owns.

blocks.title: Customer systems
blocks.note: The records the agent acts on under grants the customer issues, and the external content it reads — which comes back as context nothing has authenticated.

items.label: Business records
items.note: Reached under grants issued to the platform, ideally per tool and per agent.

items.label: External content
items.note: Documents and pages the agent reads; the platform's guardrails see it, nothing vouches for it.

blocks.title: Customer governance
blocks.note: The controls the customer owns on a platform the provider operates: agent identities, tool and agent admission, policy and guardrail configuration, evaluation gates, and the audit export that keeps the trail out of the provider's console alone.

items.label: Agent identities
items.note: A first-class, revocable principal per agent — supplied by the platform and frequently collapsed back into one shared principal by teams who do not use it.

items.label: Agent & tool admission
items.note: Which definitions may deploy and which tools may be offered. Admission, not discovery.

items.label: Policy & guardrail config
items.note: Authored by the customer, enforced by the provider inside a loop the customer cannot see.

items.label: Evaluation gates
items.note: An agent definition that has not faced adversarial input should not reach a production alias.

items.label: Audit export
items.note: Traces exported out of the provider's console, so they can be correlated with everything else.

edges.label: request / response
edges.note: The user's identity is established here and must be carried the rest of the way, or per-user authorization silently becomes a service-wide grant.

edges.label: invoke agent
edges.note: Two identities on one call — the application's and the user it acts for. Dropping the second is the confused-deputy failure this architecture makes easy to avoid and easy to commit.

edges.label: deploy
edges.note: An agent definition is a deployable artifact that decides what the agent may do. It deserves the same review, gating and provenance as application code.

edges.label: session & memory
edges.note: The scope flag on this edge is the whole control. Cross-user scope is a supported configuration whose consequence is one user's content shaping another's turn.

edges.label: code & browsing
edges.note: Generated code and web rendering go to provider-operated isolation rather than anywhere nearer the data.
Automatic for a declarative agent, opt-in for custom code. The controls on this edge are the ones the escape hatch silently drops.

edges.label: tool calls / content
edges.note: Actions land on customer systems under per-tool grants; whatever is read comes back as context indistinguishable from instruction.

edges.label: identity & admission
edges.note: Per-agent principals and the admitted tool list are applied here — where the managed identity earns its place, and where one shared principal undoes it.

edges.label: scope configuration
edges.note: Memory scope is decided here as a reviewed policy choice, not left as a default.

risks.note: Three identities are in play — the application's, the user's and the agent's — and the failure is collapsing them into one.
A managed runtime makes agents cheap to create, so the population grows faster than the inventory.
The runtime, its memory, its gateway and its sandbox are the provider's code in the path, released on the provider's schedule.
The loop is not inspectable; traces are the only window, and they only exist where the platform emits them.
Cross-user memory scope puts one user's content in another user's turn, selected by a configuration flag.
Content read through tools re-enters the loop as context; the platform's guardrails see it, nothing authenticates it.
Consequential writes on customer systems from a loop nobody watches, bounded only by the grants and policy the customer configured.
Revocable per-agent principals only help if revocation actually happens when agents are retired or repurposed.
The admitted tool list programs the agents; whoever writes it decides what every agent can be made to do.
The runtime's response is unauthenticated content, and only the application knows whether it is about to be rendered or executed.

capabilities.note: Use the platform's per-agent identities — distinct, revocable principals — instead of collapsing every agent onto one service principal.
Establish the user's identity here and propagate it to the tool call, so authorization stays per-user.
Per-tool, per-agent grants configured at the gateway, not a standing credential shared by everything.
Admit and inventory agent definitions like deployable code, because that is what they are.
Verify guardrail coverage on the custom-code path explicitly — declarative agents get it free, the escape hatch does not.
Set memory scope per session or per user as a reviewed decision; treat cross-user scope as a design exception.
Keep code execution and browsing in the provider's isolation as the only path, not an option.
Author per-invocation policy the platform enforces inside the loop — the customer's half of the shared-responsibility shape.
Traces of steps, tool calls and decisions are the only window into an unreadable loop; turn all of it on.
Export the trail — a trace that lives only in the provider's console cannot be correlated with anything else.
Gate every definition change behind adversarial evaluation before it reaches a production alias.
The isolation guarantee is a vendor claim the customer cannot test; assure it the way any critical vendor control is assured.

scenarios.title: A user's request becomes a tool call

steps.note: The user's identity is established at the customer's own surface.
The invocation carries two identities — the application's and the user's.
The loop plans; the tool call leaves under the agent's own principal, scoped per tool.
The action lands on customer systems under the grant the customer issued.
Whatever was read returns as context nothing has authenticated.
The response comes back; output handling is still the application's job.

scenarios.title: A team takes the code escape hatch

steps.note: The declarative definition is replaced with custom loop code after hitting a limitation.
Tool brokering now happens only if the code calls the gateway — nothing routes it there automatically.
The guardrails and scoping the declarative harness applied for free now apply only where the code asks. Nobody notices which controls stopped.
User A's turn runs, and the agent writes what it learned.
The write lands in a store whose scope flag was left at a shared default.
User B's turn reads it back as context — one user's content shaping another's session, looking like a feature.

archetypes.title: Managed model API consumption
summary: Consuming a cloud provider's hosted models as a dependency of applications the organisation operates: every caller reaches the provider through one gateway, on brokered credentials, under quotas, with the data-handling terms and version policy owned in one place. The most common AI architecture there is, and the one most often treated as a library call rather than a boundary crossing.
description:
This is drawn as its own architecture because it is the shared substrate beneath most cloud AI workloads, and the decisions made here are made once and inherited by all of them. Where the gateway sits, how the credential is issued, whether redaction is on the request path and whether the log is complete are properties of this layer, not of each application above it.
The essential move is that the provider is a boundary and the crossing needs one place. A model call made directly from each service with an SDK and a key in a config map produces no complete log, no consistent policy and no single place to rotate. Consolidating on a gateway turns a scattered dependency into a governed one, and it is much cheaper before there are twenty callers than after. The gateway is a convention until network egress makes it the only reachable path.
The provider-side controls are real and worth using: managed guardrails, abuse monitoring, content filtering, regional routing and retention configuration all exist and all cost less than building equivalents. They are also configuration the consumer authors and the provider enforces — the classic shared-responsibility shape — and their defaults are usually permissive.
Three things catch organisations out: data handling terms, model version churn and cost. What the provider retains and whether it trains on inputs is a contract question with a per-service answer. Versions are deprecated on the provider's schedule, so pinning and a tested upgrade path are availability controls. And a token-metered dependency with no quota is an open financial commitment reachable from anything that can loop.
distinguishedBy:
Against self-hosted inference: the same capability with the serving tier, the supply chain and the capacity problem on the provider's side. Almost every control in that architecture is replaced here by a contract term and a configuration setting.
Against the AI gateway architecture: that one is about operating the gateway as a platform for many teams and several providers. This is about the consuming relationship itself, and the two are usually built in that order.

exemplars.name: Cloud provider model services
exemplars.note: Hyperscaler-hosted model endpoints with managed guardrails, regional routing and account-level data-handling terms, reached with the account's own identity system.

exemplars.name: Direct provider APIs
exemplars.note: A model vendor's own API, reached with a provider-issued key. Fewer platform controls, and the credential is not part of the organisation's existing identity fabric.

blocks.title: Context from elsewhere
blocks.note: Whatever the applications put in context — documents, tickets, tool output. This layer cannot tell trusted from untrusted, which is why gateway-level guardrails are a backstop rather than the primary defence.

items.label: Untrusted content
items.note: Arrives already mixed into prompts by the applications above.

blocks.title: Application users
blocks.note: The people using whatever the applications build on top of this dependency.

blocks.title: Agents & pipelines
blocks.note: Unattended callers that can loop. Against a token-metered dependency, retry logic without a ceiling is an open financial commitment.

blocks.title: Application services
blocks.note: Many callers, written by different teams at different times. Whether they can reach the provider directly — rather than only through the gateway — decides whether this architecture holds.

items.label: Service callers
items.note: Every service that wants a completion, each with its own deadline pressure.

items.label: Prompt assembly
items.note: Where system instruction, context and user turn combine. Only this layer knows which part it assembled and which arrived from elsewhere.

items.label: Output handling
items.note: Context-correct treatment of completions, because only the application knows where the text is about to be rendered or executed.

blocks.title: Model gateway
blocks.note: One egress point for model traffic: routing, per-caller quotas, redaction and a complete log. The difference between one governed dependency and twenty ungoverned ones.

items.label: Model routing
items.note: Approved, pinned versions — one place to test and roll an upgrade.

items.label: Prompt redaction
items.note: The last chance to stop a secret or an identifier crossing the boundary.

items.label: Per-caller quotas
items.note: A retry loop in one service must not be able to exhaust the account.

items.label: Call log tap
items.note: Complete only because everything crosses in one place.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published interfaces: inference, managed guardrails, and the data-handling configuration surface. Everything behind them is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: A version identifier with a deprecation date attached to it.

items.label: Managed guardrails
items.note: Configured by the consumer, enforced by the provider, permissive by default.

items.label: Data-handling controls
items.note: Retention, training use and region — configuration the consumer authors and cannot verify.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Where the consuming relationship is owned: the credential broker, the spend policy, the version registry and its evaluation gate, the usage log, and the contract terms that are the only control over what the provider retains.

items.label: Credential broker
items.note: Short-lived, per-workload credentials. The provider key never appears in any application's configuration.

items.label: Quota & spend policy
items.note: Per-caller token and cost ceilings, enforced at the gateway rather than trusted to each caller.

items.label: Version registry & evals
items.note: A provider version becomes approved by passing tests, not by being available.

items.label: Usage & prompt log
items.note: What was sent, by whom, to which model, at what cost.

items.label: Data-handling terms
items.note: Retention, training use, region and subprocessors — per service and per tier, re-read when the provider ships a new product.

edges.label: untrusted context
edges.note: Content assembled into prompts from documents, tickets and tool output. Only the application knows which parts it wrote and which arrived from elsewhere.

edges.label: request / response
edges.note: The application experience this whole dependency exists to serve.

edges.label: unattended calls
edges.note: Loops and schedules that call the model with nobody watching the bill.

edges.label: model call
edges.note: The application proves what it is with a workload identity; the provider credential never reaches it. That is what makes per-caller quota and attribution possible at all.

edges.label: brokered call
edges.note: Out on a short-lived brokered credential, redacted and logged; back as a completion whose transport is authenticated and whose content is not.

edges.label: credentials & limits
edges.note: The broker issues per-call credentials and the spend policy sets per-caller ceilings — one rotation point and one brake, instead of one per service.

edges.label: terms & version policy
edges.note: The contract is the only control over what the provider does with what it receives, and the version registry tracks deprecations that arrive on the provider's schedule.

risks.note: Context assembled from documents and tool output is a steering surface the gateway sees only as text.
Any service that can reach the internet can reach a model provider. Everything on this diagram depends on egress policy making the gateway the only available path.
Unattended callers that can loop meet per-token billing on the other side of this boundary.
A shared key instead of per-workload identity makes every downstream record anonymous and every quota collective.
A metered dependency with no ceiling is an open financial commitment; the quota here is the only brake.
Everything in the prompt crosses the boundary. Redaction on this edge is the last chance to stop a secret leaving.
What the provider retains and for how long is a contract term, not an observable property.
Whether inputs feed training is a per-service, per-tier answer that changes when the provider ships a new product.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and only the application knows whether it is about to be rendered, executed or stored.
Model versions change under the consumer on the provider's schedule; pinning, evaluation and staged rollout together are the answer.

capabilities.note: One crossing for all model traffic — routing, quotas, redaction and the log in a single place.
Default-deny to model endpoints with the gateway as the sole exception. Without it the gateway is a convention, and conventions lose to deadlines.
Provider credentials brokered at call time, short-lived, with one rotation point for the organisation.
A workload identity per calling service, so quota, attribution and the log all key off who actually called.
Per-caller token and spend ceilings enforced at the crossing, not trusted to each caller's retry logic.
Detect and mask secrets and identifiers on the way out, uniformly rather than per team.
A complete record of every call — complete only because there is exactly one crossing.
Configure the managed guardrails deliberately; the defaults are permissive and the enforcement is the provider's.
Own the data-handling terms — retention, training use, region, subprocessors — per service and per tier.
Re-test behaviour when the provider ships a new version; a model upgrade is a dependency upgrade with no diffable changelog.
A registry of which provider models and versions are approved, pinned and nearing deprecation.
Find the services calling providers directly, because the population grows faster than the architecture diagram.

scenarios.title: A model call crosses the boundary

steps.note: A user request becomes a prompt — system instruction, context, user turn.
The call arrives on a workload identity; the quota and the log key off it.
Redacted, logged, and sent on a brokered credential that expires.
The completion returns — authenticated transport, unauthenticated content.
The application handles the output for its own context; only it knows where the text lands.

scenarios.title: A retry loop meets per-token billing

steps.note: An unattended pipeline starts looping on an error path.
The per-caller quota is the brake — one service's loop cannot exhaust the account.
Within-ceiling traffic proceeds; the rest is refused at the crossing, not on the invoice.
The deprecation lands in the version registry on the provider's schedule, not yours.
The replacement version passes evaluation, then the pin rolls at the gateway — one change instead of twenty.
Callers are unchanged; the upgrade was a gateway event, which is the payoff of the whole architecture.

archetypes.title: Embedded retrieval assistant
summary: A conversational surface inside an application you operate, answering from your own corpus by retrieving context at query time and grounding a model response in it. The most common production AI architecture, and the one where the index is the trust boundary.
description:
Two pipelines meet at the index and they have different threat models. The query pipeline runs per request: the front end authenticates the user, orchestration retrieves context and assembles a prompt, the gateway carries it to the model, and the answer renders back. The ingest pipeline runs offline on a schedule, reads the systems of record under a service identity, chunks and embeds, and writes the index. Almost every serious failure in this architecture is a mismatch between what the two pipelines assume.
The index is a second copy of your data with its own permissions model. The source has ACLs a decade of access reviews has shaped; the index has whatever the ingest pipeline chose to carry over, evaluated whenever it last ran. Retrieval-time filtering against live entitlements is the control that keeps the two in step — an index filtered after fetching has already put the content into the process assembling the prompt.
Retrieved content is untrusted input. It lands in the same context window as the system instruction and the user's question, and where the corpus contains anything a third party can write — tickets, uploads, reviews, mail — retrieval is an injection path that reaches every user who later asks a related question. The contrast with the action-agent architectures is that outputs here are answers rather than writes, which is why the control set is grounding, encoding and entitlement filtering rather than approval gates and reversibility.
distinguishedBy:
Against an autonomous action agent: this architecture answers, that one acts. Adding a single tool that mutates a record moves an assistant into that architecture and its entire control set, which is why the boundary is worth naming rather than blurring.
Against the tenant-wide vendor assistant: the same user-facing capability with every control point on the opposite side of the boundary. Here you own the index, the retrieval-time ACL check, the guardrails and the logs, and the work is designing them.

exemplars.name: In-product help and knowledge assistants
exemplars.note: A panel inside an application answering from that product's documentation and the tenant's own records. The most common shipped form of this architecture.

exemplars.name: Internal knowledge assistants
exemplars.note: Built on a managed model API plus a vector store, over a wiki, a ticket system and a document repository. Usually the first AI system an organisation operates itself, and usually built before anyone has asked the retrieval-time-ACL question.

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: An authenticated user of the application, with entitlements the answer must respect. The assistant is only as scoped as the identity that survives into retrieval.

blocks.title: Content authors
blocks.note: Anyone who can write into an indexed source — a customer filing a ticket, a colleague uploading a file, an external system syncing records. Their text is model input later.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: Authenticates the caller, validates the turn and applies quotas before anything reaches retrieval. The user's identity has to survive this hop or the retriever cannot filter.

items.label: App & API endpoint
items.note: The published surface, and where per-user rate and cost limits belong.

items.label: Identity & input checks
items.note: Who is asking, and classification of the turn. Catches the direct injection attempt and none of the indirect one, which is the more common of the two.

blocks.title: Query orchestration
blocks.note: Assembles the prompt from system instruction, retrieved context, conversation state and the user's turn — the component that decides what the model is allowed to see, and the one that checks and encodes what comes back.

items.label: Prompt assembly
items.note: Merges instruction, context and turn into one prompt the model cannot tell apart.

items.label: Retriever
items.note: Selects context for this turn. The last point at which content can be excluded rather than merely dropped after fetching.

items.label: Grounding & encoding
items.note: Checks the answer against what was actually retrieved, then encodes it for wherever it lands. Both halves are skipped together when a demo works without them.

blocks.title: Index & session state
blocks.note: A second copy of the corpus with its own permission model and its own freshness — the trust boundary of this architecture, and the asset most worth threat modelling on its own.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: What every future answer is grounded in. Write access here deserves deploy-credential scrutiny.

items.label: Conversation state
items.note: Session-scoped and per-user. A cache keyed loosely enough to collide across users leaks by construction.

blocks.title: AI gateway & guardrails
blocks.note: One enforcement point in front of every model call: routing, quotas, content policy, and the log of what was actually sent. A gateway that traffic can go around is not a gateway.

items.label: Content guardrails
items.note: Policy on the assembled prompt and on the completion, applied in the request path.

items.label: Credential broker
items.note: The gateway holds the provider credential so no application service has to.

items.label: Rate & cost limits
items.note: The brake on per-token spend, enforced where every call passes.

items.label: Logging tap
items.note: Records what was sent and returned, without asking the application to volunteer it.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface. Everything behind it is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The prompt leaves your tier with whatever context retrieval put into it.

blocks.title: Sources & ingest
blocks.note: The offline half: systems of record read on a schedule by connectors, chunked, embedded and written to the index. Its permission decisions are frozen into the index until it runs again.

items.label: Systems of record
items.note: The authoritative content and the authoritative permissions.

items.label: Source connectors
items.note: Read on a service identity whose reach is broader than any single user's — by design, which is what makes the retrieval-time filter mandatory.

items.label: Chunk & embed
items.note: Whatever permission metadata is not carried across here cannot be enforced at query time, however good the retriever is.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Identity, evaluation, audit and posture — the full set, because the operating organisation runs this system itself. This is what the equivalent SaaS deployment does not have and cannot obtain.

items.label: Identity provider
items.note: Establishes the user and the entitlements the retriever filters against.

items.label: Evaluation & red teaming
items.note: Continuous adversarial testing against the live index, because the corpus changes daily and a pre-launch result expires with it.

items.label: Audit sink
items.note: Prompts, retrieved document ids and responses. Retrieved ids are the part most often omitted and the part an investigation needs first.

items.label: AI posture management
items.note: Inventory of models, indexes and endpoints in use, and their configuration drift.

edges.label: question / answer
edges.note: The question carries the identity the retriever must filter against; the rendered answer comes back encoded for where it lands.
The user's identity has to survive this hop or the retriever cannot filter. Dropping to a service identity here is the single most common cause of over-broad retrieval.

edges.label: filtered retrieval
edges.note: Two distinct questions: what the service may read, and what this user may see. Only the second is per request, and only the second stops one user's question returning another's document.

edges.label: prompt / completion
edges.note: Every model call passes through the gateway's policy, limits and logging. There is no side door.
Inference on a brokered, expiring credential. The transport is authenticated and the completion is not — everything downstream treats it as untrusted input.

edges.label: authored content
edges.note: The existing write path into the systems of record. Nothing here knows the content will later be read by a model on behalf of a different user.

edges.label: embeddings & metadata
edges.note: Write access to the index is write access to what every future answer is grounded in. It deserves the scrutiny of a production deploy credential, and rarely gets it.

edges.label: policy & credentials
edges.note: Gateway policy is authored in the governance plane and enforced in the request path.

edges.label: evaluation
edges.note: Model and prompt changes pass an evaluation gate before they serve traffic.

risks.note: Injection enters at authoring time, through a pipeline that runs days earlier, and surfaces in another user's answer.
Whoever can write embeddings decides what every future answer is grounded in.
The index's permissions are whatever ingest carried over. Without a live entitlement filter, one user's question returns another's document.
The connector's standing grant is broader than any user's access, and its scope sets the maximum reach of a retrieval-time filtering mistake.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and it drives what renders to the user.
Per-token inference behind a per-request surface makes unbounded input a financial exposure.
Conversation state keyed loosely enough to collide across users leaks by construction.
Embedding models, vector stores and retrieval libraries are third-party code in the request path, and the index format is a deserialization surface.

capabilities.note: Retrieval-time filtering against live entitlements — enforced before fetching, not by dropping content after it.
Classify retrieved content as untrusted before it enters prompt assembly.
Harden the index: write-path least privilege, permission metadata, freshness checks.
Sanitize content and carry permission metadata across at ingest, where exclusion is still cheap.
One enforcement point in the path of every model call — routing, quotas, policy, logging.
Content policy on the assembled prompt and on the completion, applied per call.
Check the answer against what was actually retrieved before rendering it.
Per-user quotas and cost ceilings at the edge, before token spend is committed.
Brokered, short-lived credentials for the model API and the connectors — no keys at rest in services.
Log prompts, retrieved document ids and responses; the ids are what an investigation needs first.
Continuous adversarial evaluation against the live index, through the same gateway traffic uses.

steps.note: The question arrives with the identity the whole pipeline must preserve.
The authenticated turn enters orchestration with its entitlements intact.
Retrieval filters against live entitlements — the last point content can be excluded.
The assembled prompt passes gateway policy and logging.
Inference on a brokered credential; the completion returns as untrusted content.
The grounded, encoded answer renders back to the user.
A third party writes instructions into a ticket or document, days before any query.
The ingest pipeline embeds it and writes it into the index like any other content.
A related question from any user retrieves the poisoned chunk into their prompt.
The injected text sits beside the system instruction with nothing marking it apart.
The model follows whichever instruction it takes to be authoritative.
Permission decisions are frozen into the index at ingest time.
The retrieval-time entitlement filter is the only control that keeps pace with revocations.
The answer is exactly as scoped as that filter — no more, and no less.

archetypes.title: Remote MCP server you publish
summary: A tool server operated as a service for other people's agents: an OAuth resource server whose clients are language models. The scopes, the tenancy and the tool descriptions are all your design decisions — and the descriptions execute as instruction inside somebody else's model.
description:
The inversion is what makes this its own architecture. Every other cloud archetype here calls tools; this one is the tool. The caller is an autonomous agent acting for a user, the arguments were produced by a model, and the tool descriptions this server publishes become instructions inside that model's context. A poorly worded description causes misuse; a deliberately worded one is an attack on the caller. Publishing a server means treating changes to descriptions and error messages with the seriousness of an API contract change.
Authorization is the second inversion. Standard OAuth answers "may this client act for this user", and here that is necessary and not sufficient: the client is an agent that may have been steered by content it read elsewhere. Scopes therefore need to be narrow enough that a hijacked agent's blast radius is bounded, and consequential operations need confirmation semantics the protocol can express, rather than relying on the client to prompt its user.
The operational shape is otherwise a well-understood multi-tenant service, and the ordinary disciplines apply with unusual force: every read and write checks both that the scope permits the operation and that the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record; rate limits are sized for machine callers that retry, loop and parallelise; and results are bounded in size, because an oversized result is both a cost problem for the caller and a way to crowd their context window. There is no model anywhere in this service — every distinctive control follows from the client being one.
distinguishedBy:
Against a third-party MCP server you consume: opposite side of the same boundary. There the scopes are someone else's design and the work is admission and observation; here the scopes, the tenancy and the descriptions are all design decisions.
Against an AI-augmented API backend: that one has AI inside it and a conventional client. This one has no AI inside it at all and a model as the client. The security work is entirely about the caller's nature.

exemplars.name: Product MCP servers
exemplars.note: SaaS vendors publishing remote tool servers for their own products so customer agents can act without a bespoke integration.

exemplars.name: Internal MCP servers
exemplars.note: The same pattern inside one organisation, exposing internal systems to internal agents. Same architecture, and the temptation to skip the authorization work is much stronger.

blocks.title: Delegating user
blocks.note: The person the calling agent acts for, and the source of the authorization. Not present at call time, which is why consequential operations cannot rely on them being asked.

blocks.title: Calling agent
blocks.note: Someone else's agent, with arguments composed by a model that may have read hostile content. A non-human caller that is neither a person nor a bot to block.

blocks.title: Authorization server
blocks.note: Issues scoped, expiring, audience-restricted tokens to named clients. The one place a compromised agent's access can be withdrawn without redeploying anything.

items.label: Token issuance
items.note: Short-lived and audience-restricted — a token other resource servers accept turns one compromised agent into a multi-service problem.

items.label: Consent records
items.note: Which user authorised which client for which scopes, and when.

blocks.title: Protocol endpoint
blocks.note: The published MCP surface where agent traffic arrives, is authenticated, throttled and given a session. Session handling here is a security surface, not plumbing.

items.label: MCP transport
items.note: Session identifiers that can be guessed or replayed hand one caller another's context.

items.label: Session handling
items.note: Binds each session to the authenticated client and user, never to a guessable id.

items.label: Rate & cost limits
items.note: Sized for machine callers, which retry, loop and parallelise in ways human clients do not. A limit tuned for people is not a limit here.

blocks.title: Tool definitions
blocks.note: Names, descriptions and schemas — not documentation, but text the calling model treats as instruction. Changing them is changing somebody else's prompt.

items.label: Tool descriptions
items.note: Versioned, reviewed artifacts, because they execute inside another organisation's model.

items.label: Input schemas
items.note: The contract model-generated arguments are validated against.

items.label: Confirmation flags
items.note: Operations marked as requiring the caller to confirm with its user. The server cannot enforce it; declaring it is the only lever it has.

blocks.title: Tool handlers
blocks.note: The implementations. Arguments arrive model-generated, so validation assumes plausible nonsense rather than the malformed input a conventional client produces.

items.label: Handler code
items.note: Executes with the request's brokered identity, never a standing service account.

items.label: Argument validation
items.note: A handler that re-resolves the tenant from an argument is trusting a model to name it. Client, user and tenant travel with the request.

items.label: Result shaping
items.note: Bounds size and structure. An oversized result costs the caller money and crowds their context window.

blocks.title: Tenant data
blocks.note: Per-tenant records the tools reach. Isolation here is the claim consuming organisations cannot verify and will ask about in assurance.

items.label: Tenant records
items.note: Every read and write checks the tenant on the token against the tenant on the record.

items.label: Tenant isolation
items.note: A discipline across every handler, not one component's job.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Scope design, description review, audit and revocation — the controls that decide a hijacked agent's blast radius long before any call arrives.

items.label: Scope catalogue
items.note: What each scope permits. Coarse scopes are the difference between a hijacked agent doing one thing and doing everything the user could.

items.label: Description review
items.note: Tool text reviewed as a security artifact, because it executes in a caller's context. A benign-looking copy edit can change how thousands of agents behave.

items.label: Call audit
items.note: Which client, for which user, called what with which arguments and what came back. Also the only way to answer a customer asking what their agent did here.

items.label: Revocation & kill
items.note: Withdraw a client's tokens or disable a tool without redeploying the service.

edges.label: consent
edges.note: The user authorises a named client for named scopes. The last point at which a human decides anything in this architecture — every subsequent call happens without them.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: Model-composed arguments in; bounded results back into the caller's context window. The identity check cannot establish whether the agent was steered by content it read elsewhere.

edges.label: token validation
edges.note: Every call is validated against the issued token — client, user, scopes, audience, expiry — before it reaches a handler.

edges.label: schema into caller's context
edges.note: Tool text crossing into another organisation's model, where it executes as instruction. No authentication applies to what a description means.

edges.label: authorised call
edges.note: Client, user and tenant travel with the request rather than being re-derived. A handler that re-resolves the tenant from an argument is trusting a model to name it.

edges.label: scoped read / write
edges.note: Two checks on every operation: the scope permits it, and the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record. Skipping the second is how cross-tenant access happens in practice.

edges.label: scope definitions
edges.note: The scope catalogue is where a hijacked agent's blast radius is actually decided — long before any call arrives.

edges.label: description review
edges.note: Because the text runs in someone else's model, editing it is closer to shipping an API change than to updating documentation.

risks.note: This server is on the causing side. Its descriptions, errors and results all land in a caller's context, so its output hygiene is somebody else's input security.
Tool text treated as editable copy rather than a versioned artifact — a quiet edit changes how every consuming agent behaves.
The token proves a user consented; it cannot prove the agent still represents their intent. Scope design is the whole of the answer.
Long-lived or unrevocable tokens keep a decommissioned or compromised client alive. Expiry and revocation are the only levers after issuance.
Session identifiers that can be guessed or replayed hand one caller another's context and tenant.
Machine callers retry, loop and parallelise. Limits tuned for human clients are not limits here.
Arguments are model-generated plausible nonsense, and the user is not present to be asked. Confirmation semantics are declared, not enforced, by this side.
Every read and write needs the tenant on the token checked against the tenant on the record. It is a discipline across all handlers, not one component's job.
The read path carries the volume. A coarse scope plus a broad query returns everything the user could see, to an agent that may have been steered.
Results enter the caller's context as content. An oversized or manipulative result is a denial-of-service against a model rather than a server.

capabilities.note: Bind consent to a named client and named scopes, recorded and reviewable — the delegated grant every later call traces back to.
Named clients with short-lived, audience-restricted tokens and working revocation. The calling agent is a non-human identity you did not create but must manage.
Design scopes narrow enough that a hijacked agent's blast radius is one operation, not everything the user could do.
TLS, unguessable session identifiers, and sessions bound to the authenticated client — session handling is where transport hijacking is decided.
Per-client and per-tenant limits sized for machine callers, with idempotency keys because agents retry.
Enforce both checks on every operation: scope permits it, and token tenant matches record tenant — on reads as well as writes.
Treat definitions as versioned security artifacts: schema-pinned, change-controlled, and published with provenance callers can check.
Adversarially review descriptions and error text before release — the question is what a model will do with the words, not what a human reads into them.
Declare confirmation semantics on consequential tools so the caller must confirm with its user. Declaring it is the only lever this side of the boundary has.
Bound result size and structure before it leaves — what returns becomes part of another organisation's prompt.
Record client, user, tool, arguments and result per call — the trail that answers a customer asking what their agent did here.

steps.note: Consent binds a named client to named scopes. The last human decision in the flow.
The agent calls in with its scoped token; the user is no longer present.
Client, user, scopes, audience and expiry are validated per call.
The authorised identity travels with the request — nothing is re-derived from arguments.
Scope check plus tenant-match check, on this and every subsequent operation.
The agent was steered by content it read elsewhere. Its token is valid and every identity check passes.
Rate limits and argument validation constrain the mechanics, not the intent.
The tenant check bounds reach to the one tenant; the scope bounds it to named operations.
The blast radius was decided by scope design long before this call arrived.
The edit is reviewed as an interface change — text a model will act on, not copy.
The new wording lands in every consuming agent's context on their next session.

archetypes.title: Sandboxed agentic execution service
summary: A service that runs agents in disposable isolated environments — cloud coding agents, autonomous operations agents, agentic browsing. Untrusted code and untrusted instructions execute together, and the isolation is the product.
description:
Everything here follows from one design commitment: the agent is assumed to be compromisable, and the architecture is arranged so that it does not matter very much when it is. The sandbox is not a hardening measure applied to an otherwise-trusted workload; it is the trust boundary the whole service is organised around.
Three properties make the isolation real. The environment is disposable, so persistence is impossible without escaping — a compromise lasts for one task rather than indefinitely. Egress is default-deny with a per-task allowlist, so an agent steered into exfiltrating cannot reach a collection endpoint. And credentials are injected outside the sandbox rather than handed into it: the agent asks a proxy for an effect — the push, the API call, the deployment — and the proxy holds the token. A compromised agent gets the capability and never the secret.
Multi-tenancy at the isolation layer is the remaining hard part. Containers sharing a kernel are a different security claim from microVMs with their own, and running many customers' agents on shared hosts makes the isolation technology a load-bearing security decision rather than an operational one. The output is where the boundary is crossed on purpose: whatever the agent produces leaves as a reviewable artifact — a pull request, a change, a report — down the same review and CI path a human's change takes. That human review is the last control, and the one that erodes fastest as volume grows.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint coding agent: the same loop, hosted. The endpoint version runs on a machine that also holds SSH keys, cloud credentials and a browser profile, and nothing separates them. Here the environment contains nothing but the task, and is destroyed afterwards.
Against the durable multi-agent workflow: that one is about surviving failure across a long process; this one is about containing a compromise inside a short one. A workflow may use this as a step; they are not the same concern.

exemplars.name: Cloud coding agents
exemplars.note: Vendor services that clone a repository into an isolated environment, run an agent against the task, and open a pull request for review.

exemplars.name: Autonomous operations and SRE agents
exemplars.note: Agents given a contained environment and read access to production telemetry, proposing or applying remediations through a reviewed path.

exemplars.name: Agentic browsing services
exemplars.note: Hosted browser automation driven by an agent, where the browser runs in the sandbox rather than in the user's own session.

blocks.title: Task requester
blocks.note: Describes the outcome, and reviews the artifact at the end. Absent in between — their entitlements bound what the broker will do for the task.

blocks.title: Arbitrary internet
blocks.note: Where a compromised agent would send what it found. Drawn because the default-deny egress policy exists precisely to make this edge fail.

items.label: Collection endpoints
items.note: The destination a successful injection needs and cannot reach.

blocks.title: Task control plane
blocks.note: Accepts work, provisions one environment per task with a fresh identity, and tears it down at the end. Deliberately outside the sandbox, which is the point.

items.label: Task scheduler
items.note: One task, one environment, destroyed afterwards. Resource ceilings bound the run.

items.label: Environment provisioning
items.note: A fresh workload identity per task, expiring with it — persistence would undo the design.

blocks.title: Egress gate
blocks.note: Default-deny with a per-task allowlist, enforced by the platform outside the thing it contains. The control that makes a successful injection unprofitable rather than merely detected.

items.label: Per-task allowlist
items.note: Scoped to the task's actual dependencies, not the service's union of all needs.

items.label: Attempt logging
items.note: Denied attempts are the highest-value signal in this archetype — they are what a successful injection looks like when the architecture worked.

blocks.title: Sandboxed runtime
blocks.note: One task's agent loop, workspace and browser, in an environment that is assumed compromised and arranged so a compromise expires with the task. It holds no secrets and no standing authority.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Plans and executes with no credentials of its own — it can only ask the proxy for effects.

items.label: Workspace & shell
items.note: Filesystem and toolchain containing the task and nothing else — no other repo, no other customer.

items.label: Clean browser
items.note: No pre-existing sessions; nothing of the user's to steal.

items.label: Isolation boundary
items.note: Container versus microVM is a security claim, not an operational choice, once tenants share hosts. The sandbox must not reach its own configuration.

blocks.title: Repository & web content
blocks.note: Code, issues, dependency metadata and pages the agent reads. Assumed hostile — the architecture makes the reader disposable rather than the content safe.

items.label: Cloned repositories
items.note: Including README files, issues and configs that are all model input.

items.label: Web pages & docs
items.note: Attacker-writable content read as context inside the sandbox.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface, reached through the egress allowlist like everything else. Even the model call does not put a secret inside the environment.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: On the allowlist, with the credential attached outside the sandbox.

blocks.title: Broker & action proxy
blocks.note: Holds the task's tokens and performs privileged operations on the agent's behalf — the push, the API call, the deployment. Credential isolation happens here rather than being asserted.

items.label: Credential broker
items.note: Short-lived, task-scoped tokens that never pass inward, and never exceed what the requester could do themselves.

items.label: Proxied operations
items.note: The agent asks for an effect; the proxy performs it and logs it.

items.label: Artifact creation
items.note: Work leaves as a reviewable artifact, not a direct change — which keeps the human gate meaningful.

blocks.title: Target systems
blocks.note: The systems that will trust the artifact once someone merges or applies it. Deliberately reached by the same review, CI and deployment path a human's change takes.

items.label: Target repositories
items.note: Where the pull request lands, behind branch protection and review.

items.label: Infrastructure & records
items.note: Where an applied remediation becomes a real change.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Isolation policy, artifact review, session audit and termination — each enforced by the platform, outside the environments they govern.

items.label: Isolation & egress policy
items.note: Which isolation technology, which allowlist, which resource ceiling. Whether tenants share a kernel is a security decision that often gets made as an operational one.

items.label: Artifact review
items.note: A human reading the diff before it lands. The last control, and the one that erodes fastest as volume grows.

items.label: Session audit
items.note: Prompts, commands, network attempts and proxied actions — including every denied egress attempt.

items.label: Task termination
items.note: Destroying the environment. Cheap here in a way it is nowhere else, because the environment was disposable by design.

edges.label: task / artifact link
edges.note: The requester's entitlements bound what the broker will later be willing to do for the task; the finished artifact comes back for their review.

edges.label: provision per task
edges.note: A fresh environment and a fresh identity, both expiring with the task. Persistence across tasks would undo the main property this architecture is built for.

edges.label: cloned content
edges.note: Assumed hostile on arrival. The architecture does not try to make this content safe; it makes the environment that reads it disposable.

edges.label: outbound attempt
edges.note: Every byte leaving the sandbox passes the gate — there is no other network path.

edges.label: allowed — inference
edges.note: On the allowlist, with the credential attached outside the sandbox. The one channel that always leaves, and therefore the one worth inspecting.

edges.label: denied by default
edges.note: Drawn because it fails. Making exfiltration unprofitable is a stronger position than making injection unlikely, and it is the one this architecture can actually achieve.

edges.label: privileged operation request
edges.note: The defining crossing. The agent asks for an effect; the proxy holds the credential and performs it. A compromised agent gets the capability and never the secret.

edges.label: reviewed artifact
edges.note: The pull request or change lands by the same review, CI and deployment path a human's change takes, so the existing controls apply unchanged.

edges.label: credential policy & audit
edges.note: The broker's grants never exceed the requester's entitlements, and every proxied action is recorded off the agent's write path.

edges.label: artifact review
edges.note: A human reads the diff before merge or apply. Keeping everything upstream strong is what keeps this gate meaningful as volume grows.

risks.note: Not mitigated here — contained. The agent is assumed to be steered by what it reads, and the consequences are arranged to expire with the task.
Dependencies, build scripts and setup instructions arrive with the clone and execute in the workspace. Admission is whatever the repository says about itself.
The exfiltration path this architecture is built to close. A denied attempt here is what a successful injection looks like when the design worked.
The inference channel is always on the allowlist, so it is the covert path that remains once everything else is denied.
Many customers' agents on shared hosts make the isolation technology the claim: a shared kernel is a different promise from a microVM with its own.
The agent's own authority is deliberately nil, so rogue actions reduce to what the proxy will perform — which is why its scope check carries the weight.
The proxy acts on the agent's word with real credentials. It must never exceed what the requester could have done, or delegation becomes escalation.
The artifact is model output that target systems will trust once merged. Human review is the last control, and it erodes as volume grows.
An unattended loop burns compute and inference spend until the scheduler's ceilings end it — nobody is watching the task run.

capabilities.note: Disposable per-task isolation, microVM-grade where tenants share hosts, with configuration the sandbox cannot reach.
Keep every secret outside the sandbox: the agent requests effects, the proxy holds the tokens and performs them.
Default-deny with a per-task allowlist scoped to actual dependencies, enforced by the platform outside the environment.
Broker short-lived, task-scoped credentials bounded by the requester's own entitlements; nothing long-lived, nothing inward.
A human review gate on every artifact before merge or apply — sized and staffed so it does not rubber-stamp at volume.
Record prompts, commands, proxied actions and every denied egress attempt — the denied attempts are the signal most often not collected.
Terminate by destroying the environment. Cheap and complete, because the environment was disposable from the start.
A fresh workload identity per task, expiring at teardown, so nothing survives to be reused by the next compromise.
Inspect what leaves on the allowed inference channel — the one egress path a steered agent always has.
Per-task resource, time and spend ceilings, enforced by the scheduler because no human is present to abandon a runaway run.
The proxy performs only the operations the task was granted — a per-operation scope, not the requester's whole reach.

scenarios.title: A coding task runs end to end

steps.note: The task arrives; the requester's entitlements bound everything that follows.
A fresh environment and identity are provisioned — no secrets inside.
The repository is cloned in, assumed hostile.
The agent works; every outbound byte passes the gate.
Inference is on the allowlist, credential attached outside the sandbox.
The agent asks for the push; the proxy holds the token and performs it.
A pull request opens, on the same review and CI path as a human change.
The artifact link comes back; the environment is destroyed.
A hostile instruction rides in on a README, an issue or a fetched page.
The steered agent tries to send what it found.
Denied by default. The attempt is logged — this is the architecture working.
An out-of-scope operation is refused; the proxy's grant never exceeded the task.
The malicious diff still has to pass a human reviewer before anything trusts it.
An unbounded loop hammers the allowed channels; ceilings and logs accumulate.
The audit trail shows the pattern; termination is invoked.
The environment is destroyed — the kill is cheap because nothing was meant to persist.

archetypes.title: Self-hosted open-weights inference
summary: Open-weights models served on GPUs the organisation operates: weights fetched from public hubs, scanned and promoted through a registry, loaded onto a shared accelerator fleet, and exposed to internal callers through one inference gateway. The whole model-provider role moves inside the boundary.
description:
The trade is explicit: a data-disclosure risk goes away and a supply-chain, availability and safety risk arrives. There is no provider applying content policy, no provider absorbing a traffic spike, and no provider patching the serving stack. Every control a managed API supplies by default is now a component this organisation runs or does without.
The supply chain is the distinctive risk. Weights are large artifacts from public hubs, and several distribution formats execute code on load. The control is scanning and format policy in the promotion pipeline, before an artifact reaches a node — a blocking gate, not a report. The registry with provenance and that gate is what separates this architecture from the same software installed by one person on a workstation.
Multi-tenancy on accelerators has no equivalent elsewhere in this catalogue. Continuous batching mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass, the KV cache holds their context, and prefix caching across tenants is a performance feature that is also a disclosure path. Whether cache entries may be shared across tenants is a serving-configuration flag with data-protection consequences, and it rarely reaches a review.
Availability is a security property here in a way it is not with a managed API. GPU capacity is finite and expensive, admission control at the gateway is what stops one caller becoming everyone else's outage, and quotas are a control rather than a billing feature.
distinguishedBy:
Against an endpoint local runtime: identical software, entirely different operational position. There it was installed by one person and has no inventory entry; here it has a pipeline, a network policy, an identity and someone on call.
Against consuming a managed model API: this architecture replaces one boundary crossing with a whole subsystem. The guardrails, abuse monitoring, capacity management and patching the provider was doing are now blocks on this diagram.

exemplars.name: Serving runtimes on Kubernetes
exemplars.note: Open-source inference servers with continuous batching and paged attention, scheduled onto GPU node pools with an inference-aware gateway in front.

exemplars.name: On-premises inference for data residency
exemplars.note: The same stack in a datacentre because the data cannot leave. The most common non-cost reason organisations take on this architecture.

blocks.title: Public model hub
blocks.note: Where the open weights are published. Publisher identity is verifiable to a degree; what an artifact does on load is a property of its format, not its publisher.

items.label: Published weights
items.note: Multi-gigabyte artifacts, in formats some of which execute code on load.

blocks.title: Consuming applications
blocks.note: Internal applications and agents sharing one cluster. Their isolation from each other is a property of the serving configuration, not of the network between them.

blocks.title: Inference gateway
blocks.note: Model routing, admission control and per-tenant quotas in front of finite GPU capacity. With no provider applying content policy, the guardrail checks here are a service the organisation runs itself or does without.

items.label: Admission & quotas
items.note: Per-tenant ceilings on finite capacity. What stops one caller becoming everyone's outage.

items.label: Guardrail checks
items.note: Content and injection classification on both legs, run inline rather than advisory.

items.label: Model routing
items.note: Which model version serves which tenant's request.

blocks.title: Model registry & weights
blocks.note: Versioned artifacts with provenance, encrypted storage and a promotion gate. The single control that separates this architecture from an ungoverned copy of the same software.

items.label: Versioned registry
items.note: Provenance and promotion state per artifact. Nothing serves that was not promoted.

items.label: Weight storage
items.note: Expensive to reproduce, trivial to copy. Encryption and access control protect both facts.

blocks.title: Serving runtime
blocks.note: Continuous batching and paged attention across tenants. The batching that makes it efficient is also what puts several tenants' context in one process, and the serving stack itself is third-party code with its own CVE stream.

items.label: Continuous batching
items.note: Mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass. Efficiency and co-tenancy are the same mechanism.

items.label: Serving stack
items.note: An open-source inference server with its own CVE stream and nobody upstream patching it for you.

blocks.title: KV & prefix cache
blocks.note: Recent context held to avoid recomputing it. Sharing prefixes across tenants is a performance feature and a disclosure path, and the choice between them is a configuration flag that rarely reaches a review.

items.label: KV cache
items.note: Tenants' live context in accelerator memory.

items.label: Prefix sharing
items.note: Cache hits across tenants cut latency and cross a data boundary in the same operation.

blocks.title: Models on GPU
blocks.note: The weights in memory across a shared node pool. A high-value exfiltration target — the artifact is expensive and portable — and a shared physical substrate for every tenant at once.

items.label: Loaded weights
items.note: Verified against the registry digest at load, or the promotion gate can be bypassed by writing to storage.

items.label: GPU node pool
items.note: Shared accelerators. Tenancy here is a hardware property, not a namespace one.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: The controls a managed provider would have supplied, now operated in-house: artifact scanning, per-version evaluation, posture over serving configuration, and workload identity for callers and pipeline alike.

items.label: Artifact scanning
items.note: Format and content inspection as a blocking gate in the promotion pipeline, before any node opens the file.

items.label: Evaluation & red teaming
items.note: Per model version, because a new checkpoint from the same publisher is a new model nobody else has tested.

items.label: Posture & inventory
items.note: Which versions serve where, at what configuration — including whether cross-tenant cache sharing is on.

items.label: Workload identity
items.note: Short-lived credentials for callers and for the pipeline that promotes artifacts.

edges.label: weights fetch
edges.note: Provenance establishes who published the artifact and nothing about what it does on load — which is why the scan gate sits between this edge and any node that will open the file.

edges.label: inference request
edges.note: The tenant on the token is what quotas and cache-isolation decisions key off. A request that arrives without one gets whatever the default tenant can do.
Admitted requests scheduled into the batch; completions back through the guardrail. Output-side policy is the half most often omitted when self-hosting.

edges.label: forward pass
edges.note: The batch executes on shared accelerators, several tenants per pass.
Context written and reused across requests. Whether a cache entry may serve another tenant's request is the configuration decision that matters most on this edge.

edges.label: verified load
edges.note: The digest is verified at load time, which is what makes registry promotion meaningful. Without it the gate can be bypassed by writing to storage directly.

edges.label: scan & promotion gate
edges.note: Scanning and evaluation gate promotion — blocking, not advisory. A scan that runs after deployment has documented an incident.

edges.label: posture & drift
edges.note: Posture watches serving configuration for drift, including the cache-sharing flags. A posture tool that can read the cache has joined the data path it was meant to observe.

risks.note: Publisher identity is the only assurance the hub offers, and it says nothing about the artifact's behaviour.
Several weight formats execute code on load. Format policy on this edge is the only place that fact can be addressed once for everything downstream.
The stored artifact is expensive to reproduce and trivial to copy, which makes storage access control an asset-protection question.
A load path that skips digest verification turns the promotion gate into a suggestion.
The serving stack is third-party code with its own CVE stream, and no provider is patching it on anyone's behalf.
Batching puts several tenants' requests in one forward pass; isolation is a property of several configuration choices at once.
Cross-tenant prefix sharing puts one tenant's context where another's request can reach it, and it looks like a cache hit rather than an incident.
A poisoned cache entry serves every later request that matches it.
Shared accelerators are a physical substrate common to every tenant, below every namespace boundary.
GPU capacity is finite and there is no provider to absorb a spike. Admission control here is an availability control, not a billing feature.
With no provider applying output policy, an unguarded return leg hands raw completions to every caller.

capabilities.note: Format and content scanning as a blocking gate in the promotion pipeline, before any artifact reaches a node.
Safety and adversarial evaluation per model version — a new checkpoint is a new model with new behaviour.
One governed front door for every caller: routing, admission and policy at a single crossing.
Workload identity per calling tenant, issued by the platform rather than a shared key in a config map.
Per-tenant quotas on finite GPU capacity, enforced at admission rather than discovered at saturation.
Content and injection classification on both legs, because no provider is applying policy for you.
Reviewed serving configuration — batching, cache sharing, tenancy flags — treated as security settings, not tuning knobs.
Tenant-scoped cache keys, so a prefix hit can never cross a tenant boundary.
Encryption, access control and integrity digests on weights at rest, matched by verification at load.
Track and patch the serving stack's CVE stream on your own schedule, because nobody upstream will.
Hardware-backed isolation for the highest-sensitivity tenants where shared accelerators are not acceptable.
Continuous posture over which versions serve where and at what configuration, catching drift before an incident does.

steps.note: The artifact is fetched with provenance recorded — who published it, not what it does.
Scanning and per-version evaluation gate the promotion. Blocking, or it is not a gate.
The promoted artifact loads onto nodes, digest-verified against the registry.
The workload identity on the request decides its quota and its cache scope.
The admitted request is scheduled into a batch alongside other tenants' traffic.
Prefix lookup — a hit is cheap, and tenant-scoped keying is what keeps it safe.
The forward pass executes on shared accelerators.
The completion returns through the guardrail's output leg, not around it.
Admission control decides who waits. There is no provider to absorb the spike.
Within-quota traffic is scheduled; everything else is shed at the front door rather than at the accelerator.
