archetypes.title: Fine-tuning and model registry pipeline
summary: A build system whose artifact is a model. Curated data goes in, a tuned checkpoint comes out, and everything that is true of a compiler and its supply chain is true here — except that the output cannot be diffed and the defects cannot be found by reading it.
description:
Treating this as a build pipeline is the whole of the correct framing. It has source inputs, a build environment, dependencies, an artifact, a registry and a promotion path, and it deserves the controls a software pipeline gets: reproducibility, provenance, signed artifacts, and a promotion gate nothing bypasses. Where the analogy breaks is inspection: a compiled binary can be decompiled and diffed; a tuned checkpoint cannot be read for backdoors in any practical sense. Input control and evaluation are the substitutes for code review — what went into the training set and how the result behaves are the only two things anyone can actually examine.
Poisoning is therefore the primary risk and it is durable. A poisoned example influences every inference the model ever makes, survives redeployment, and is not removable without retraining. A targeted poisoning that only activates on a trigger phrase is invisible to accuracy metrics and to any evaluation that does not know what to look for — which is why curation is the last place a bad example can be removed rather than baked in, and why lineage from every promoted model back to its exact dataset is what makes a discovered poisoning scopeable at all.
Training data is also a disclosure surface in a way inference data is not. Memorised examples can be extracted from the model afterwards, so restricted-access content in the corpus becomes part of an artifact served far more widely than the dataset ever was. The two access questions to settle early: who may promote a checkpoint to production, and who may read the corpus. Both default to a broad platform-team role, and both are higher-privilege than they look — which is why promotion is a separated human decision and the signing key lives outside the training environment, so a compromised job cannot sign its own output.
distinguishedBy:
Against the batch pipeline: same build-system trust properties, different artifact. That produces data; this produces a model. The data can be corrected in place; the model cannot.
Against self-hosted inference: that consumes artifacts, this produces them. They meet at the registry, and the promotion gate between them is where both archetypes' supply-chain controls concentrate.

exemplars.name: Managed fine-tuning services
exemplars.note: Provider-hosted tuning against a customer dataset, producing a private checkpoint served from the same platform. Availability varies sharply by provider and by year.

exemplars.name: Self-operated tuning on accelerator fleets
exemplars.note: Adapter or full fine-tuning on the organisation's own hardware, with a registry and promotion pipeline built alongside.

exemplars.name: Adapter and preference tuning
exemplars.note: Lightweight tuning producing an adapter rather than a full checkpoint. Smaller artifact, same supply-chain questions, and an additional one about who may load an adapter at serve time.

blocks.title: Labelling workforce
blocks.note: Human or model-generated labels and preferences, frequently from an outsourced workforce. A supply chain with a direct path into model behaviour and almost no scrutiny.

blocks.title: Training content origins
blocks.note: Scraped corpora, purchased datasets, user-generated content and internal records. Each carries a different provenance claim and most carry none.

items.label: Scraped & purchased sets
items.note: Authored by parties the pipeline never authenticates.

items.label: Internal records
items.note: Often restricted-access data about to be baked into a widely served artifact.

blocks.title: Curation & filtering
blocks.note: Deduplication, quality filtering and removal of sensitive or improperly sourced content. The last point at which a poisoned example can be removed rather than baked in.

items.label: Quality & safety filters
items.note: After training, a bad example is in the weights and cannot be taken out.

items.label: Sensitive-content removal
items.note: What stays in can later be extracted from the model by anyone who can query it.

items.label: Provenance capture
items.note: Per-example source and licence, recorded now because it cannot be reconstructed later.

blocks.title: Training corpus
blocks.note: The assembled, versioned dataset. Read access is higher-privilege than it looks — it is the union of everything the organisation decided a model should learn.

items.label: Dataset versions
items.note: Immutable and versioned, so a run can be tied to exactly what it saw.

items.label: Corpus access control
items.note: Writes decide what the model will learn; the write path deserves a production deploy's review.

blocks.title: Base model & deps
blocks.note: The starting checkpoint and the training frameworks, pulled from outside. Everything the base model already contains is inherited — tuning adds behaviour and does not subtract it.

items.label: Base checkpoint
items.note: A backdoor in the base survives tuning and every benchmark that does not know its trigger.

items.label: Frameworks & dependencies
items.note: An ordinary software supply chain executing with access to the corpus and the artifact.

blocks.title: Training job
blocks.note: The build. Reproducibility — same data, same code, same seed, same artifact — is what makes an incident investigable at all.

items.label: Tuning run
items.note: Scoped to the dataset approved for this run, so a job cannot quietly widen its own inputs.

items.label: Reproducibility record
items.note: Data version, code version, seed and base model, captured during the run.

items.label: Write-once output
items.note: Candidate-only writes, so a job cannot overwrite an already-promoted artifact. The signing key lives outside this environment for the same reason.

blocks.title: Evaluation & red teaming
blocks.note: Capability, safety, backdoor and memorisation testing — the substitute for reading an artifact nobody can read. Blocking, because a report on an unreadable artifact changes nothing on its own.

items.label: Capability & safety evals
items.note: A targeted poisoning passes every benchmark that does not know its trigger.

items.label: Backdoor probing
items.note: Adversarial search for triggers and behavioural anomalies against the previous version.

items.label: Memorisation testing
items.note: Extraction and membership-inference testing before promotion — the only way to learn the artifact remembers its training data before someone else does.

blocks.title: Model registry
blocks.note: Versioned artifacts with lineage back to the exact dataset and code that produced them, and a promotion gate to production that nothing bypasses.

items.label: Candidate checkpoints
items.note: Unpromoted, unsigned, and served to nobody.

items.label: Lineage metadata
items.note: Which examples, which code, which base model, which run — recorded, not reconstructed.

items.label: Signed releases
items.note: Signature applied at promotion and verified at load, which is what makes the gate meaningful.

blocks.title: Serving & consumers
blocks.note: The inference platforms that pull promoted models. This archetype ends at the registry; the promotion gate is the seam between producing the artifact and serving it.

items.label: Inference platforms
items.note: Verify the signature at load — a registry bypass shows up here or never.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Lineage, promotion authority and signing — the record of what produced what, and the separated decisions about what may ship.

items.label: Data & model lineage
items.note: The only route to scoping the damage when a dataset turns out to have been poisoned or improperly sourced months later.

items.label: Promotion authority
items.note: Separation of duties: whoever runs training cannot promote unilaterally. The default configuration usually grants both to the same role.

items.label: Artifact signing
items.note: Keys held outside the training environment, so a compromised job cannot sign its own output. Verification happens at load, in whichever platform serves it.

edges.label: raw content
edges.note: Curation is the only place a poisoned or improperly sourced example can still be removed. After training it is in the weights.

edges.label: labels & preferences
edges.note: Frequently an outsourced workforce with a direct influence on model behaviour and very little scrutiny relative to that influence.

edges.label: curated dataset
edges.note: Corpus writes decide what the model will learn. The write path deserves the review a production deploy gets.

edges.label: approved training data
edges.note: Scoped to the dataset version approved for this run, so a job cannot quietly widen its own inputs.

edges.label: base checkpoint & dependencies
edges.note: Everything already in the base model is inherited, and the frameworks execute with access to the corpus and the artifact.

edges.label: candidate checkpoint
edges.note: Write-once and candidate-only — a job cannot overwrite a promoted artifact, and cannot sign anything.

edges.label: evaluation gate
edges.note: Blocking, before promotion: capability, safety, backdoor and memorisation results are the substitute for code review on an artifact nobody can read.

edges.label: promoted model
edges.note: Pulled only after promotion, with the signature verified at load. Deliberately the only path from training to traffic.

edges.label: signing & promotion
edges.note: A separated human promotion decision, a signature applied outside the build, and lineage recorded during the run rather than reconstructed later.

risks.note: A poisoned example that survives curation influences every inference the model ever makes, and is not removable without retraining.
Labels and preference data steer behaviour directly, and the workforce producing them gets almost no scrutiny relative to that influence.
A licensing or privacy defect discovered after training is a retraining decision, not a deletion. Irreversibility starts at the training job.
Corpus read access is the union of everything a model should learn, and it defaults to a broad platform-team role.
A tampered base checkpoint or dependency is inherited whole — tuning adds behaviour and does not subtract it.
Training frameworks and their transitive dependencies execute with access to the corpus and the artifact — an ordinary supply chain in an unusually valuable position.
The checkpoint may have memorised its inputs, turning a restricted dataset into an artifact with broad access. There is no runtime control for this path.
A targeted poisoning activates only on its trigger and passes every benchmark that does not know it — the gate is necessary and insufficient alone.
The registry holds the crown-jewel artifacts. Read access to checkpoints is model theft with none of the serving-side telemetry.
Whoever runs training should not be able to promote unilaterally. The default configuration usually grants both to the same role.

capabilities.note: Record per-example source and licence at ingestion — provenance cannot be reconstructed later, and it is the only route to scoping a poisoning.
Filter poisoned, sensitive and improperly sourced content here — the last point where removal is deletion rather than retraining.
Make evaluation a blocking gate on promotion: capability, safety and regression against the previous version, with results recorded per candidate.
Probe candidates adversarially for backdoors and trigger behaviour — the tests that assume the training data was hostile.
Run extraction and membership-inference tests before promotion, because a model that memorised its corpus has widened that data's audience permanently.
Encrypt checkpoints at rest, restrict reads, and sign at promotion so serving can verify the artifact it loads.
Gate corpus reads and writes separately, and scope each training job to its approved dataset version.
Promotion is a human decision by someone who did not run the training — separation of duties on the highest-privilege action in the pipeline.
Scan base checkpoints and loaders before use — serialised model formats are a code execution vector, not just data.
Maintain the lineage record — dataset version, code, base model, run — for every artifact in the registry, recorded during the run.
Promote gradually behind traffic splitting, with the signature verified at load and a rollback target retained.
Hold signing keys outside the training environment, so a compromised job cannot sign its own output.

scenarios.title: A tuning run ships a model

steps.note: Raw content arrives with mixed and mostly absent provenance claims.
What survives filtering becomes a versioned, provenance-stamped dataset.
The job reads exactly the approved dataset version, nothing wider.
The base checkpoint and frameworks come in — everything they contain is inherited.
The candidate lands write-once, unsigned, served to nobody.
Capability, backdoor and memorisation testing gate the candidate.
A separated human promotes; the signature is applied outside the build.
Serving pulls the promoted artifact and verifies the signature at load.

scenarios.title: A poisoning is discovered months later

steps.note: Lineage maps the poisoned examples to every model version that learned from them.
Affected versions are rolled back to the last clean checkpoint.
The poisoned examples are removed and the dataset re-versioned.
Retraining is the only removal — the weights cannot be edited.
The trigger behaviour rides in with the checkpoint; scanning and provenance are the only upstream checks.
The candidate carries the backdoor intact — tuning did not remove it.
A gate that does not know the trigger passes it, which is why base-model provenance matters before this point.

archetypes.title: Realtime voice agent
summary: A conversational agent over a live audio channel, handling calls and acting on what it hears. Injection arrives as speech, the caller's identity is asserted by a voice, and there is no moment to pause and check anything.
description:
Realtime changes what is possible rather than what is at stake. Every asynchronous architecture can insert a filter, a check or a human between the input and the effect. Here the budget is a few hundred milliseconds before the pause becomes audible and the conversation breaks, which means guardrails have to be streaming and partial, and human oversight means transferring the call rather than blocking on a queue.
Identity is the harder problem. A voice is not an authenticator and has not been one for several years — cloned voices are cheap — and the calling number is spoofable, so anything consequential needs a second factor on another channel: a code to the registered device, a callback, an in-app confirmation. Systems that treat the calling number plus a plausible voice as authentication are the ones this architecture's incidents come from.
Audio is also the worst medium for detection. Speech-to-text loses tone, homophones and overlapping speakers, so the transcript the guardrail inspects is not what was said. Where only the transcript is retained, an investigation cannot recover what happened; where audio is retained, that is biometric data with its own regulatory weight. And the telephony edge brings an exposure the rest of the catalogue lacks: a voice agent on a public number is an always-open endpoint with per-minute inference costs behind it.
distinguishedBy:
Against the autonomous action agent: the same act-on-a-request shape with the latency budget removed. Every deliberative control that architecture relies on — filtering, approval queues, reconsideration — is unavailable, so the compensating controls move to identity and to limiting what a voice alone may do.
Against a text chat assistant: the medium changes the threat model. Audio cannot be reliably inspected, transcription is lossy, the caller is anonymous by default, and the recording is biometric data.

exemplars.name: Realtime speech APIs with tool calling
exemplars.note: Provider APIs handling speech in and out with low latency and function calling in-session, increasingly with direct telephony integration.

exemplars.name: Contact-centre voice agents
exemplars.note: Agents answering customer calls end to end, with escalation to a human and access to account records. The mainstream commercial deployment of this architecture.

blocks.title: Caller
blocks.note: Claims an identity by speaking. A voice is not an authenticator and a calling number is spoofable, so this claim needs corroboration before anything consequential happens.

blocks.title: Telephony edge
blocks.note: Carrier and session border. Caller identification arrives here already untrustworthy — a hint, not a fact — and the network in the middle of every call is a third party.

items.label: Session border
items.note: Where the call arrives, and where admission, fraud signals and concurrency caps belong.

items.label: Caller ID & carrier signals
items.note: Spoofable, and treated as routing input rather than authentication.

blocks.title: Realtime session
blocks.note: The live conversation: streaming audio in and out, the dialogue agent deciding when to call a tool, and guardrails that must rule on partial transcripts within the latency budget.

items.label: Stream handling
items.note: Audio in, audio out, continuously. Any inspection here has a few hundred milliseconds before the pause is audible.

items.label: Dialogue agent
items.note: Decides in real time, with no opportunity to reconsider before the words are spoken.

items.label: Streaming guardrail
items.note: Partial-transcript classification, inbound and outbound. Necessarily weaker than a batch filter, because it must decide before the utterance is finished.

items.label: Human transfer
items.note: Escalation to a person — this architecture's only form of human oversight, because a queue is not available while the caller is on the line.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: Streaming speech-to-speech inference. It holds the caller's audio for the duration of the call, which makes the provider's retention terms a biometric-data question.

items.label: Realtime speech API
items.note: Speech in, speech and tool calls out, under a latency budget nothing else in the catalogue has.

blocks.title: In-session tools
blocks.note: Account lookups and transactions invoked mid-conversation. The gap between reads and writes is where the verification requirement belongs, and the permitted set changes when verification completes mid-call.

items.label: Account lookup
items.note: Reads on an unverified call should be narrower than reads on a verified one.

items.label: Transactions
items.note: Consequential writes wait for the out-of-band factor; conversation does not.

blocks.title: Customer records
blocks.note: What the agent reads and changes, scoped to whoever the caller has actually been proven to be — not to who they said they are.

items.label: Accounts & history
items.note: The state a wrong action changes, and the data a wrong read discloses aloud.

blocks.title: Audio & transcripts
blocks.note: Biometric data with its own regulatory weight, plus a transcript that is not a faithful record of what was said. Retaining both has consequences; retaining neither leaves incidents unreconstructable.

items.label: Call audio
items.note: A voiceprint of every caller, for as long as the retention policy says.

items.label: Transcripts
items.note: Lossy by construction — tone, homophones and overlapping speakers are already gone.

blocks.title: Governance plane
blocks.note: Verification, action limits, retention and review — the deliberative controls, all moved outside the call because there is no room for them inside it.

items.label: Out-of-band verification
items.note: A code to the registered device, a callback, an in-app confirmation. The substitute for an authenticator, required before anything consequential.

items.label: Action limits
items.note: What may happen on a call with only a voice behind it, re-evaluated when verification completes partway through.

items.label: Retention policy
items.note: How long audio and transcripts are kept, and who may replay them. A genuine tension between investigability and biometric minimisation.

items.label: Post-call review
items.note: Sampled review after the fact — the only deliberative control available, arriving after the effect.

items.label: Kill switch
items.note: Takes the number offline and drops live sessions when the agent is the thing misbehaving.

edges.label: call audio
edges.note: Whoever they are, over a network nobody here controls. Spoken instructions and the agent's synthesized replies share this channel.

edges.label: media stream
edges.note: Transport is secured; the speaker is not identified. Everything the session hears is untrusted input that cannot be filtered as reliably as text.

edges.label: streaming inference
edges.note: The caller's audio flows to the provider for the duration of the call, and the streamed response drives speech and tool calls with the same few hundred milliseconds of scrutiny.

edges.label: tool call
edges.note: Decisions land in real time. What a voice alone may invoke is bounded by policy, not by the model's judgement.

edges.label: read or transact
edges.note: Scoped to what the caller has been proven to be. Reads on an unverified call stay narrow; writes wait for the out-of-band factor.

edges.label: audio & transcript
edges.note: Biometric data plus a lossy transcript, captured continuously. Both need access control on replay, not only on storage.

edges.label: verification & limits
edges.note: Consequential actions wait for out-of-band proof; the permitted set changes the moment verification completes.

risks.note: Injection arrives as speech, into a channel that cannot be inspected as reliably as text, within a latency budget too short for a thorough check.
A voice is not an authenticator and the calling number is spoofable, so every action on an unverified call is taken for someone who has not been identified.
Tool decisions land in real time, with no filter, queue or reconsideration between decision and effect.
What the agent reads, it may say aloud — to a caller who has only claimed to be the customer.
Retained audio is a voiceprint; retained transcripts are conversation content. Both outlive the call by whatever the retention policy says.
The provider holds the caller's audio for the duration of the call — a biometric retention question.
Outbound speech gets the same few hundred milliseconds of checking as inbound, so what is said is less vetted than anyone would like.
A public number is an always-open endpoint with per-minute inference behind it; dialling it is the whole attack.

capabilities.note: Out-of-band verification — registered device, callback, in-app — before any consequential action; a voice alone proves nothing.
Split the tool set by verification state: narrow reads for a voice, transactions only after the second factor lands.
Human oversight as live transfer, not a queue — sized so escalation is instant, not deliberative.
Streaming, partial-transcript guardrails on both directions, tuned for the latency budget they have.
Classify partial transcripts as untrusted input, knowing the transcript is not what was said.
Call admission, concurrency caps and per-caller pacing at the border, where cost begins.
Per-call policy on what a voice alone may do, re-evaluated when verification completes mid-call.
Redact what is captured before it is stored; the recording outlives every other artifact of the call.
Classify and govern recordings as biometric data, with replay access controlled and logged.
Hold the provider's audio retention and processing terms to a biometric standard, not a general one.
Post-call sampled review of transcripts and actions — and log reviewer access to recordings too.
A stop that takes the number offline and ends live sessions, without a deploy.

scenarios.title: A caller asks to change their payout account

steps.note: The call arrives with a plausible voice and a caller ID worth nothing.
The conversation proceeds — nothing about talking requires identity.
Streaming inference drives the dialogue within the latency budget.
The agent proposes the change; the write is consequential.
Out-of-band verification fires — a code to the registered device, not to the caller.
Only after the factor lands does the write execute, scoped and logged.
The confirmation is spoken back on the same channel the request arrived on.
The voice matches, the number is spoofed to match, and both are hints, not proof.
The conversation is fluent; nothing in the audio gives the clone away reliably.
Reads stay narrow because the call is unverified — the clone learns little.
The consequential ask triggers verification on the registered device, which the attacker does not hold. The attack ends there or not at all.
Dialers hit the public number; each answered call is an open streaming session.
Admission control and concurrency caps at the border decide how many get this far.
Per-minute inference cost accrues on every session that survives — the meter is the target.

archetypes.title: Agentic browser and AI extension
summary: AI operating inside the user's web browser, in two shapes: a dedicated agentic browser whose built-in agent navigates and clicks for you, or a browser extension that lets an assistant read and drive the user's own tabs. Either way the agent works inside sessions that are already logged in — the page is the untrusted input, and the session cookies are the credential.
description:
Every other endpoint archetype has some separation between the content it reads and the authority it holds. Here there is none: the agent acts inside a session that is already authenticated to the user's mail, bank, source control and internal applications, and the instruction it is following arrives as text on a page served by whoever owns that page. Same-origin policy is the boundary the web is built on, and this archetype's job is to cross it — an agent that reads one origin and acts on another has done exactly what a decade of browser security is designed to prevent, with the user's cookies attached.
Two variants share the shape, and neither is a coding agent or OS-level computer use. A dedicated agentic browser is a browser product with the agent built in, driving navigation and clicks as tools. An extension or plugin connects an assistant to the browser the user already runs, reading the DOM of named tabs and often acting on them. The extension variant is the broader exposure in practice — host permissions on all sites see every page including the ones the user would never point an agent at, and the automatic update channel is a supply chain nobody enrolled.
The controls that work constrain what the session can reach rather than what the agent may say. A separate browser profile with a narrow set of logged-in origins converts an unbounded blast radius into a bounded one, and is worth more than any prompt filter. In-browser inspection is the only vantage point with visibility into what the agent actually saw and clicked.
There is no governance column in this drawing, and that absence is the finding. No policy engine sits between the page and the click, no audit sink records the session unless the browser itself does, and the applications being acted on cannot tell the agent from the user. What remains enforceable — profile scope, managed browser policy, egress inspection — has to be imposed on the endpoint from outside this architecture.
distinguishedBy:
Against a coding agent: that one reads a repository the developer chose and acts on a filesystem. This one reads pages an attacker serves and acts through credentials the user already holds, with no working directory to scope it to.
Against a desktop assistant with computer use: that one drives the whole machine through the GUI — any application, via screenshots and synthetic input — and its blast radius is the OS session. This one lives inside the browser and speaks its APIs (DOM, tabs, navigation), and its blast radius is the set of websites the user is signed in to. Overlapping products exist, but the authority, the permission model and the extension update channel are different problems.

exemplars.name: Agentic browsers
exemplars.note: Browsers with a built-in agent that navigates, reads and clicks on the user's behalf inside their existing signed-in session.

exemplars.name: Assistant sidebars in mainstream browsers
exemplars.note: An assistant panel with access to the current page's content, and increasingly to act on it. Ships enabled to a very large installed base.

exemplars.name: Assistant browser plugins from model vendors
exemplars.note: Extensions that connect a general assistant to the user's browser so it can read and drive named tabs — Claude's browser extension is the widely deployed shape of this variant.

exemplars.name: AI browser extensions
exemplars.note: Third-party extensions requesting host permissions across all sites. The permission grant is one click, the update channel is automatic, and the reviewer is the store.

blocks.title: User
blocks.note: Sets the goal, and is usually not reading the pages the agent reads on the way to it.

blocks.title: Agent loop
blocks.note: Reads the extracted page, decides the next navigation or click, and repeats. Once page text is in context it is indistinguishable from the user's goal.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Plans the next action from the goal and everything the browser has shown it.

items.label: Page extraction
items.note: Turns a rendered page into context — the only point where hidden and off-screen content can be stripped before it becomes instruction, and the step most implementations skip.

items.label: Action confirmation
items.note: Blocks before a consequential click — a purchase, a send, a permission change. Which actions count is a product decision, usually narrower than users assume.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface. It receives page content from authenticated sessions, which is frequently more than the user realises they shared.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The completion that comes back selects the next click.

blocks.title: Browser runtime
blocks.note: Navigation, DOM reading and clicking, offered to the model as tools. Its authority is the profile's cookie jar, and from the browser's perspective the agent's action is the user's.

items.label: Navigation & input
items.note: Clicks and keystrokes indistinguishable from the user's own.

items.label: DOM reader
items.note: Visible text, hidden text, alt attributes and comments — all of it becomes model input.

items.label: Extension host & updates
items.note: Where the extension variant lives. An automatic update channel into a component with permission to read every page.

blocks.title: Browser profile
blocks.note: Cookies, saved passwords and session tokens for every origin the user has signed into. The session cookies are the credential — narrowing this profile is the highest-value control in the archetype, and it is a configuration choice rather than a product feature.

items.label: Session cookies
items.note: Standing authentication to every signed-in origin, presented on every request.

items.label: Saved passwords & autofill
items.note: Credentials the browser will happily type into a form the agent navigated to.

blocks.title: Signed-in applications
blocks.note: Mail, banking, source control and internal tools. The agent acts on these as the user, and the applications cannot tell the difference — no grant was ever issued to an agent.

items.label: Mail & calendar
items.note: Readable and sendable as the user, on every turn.

items.label: Banking & payments
items.note: Where a wrong click is a transaction.

items.label: Source control & internal apps
items.note: Corporate surfaces reached through a consumer browser session.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: Every page is authored by someone else, and the agent reads all of them with the same standing. A hostile page does not need a vulnerability — its text is already model input.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike, served by whoever owns the page.

edges.label: goal / confirmation
edges.note: The user states an outcome and answers confirmations. The pages that determine how the outcome is reached are not theirs.
Page content — including content from authenticated pages — leaves for inference; the completion that returns selects the next click and is not authenticated content.
Actions out as navigation and clicks; extracted page content back in as context.

edges.label: session tokens
edges.note: The cookie jar rides along on every request the agent causes. Whatever origins the profile is signed into, the agent can act on.
Authenticated requests out with the user's cookies; authenticated content — mail, records, internal pages — back in as model input.
Browsing out; page text back in. The primary injection path — any page the agent reads can steer what it does on every other origin the profile reaches.

risks.note: Page text is instruction once extracted — visible or hidden — and the author is whoever owns the page the agent happened to read.
Instructions from one origin act on another with the user's cookies attached. The application receives a request it cannot distinguish from the user's.
A purchase, a send or a permission change is one click, and the set of actions the gate covers is narrower than users assume.
Authenticated page content leaves for inference. The user consented to an assistant, not to a transcript of their mail.
The completion selects a click on a real, signed-in application, and nothing authenticates its intent.
Every authenticated origin in the profile is in scope for every page the agent reads — authority pooled in one cookie jar.
The extension update channel is automatic: one silent update changes the code that reads every page, with no further decision by anyone.
An extension is one click to install and appears in no inventory; assistant sidebars ship enabled to an installed base nobody enrolled.

capabilities.note: A dedicated profile with a narrow set of signed-in origins — the control that converts an unbounded blast radius into a bounded one.
Confirmation before consequential clicks, with the covered set defined by consequence rather than by what the product found convenient.
Strip hidden and off-screen content at extraction, before the page becomes context. Bounds the injection rather than preventing it.
In-browser inspection of what the agent read and clicked — the only vantage point that sees either, and often the only telemetry available.
An allowlist on where the agent may browse and what may leave with it, enforced outside the loop.
Classify and redact what page content may leave for inference, because the pages are authenticated ones.
Review and narrow the standing sessions the profile holds; each signed-in origin is authority the agent inherits.
Bound the pace of authenticated actions, because the applications themselves will not distinguish agent from user.

scenarios.title: A hostile page steers the agent

steps.note: The user asks for something routine — compare prices, book a slot.
The agent navigates; the browser fetches whatever the task surfaces.
A page comes back carrying hidden text addressed to the agent.
The page becomes context, indistinguishable from the user's goal.
The next click lands on a signed-in origin with the user's cookies attached.
A legitimate request against the user's own mail.
The browser fetches the inbox on the standing session.
Mail content returns — including messages written by strangers, which are now model input.
The inbox leaves for inference, which is more than the user pictured sharing.
A silent update arrives over the store's channel into the extension host — the code that reads every page has changed with no decision by the user.
The updated extension sees and can act on every authenticated page the profile reaches.

archetypes.title: Vendor coding and coworker agent
summary: A vendor-built agent loop in a terminal or editor, driven by a developer who is present, with read and write access to a working tree, a shell, and whatever tool servers the project's configuration file admits — a file that arrives with the clone.
description:
The defining property is the human in the loop and the fact that the loop is scoped to a task. The developer starts it, watches it, and is the approval gate for the actions that matter. Most of this archetype's security posture rests on that gate being real rather than nominal — and approval fatigue is the failure mode that makes everything else matter. A gate that fires on every file write trains the developer to accept, so the architectures that hold up narrow what needs approving: sandboxed execution, tool permissions scoped in advance, and default-deny egress, so the prompts that do fire are rare enough to read.
The tool plane is what makes it more than an editor plugin. The agent reads a project configuration file to decide which tool servers to launch and trust, and that file usually ships in the repository — cloning a project can register tool providers the developer never chose. The disclosed vulnerability pattern in this archetype is overwhelmingly about that file: injecting into it, swapping its contents after approval, or getting it auto-registered without a prompt. Meanwhile everything the agent reads — source files, manifests, issue text, tool output — is untrusted input with the same standing as the developer's instruction.
Unlike the other endpoint archetypes, this one partially has a governance plane — but it belongs to the vendor, and it is drawn that way: managed settings, a tool-server allowlist and audit export are published surfaces of the vendor's control plane, not services the organisation operates. In a managed deployment they are the difference between a governed tool and a shadow one; in the default install none of them are on, and the same binary runs with no policy, no audit and no inventory entry. There is no independent governance column to draw.
distinguishedBy:
Against the personal autonomous harness: this agent is invoked, not triggered; reads content the developer chose to clone, not messages from strangers; holds credentials the vendor issued for a session, not long-lived keys in a dotfile; and is an outbound client with no listening port. It also has an administrator available — managed settings, an audit trail and a policy file — which the harness archetype cannot have at all.
Against a sandboxed cloud execution service: the same agent run by the vendor on their infrastructure gets an isolated filesystem, default-deny egress and a clean teardown. Here it runs on a machine that also holds the developer's SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profile, and nothing separates them from the agent's shell.

exemplars.name: Terminal and CLI coding agents
exemplars.note: Vendor agent loops that run in a shell against a working directory, with a permission model for file writes and command execution and support for project-scoped tool servers.

exemplars.name: IDE-embedded agents
exemplars.note: The same loop inside an editor, where the tool-server configuration lives in a dotfile in the repository. This is the specific location that has repeatedly proven to be a code-execution path when it can be written or swapped between approval and use.

exemplars.name: Managed enterprise deployments
exemplars.note: The same product with centrally managed settings, an allowlist of permitted tool servers and exported audit. The architecture is unchanged; the vendor control plane being switched on is the difference.

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: Present, watching, and the approval gate. The archetype's posture depends on that staying true, which is why every other control exists to keep the prompts rare enough to read.

blocks.title: Repository content
blocks.note: Source files, dependency manifests, issue and PR text — and the agent configuration dotfile, all arriving together in the clone. Contributed to by people who are not the developer, and read into context as though it were instruction.

items.label: Code & project docs
items.note: A repository is a document the attacker may have contributed to.

items.label: Tool config dotfile
items.note: The tool-server declaration that ships with the code. The single most attacked artifact in this archetype.

blocks.title: Agent client
blocks.note: The terminal or editor the developer drives, and the vendor's loop behind it running as that developer. Outbound only — it accepts no connections, which is the single largest structural difference from a personal agent harness.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decides the next edit or command from the task and everything it has read so far.

items.label: Approval gate
items.note: Blocks on writes and commands. Effective in inverse proportion to how often it fires — a prompt on every action is a click-through.

items.label: Session credentials
items.note: Vendor-issued and session-scoped, the meaningful improvement over a long-lived key in a file. The developer's other credentials on the same machine are not.

blocks.title: Vendor service
blocks.note: The inference API plus the published surfaces of the vendor's control plane — the partial governance this archetype has, operated by the vendor rather than the organisation. Everything behind the published interfaces is the vendor's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The published interface. The completion it returns drives file writes and commands.

items.label: Managed settings
items.note: Centrally enforced permissions and a tool-server allowlist the developer cannot override. Off by default; the difference between a governed deployment and a shadow one.

items.label: Session audit export
items.note: Exported prompts, tool calls and approvals. In an unmanaged install there is no record at all.

blocks.title: Tools & servers
blocks.note: Everything here runs as the developer, on a machine that also holds their SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions. Admission is the configuration file — which arrived with the clone.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read and write across the working tree, and often beyond it. Scope is a setting, not a boundary.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution with the developer's full authority when it runs outside the sandbox.

items.label: Local MCP servers
items.note: Child processes launched over stdio with the developer's privileges, admitted by the config file.

items.label: Tool configuration
items.note: The admission decision for the whole plane. Injection into it, swapping it after approval, and auto-registration are this archetype's disclosed code-execution paths.

blocks.title: Sandboxed execution
blocks.note: Where builds, tests and shell commands run when isolation is on. Containing execution is what turns "approve every command" into "approve the ones that leave the box".

items.label: Isolated runtime
items.note: A container or VM whose own configuration the agent must not be able to reach.

blocks.title: Remote services
blocks.note: What the tool plane reaches over the network: remote tool servers, package registries and the web — and where fetched content comes back in as context indistinguishable from the developer's instruction.

items.label: Remote tool servers
items.note: Third-party providers reached over an explicit, scoped, revocable grant — a better trust story than a local child process, but their tool descriptions are still model input.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: Dependencies and their metadata, authored by strangers and read into context.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: Attacker-writable content that re-enters the loop as context, and the exfiltration path out.

edges.label: task / approval
edges.note: The developer states the task and answers the approval prompts. Whoever is at the machine is the developer, as far as the agent is concerned.

edges.label: clone — code & config
edges.note: Repository content is read into context as instruction, and the tool-server declaration arrives in the same clone. A contributor is not the developer, and nothing authenticates the difference.
Inference on a vendor-issued, session-scoped credential that expires on its own. The completion that comes back is unauthenticated content, and it drives the tool calls.

edges.label: enforced allowlist
edges.note: Managed settings pin which tool servers may be admitted, enforced outside the file they govern. Only present in managed deployments — the common install has no such edge.
Tool calls out with whatever scope the configuration granted; file contents and tool results back into context.
Command execution routed into isolation. The control that lets the approval gate fire rarely enough to be read — and still opt-in in many deployments.
Remote tool calls and package fetches out; descriptions, dependencies and page content back in as model input. Also the path an exfiltration attempt takes.

risks.note: Source files, manifests, issue text and test output are four unrelated paths into the same context window, none of which is the developer's instruction.
The configuration file admits the whole tool plane and arrives with the clone. Injecting into it, swapping it after approval and auto-registration are the disclosed paths.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and it drives file writes and shell commands.
A gate that fires on every action trains the developer to accept, and an accepted prompt is not oversight.
A binary a developer can fetch without asking anyone. Unmanaged, it has no policy, no audit and no inventory entry — and that is the common case.
The machine also holds SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions, and nothing separates them from the agent's shell on the way out.
A remote server's grant is explicit and revocable, but says nothing about whether its tool descriptions are honest — and they are model input.
Local MCP servers are third-party code running as the developer, in the same trust zone as everything else.

capabilities.note: Make isolated execution the default path for commands, so the approval gate only fires for actions that leave the box.
A managed allowlist of tool servers, enforced outside the configuration file it governs — never auto-registration from a cloned repo.
Provenance and behavioural review before a server is admitted; pin versions so an update is a decision.
Per-tool grants scoped to the working tree and the task, instead of the developer's full authority.
Non-overridable approval on consequential actions, kept rare by the surrounding controls so each prompt is actually read.
Default-deny outbound with an allowlist — the last boundary between a repository-borne injection and an attacker's collection endpoint.
Treat repository content as untrusted on read; it cannot be authenticated, only bounded.
Keep the developer's SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profile outside the agent's reachable filesystem and environment.
Turn on session audit export — prompts, tool calls and approvals — so an incident is reconstructable.
Find the installs that never enrolled, because this archetype spreads one developer at a time.

scenarios.title: The developer asks for a change

steps.note: The task is stated by a human who will stay for the whole session.
The model plans on a session-scoped credential; the completion becomes the next action.
Edits and commands execute with whatever scope the configuration granted.
Commands run contained, so only the actions that leave the box need a prompt.
The diff comes back to the person who asked, who approves what matters.

scenarios.title: A clone brings its own tool servers

steps.note: The tool configuration dotfile arrives with the code, authored by whoever last committed.
Declared servers launch as the developer — unless a managed allowlist enforced outside the file says otherwise.
A declared remote server is reached, and its tool descriptions enter context as model input.

scenarios.title: An injection in the tree phones home

steps.note: A hidden instruction in a source file or manifest is read into context.
The instruction shapes the completion, which the loop treats as the plan.
The plan becomes a file write or command, inside whatever scope the tools hold.
The exfiltration attempt has to cross the egress allowlist — the last control standing.

archetypes.title: Desktop assistant with computer use
summary: A consumer-shaped desktop application that reads local files and drives the graphical interface — moving the pointer, typing, and clicking through applications that have no API and no concept of an agent operating them.
description:
Computer use is the distinguishing capability and the distinguishing problem. When an agent acts through the GUI it inherits every application already open and signed in, through an interface built entirely on the assumption that a human is driving. There is no authorization decision available at the point of action: the application receives a click. Tool permission scoping works when tools are named and enumerable; here the tool is "the screen", and the reachable action set is everything a person at that desk could do. The controls that remain are containment — a contained desktop with its own filesystem and accounts — and the approval gate.
The input side is broad. The assistant reads whatever the user points it at: documents, spreadsheets, mail, screenshots. Any of those may have been authored by someone else, and screenshot text carries no provenance at all. Connectors are the third axis: standing OAuth grants into mail, calendar and storage, authorised once in a moment of enthusiasm, scoped to a service rather than a task, and outliving the conversation that prompted them.
There is no governance column here, and its absence is the finding. The only policy plane in this architecture is the operating system's permission prompts — one-time consent dialogs gating file access, screen recording and input control, granted per capability and never per action. They are drawn on the request path because every screen and file operation crosses a grant made once; nothing organisational sits behind them unless device management is imposed on the endpoint from outside this drawing.
distinguishedBy:
Against the agentic browser: that one's authority is a cookie jar and its input is a web page. This one's authority includes the local filesystem and every open desktop application, and its input includes screenshots — where an injection can be a picture of text.
Against the coding agent: same vendor discipline around credentials and updates, but no working directory to scope to and no repository to blame. The coding agent's blast radius is a project; this one's is a desktop.

exemplars.name: Desktop assistants with a computer-use mode
exemplars.note: A consumer application with local file access and an opt-in mode that drives the GUI, usually inside a contained virtual desktop rather than the user's own session.

exemplars.name: OS-integrated assistants
exemplars.note: Assistants shipped with the operating system, holding read access across local content and increasingly the ability to act in first-party applications.

blocks.title: User
blocks.note: Grants access, sets the task, and approves the actions the product decides to ask about. The broadest authorization decisions here are the ones made once, in a dialog.

blocks.title: Docs & screen content
blocks.note: Files, mail, spreadsheets and screenshots the assistant reads. Any of them may have been authored by someone else, and screenshot text has no provenance at all — the hardest input on this diagram to filter.

items.label: Documents & mail
items.note: Authored by anyone, read into context as though the user wrote it.

items.label: Screenshots
items.note: Text as pixels — an injection can be a picture of an instruction.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API and the vendor's connector broker — the published surfaces. Everything behind them is the vendor's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Receives document text and screenshots; the completion drives a click on a real application.

items.label: Connector broker
items.note: Holds the OAuth grants into the user's services and exercises them on the assistant's behalf.

blocks.title: Assistant application
blocks.note: The window the user talks to and the loop behind it: reads content, plans, and issues file operations or screen actions. Installed by the user, and in no inventory.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Plans the next file operation or screen action from the task and everything read so far.

items.label: Local file tools
items.note: Read and often write across the user's documents. Folder selection is a preference, not an enforced boundary.

items.label: Action approval
items.note: The only authorization point available for GUI actions, because the applications being driven have none. Its coverage is a product decision.

blocks.title: OS permission layer
blocks.note: The operating system's consent prompts — file access, screen recording, input control — are the only policy plane this architecture has. Each is granted once, per capability, and covers every future action that capability enables.

items.label: Screen recording grant
items.note: Approved once; every subsequent capture rides the same consent.

items.label: Input control grant
items.note: The grant that turns a completion into a click.

items.label: File access grant
items.note: Folder-level consent that the assistant's tools inherit wholesale.

blocks.title: Contained desktop
blocks.note: A separate virtual desktop with its own filesystem and accounts, where computer use runs in the target state. Where products run uncontained, these actions land on the user's own desktop and the approval prompt is the sole control.

items.label: Screen & input control
items.note: Pointer, keyboard and capture — the tool that cannot be enumerated.

items.label: GUI applications
items.note: Driven through interfaces that cannot tell an agent from a person.

items.label: Contained workspace
items.note: The files and sessions the agent can reach when containment is on.

blocks.title: Connected services
blocks.note: Mail, calendar and storage reached through standing OAuth grants. Authorised once, scoped to a service rather than a task, and outliving the conversation that prompted them — this archetype's reach extends well beyond the machine.

items.label: Mail & calendar
items.note: The grant that reads one invite reads the whole calendar, on every turn.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Cloud documents pulled into context through a grant the user forgot they gave.

edges.label: task / approval
edges.note: The task in and the approvals back. The consent that matters most was granted once, in a dialog, and covers every future turn.

edges.label: read into context
edges.note: Documents and screenshots become context. Screenshot text has no provenance, so nothing upstream can classify who wrote it.
Document text and screenshots leave for inference — usually more than the user pictured — and the completion that returns drives a click on a real application.

edges.label: capability use
edges.note: Every file, screen and input operation crosses a grant the OS collected once. The prompt is per capability, never per action.

edges.label: screen actions
edges.note: Granted actions land in the contained desktop; screen content comes back as context. Without containment this edge points at the user's own session instead.
The broker exercises standing grants; mail and documents return and re-enter context — the same indirect injection path as retrieval, through a grant nobody is watching.

risks.note: Documents, mail and screenshots all reach the same context window, and the screenshot path carries text with no provenance at all.
Connector content — mail written by strangers, shared documents — re-enters context through a standing grant, on every turn.
Documents and screenshots leave for inference, which is usually more than the user pictured sharing.
The completion drives a pointer on a real application, and nothing authenticates whose intent it encodes.
The driven application receives a click. There is no authorization decision available at the point of action — only containment and the approval prompt upstream.
GUI applications carry whatever authority is already signed in, and cannot tell an agent from the person the session belongs to.
Standing grants scoped to a service, not a task. Each was consented to individually; the reach is their union, and nobody consented to that.
A consumer application installed by the user, appearing in no inventory, with the OS consent dialogs as the only policy anyone applied.

capabilities.note: Keep computer use in the contained desktop with its own filesystem and accounts — never the user's own session. The archetype's primary control.
Approval before consequential actions, with coverage set by consequence — it is the only authorization the GUI path will ever have.
Classify documents and extracted screenshot text on the way in; bound what an embedded instruction can achieve.
Narrow the OS grants — folder-scoped file access, screen recording only for the contained display — so the one-time consents cover less.
Redact what document and screen content may leave for inference, because the inputs are the user's private files.
Default-deny network from the contained desktop, so a hijacked session cannot deliver its findings.
Review and narrow the standing connector grants; expire the ones no task has used.
The contained desktop gets its own accounts and sessions, not the user's — containment includes credentials.
Endpoint telemetry on the assistant process and its file reach — screen action sequences are the hardest thing here to reconstruct after the fact.

steps.note: A routine request against the user's own documents.
The folder is read into context — including files the user never opened themselves.
The documents leave for inference.
The summary returns; the data already left in step three.

scenarios.title: A poisoned document drives the screen

steps.note: An instruction embedded in a shared document — or in a screenshot as pixels — enters context.
The instruction shapes the completion, which the loop treats as the plan.
The grants were given weeks ago; no new consent is requested.
Clicks land on GUI applications. Contained, the blast radius is the virtual desktop; uncontained, it is everything signed in.

scenarios.title: The connector grant outlives the task

steps.note: The assistant asks the broker for calendar context.
The standing grant reads the whole calendar, as it can on any turn.
Content authored by strangers returns through the broker.
It re-enters context with the same standing as the user's words.

archetypes.title: Local model runtime
summary: An open-weights model served on the user's own machine, listening on a local port so other local processes can call it. Chosen to keep data off a vendor's infrastructure, which succeeds — and moves every control the vendor was providing onto the device.
description:
The reason people run this is sound: prompts and documents never leave the machine, there is no per-token cost, and it works offline. The architectural consequence is that the guardrails, rate limiting, abuse monitoring and content policy a hosted API applies on the way in and out are simply absent, and nothing replaces them by default. The guardrail block in this drawing is the target state; in the common install it does not exist, and raw model output goes straight back to the caller.
The runtime is a local network service. It binds a port, speaks an HTTP API, and historically ships without authentication because the assumed caller is a process on the same machine. That assumption fails in two directions: any local process — including a browser tab, through a permissive CORS policy — can call it, and a runtime bound to a routable interface rather than loopback is reachable from the network. Who may bind the port and who may call it are the admission decisions of this architecture, and by default nobody makes them.
The supply chain is the axis specific to this archetype. Weights are large binaries fetched from public hubs, and several serialization formats execute code on load — the format matters more than the source, because a safe-by-construction tensor format from an unknown publisher beats a pickle-based one from a known publisher. The scan has to sit in front of the fetch, because the runtime is usually the thing doing the fetching.
There is no governance column, and that absence is the finding: no model inventory, no weight scanning pipeline, no policy on binding or sources exists anywhere in the default deployment. This runtime is installed by one person in an afternoon and appears in no inventory — every control named on this page presumes someone first learns it exists.
distinguishedBy:
Against self-hosted inference in a datacentre: identical software, entirely different operational reality. There the runtime has a network policy, an identity, a scanner in the pipeline and someone on call. Here its port is protected by the assumption that nothing else on the machine is hostile.
Against the other endpoint archetypes: this one is not an agent. It has no loop, no tools and no autonomy — it is a dependency the others consume. It earns its own architecture because its risks are supply chain and local exposure rather than agency.

exemplars.name: Local inference servers
exemplars.note: Desktop applications and daemons that download open-weights models and expose an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API on a loopback port for other local software to call.

exemplars.name: OS and vendor-provided local runtimes
exemplars.note: Platform-level local inference offered as a system service, with a managed model catalogue. Narrower supply chain, same local-service exposure.

exemplars.name: Public model hubs
exemplars.note: Where the weights come from. Publisher identity is verifiable to varying degrees; what the artifact does on load is a property of its format, not its publisher.

blocks.title: Unexpected callers
blocks.note: Anything on the machine that can open a socket — including a browser tab, where the runtime allows cross-origin requests. Not the caller the API was designed for, and nothing tells them apart.

blocks.title: Local applications
blocks.note: The intended consumers: editors, agents and tools on the same machine, calling the local API instead of a hosted one — and often built expecting a hosted API's safety floor.

blocks.title: Local HTTP API
blocks.note: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on a local port, frequently unauthenticated because the caller is assumed trusted by virtue of being local. Which interface it binds and who may call it are this architecture's admission decisions.

items.label: Completion endpoint
items.note: The published local interface every consumer on the machine shares.

items.label: Interface binding
items.note: Loopback is an assumption, not a policy. Bound to a routable interface, the runtime is reachable from the network.

items.label: Cross-origin policy
items.note: A permissive CORS policy lets any web page the user visits drive local inference.

blocks.title: Local guardrails
blocks.note: Input and output classification, deployed by the device owner because nobody else will. This block is the target state — in the common install it does not exist, and its absence is the archetype's defining property.

items.label: Input classification
items.note: The screening a hosted API would have applied on the way in.

items.label: Output classification
items.note: The floor under model behaviour that the weights alone do not provide.

blocks.title: Inference runtime
blocks.note: Loads weights, batches requests, serves completions. Also the process that fetches the weights, which is why the supply-chain control has to sit in front of the fetch. Whatever safety behaviour exists is whatever the weights carry.

items.label: Weight loader
items.note: Where a pickle-based format turns file opening into code execution.

items.label: Loaded model
items.note: Open weights with no provider-side guardrail, abuse monitoring or content policy.

blocks.title: Weights on disk
blocks.note: Multi-gigabyte artifacts whose format determines whether loading them is deserialization or execution — a more useful question than who published them.

items.label: Model files
items.note: Readable by any process with the user's privileges, and swappable by the same.

blocks.title: Public model hub
blocks.note: Distribution for open weights. Publisher identity ranges from verified to arbitrary, and neither transport security nor a signature says anything about what the artifact does when the runtime opens it.

items.label: Open-weights catalogue
items.note: Declared behaviour and actual behaviour are separate facts.

edges.label: completion request
edges.note: Local software calls the local API the way it would a hosted one — usually assuming a safety floor that is not there.

edges.label: unauthenticated request
edges.note: The same endpoint, reached by callers nobody intended: a browser tab through CORS, or the network if the binding is routable. Locality is standing in for authorization.
Requests pass through classification on the way in and completions on the way out — when the block exists at all.
Filtered prompts in, raw completions back. Without the guardrail block this is a straight pipe.

edges.label: fetch / load
edges.note: The runtime fetches artifacts to disk and loads them at start. For several formats the load is an execution event, which makes this the supply chain's last step.

edges.label: weight download
edges.note: Transport is authenticated and the publisher may be verifiable. Neither says what the artifact does when opened.

risks.note: Pickle-class formats execute code on load. The risk is a property of the artifact format, not of the publisher.
Publisher identity at publish time, nothing at load time — and a hub account is a takeover target.
Any local process can saturate the runtime; a browser tab can do it from a web page.
The artifacts sit on disk with the user's file permissions — readable by anything running as the user.
Installed by one person in an afternoon, in no inventory. Responding to a bad model release presumes someone knows this runtime exists.
The serving stack itself is fast-moving native code with its own CVE history, running unsandboxed.
Where this block is absent — the common case — raw model output goes straight to callers built expecting a hosted API's floor.
With no provider-side safety layer, whatever refusal behaviour the weights carry is the whole of the defence, and it is removable by fine-tune.

capabilities.note: Format and content inspection in front of the fetch — a scan that runs after the runtime opens the file has documented an incident, not prevented one.
Authenticate local callers rather than treating locality as authorization; a browser tab is local too.
Deploy the input and output classification a hosted API would have applied — nothing supplies it here by default.
Bound what any single caller can consume, because the callers share one unmetered port.
A device-enforced policy on whether local inference may run at all, from which sources, and bound to loopback only.
Restrictive file permissions and integrity checks on the artifacts, so a swap is detectable.
Which models, at which versions, from which sources, on which machines — the precondition for every response.
Find the runtimes nobody registered, derived from the machine rather than self-reported.
Evaluate what the weights actually do before serving them to other software — there is no provider evaluation to inherit.

steps.note: A local tool calls the OpenAI-compatible endpoint as if it were hosted.
The request crosses classification — if anyone deployed it.
The model serves the completion with whatever behaviour the weights carry.
The response returns with no provider floor under it.
A well-reviewed model name, a compromised artifact — the download verifies transport, not behaviour.
The runtime opens the file. In a pickle-class format, the load is the execution event, with the user's privileges.

steps.note: A visited web page calls the local endpoint through a permissive cross-origin policy.
Nothing distinguishes this caller from the intended ones.
The page now drives local inference — for free, and invisibly to the user.

archetypes.title: Local MCP and tool plane
summary: The fleet of tool servers running on a developer's machine and the configuration files that admit them. Not an agent — the substrate every local agent shares, and the place where this surface's disclosed vulnerabilities have concentrated.
description:
Every endpoint agent in this catalogue reads a configuration file to decide which tool servers to launch and what they may do without asking. That file is the admission decision for the whole tool plane — and it is an ordinary file: writable by the user, writable by anything running as the user, and frequently committed to the repository it configures. Three failure modes recur and need three different controls: injection into the file adds a server nobody approved; swapping it after approval means the thing reviewed is not the thing that runs; auto-registration admits a server with no approval step at all.
A local server is a child process with the user's privileges. There is no sandbox between it and the filesystem, no scope on what it may read, and no identity distinguishing it from the agent that launched it — over stdio there is nothing to authenticate to. Tool descriptions are model input: a hostile server does not need a vulnerability, it can simply describe itself persuasively, and descriptions are re-read on each connection, so an approved description is not a durable fact.
This drawing has no governance column, and its absence is the finding — sharpened here by the fact that the plane does have a management-plane edge: the configuration file itself, drawn as a governance path because admission is exactly what it decides. The only management plane this surface has is a user-writable dotfile. Allowlists enforced outside that file, integrity checking on it, and an inventory of what is admitted where all have to be imposed on the endpoint; none of them exist by default, and servers accumulate — added for one task, removed never.
distinguishedBy:
Against the agent archetypes that use it: those describe a loop and its authority. This describes the admission mechanism they all share. It is drawn separately because the vulnerabilities land here rather than in any one agent, and because fixing it fixes all of them.
Against a remote MCP server you publish: that is a service with an OAuth boundary, an operator and a tenancy model. This is a child process with your privileges and no boundary at all. They share a protocol and almost nothing else.

exemplars.name: Project-scoped tool configuration files
exemplars.note: Dotfiles in a repository declaring which tool servers an agent should launch. Ship with the clone, and have been the specific location of multiple disclosed code-execution paths.

exemplars.name: User-scoped and managed tool configuration
exemplars.note: The same declaration at user or device level. Managed variants let an administrator pin an allowlist the user cannot override, which is the only durable fix for auto-registration.

exemplars.name: Community tool servers
exemplars.note: Servers installed from package registries and run as child processes. Reviewed by whoever installed them, updated automatically, and holding the user's full privileges.

blocks.title: Repo-supplied config
blocks.note: A tool-server declaration that arrived with a clone, authored by whoever last committed to the project, and read on the next agent start.

items.label: Cloned declarations
items.note: The project speaks for itself about which servers to run — and the project has many authors.

blocks.title: Agent clients
blocks.note: Whichever agents consume the plane — coding agents, assistants, harnesses. Interchangeable: the plane outlives and is shared by all of them.

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: Approves servers on first use, and is also the privilege every server runs with. The approval covers what the file said at that moment, not what it says later.

blocks.title: Tool configuration
blocks.note: The admission decision for the whole plane, held in ordinary files. In the target state the file is write-protected from the plane it governs — left user-writable, a compromised server can add its own successor, which turns one bad package into a persistent foothold.

items.label: Project-scoped file
items.note: Ships with the clone; the single most attacked artifact on this surface.

items.label: User-scoped file
items.note: The same declaration at user level, shared by every project and every client.

items.label: Auto-approve rules
items.note: What runs without a prompt — a decision as consequential as which servers exist.

blocks.title: Local tool servers
blocks.note: Child processes over stdio, holding the user's privileges. No sandbox, no scope, no identity of their own, and nothing to authenticate to.

items.label: Stdio child processes
items.note: Every server is the user, as far as the filesystem and network are concerned.

items.label: Tool descriptions
items.note: What each server tells the model its tools do — model input, author-controlled, re-read on each connection.

items.label: Server credentials
items.note: Tokens for the services each server fronts, in environment variables or the config file itself — readable by every other server in the plane.

blocks.title: Package registry
blocks.note: Where servers are installed from and updated. Publisher identity is verifiable; behaviour is not, and behaviour changes on update with no further decision by anyone.

items.label: Community packages
items.note: Declared behaviour and actual behaviour are separate facts.

items.label: Auto-update channel
items.note: The code running with the user's privileges changes whenever the publisher ships.

blocks.title: Fronted services
blocks.note: The remote APIs and accounts the servers act on with their stored tokens — and where fetched content comes back in as model input.

items.label: Remote APIs
items.note: Reached with standing tokens, on behalf of whichever agent called.

items.label: SaaS accounts
items.note: The blast radius of a leaked server token, which every other server could read.

edges.label: task / approval
edges.note: The developer drives the agents and answers first-use prompts. The approval is of a description at a moment in time.

edges.label: tool calls
edges.note: Tool calls out with the user's authority; results and tool descriptions back into the agent's context as model input.

edges.label: ships with the clone
edges.note: Project-supplied declarations should be proposals admitted against an allowlist enforced outside the file. Auto-registration on clone is the failure that replaces.

edges.label: admits & launches
edges.note: The admission decision for the plane — the only management-plane relationship this surface has, and it is a user-writable file deciding it.

edges.label: install & update
edges.note: Publisher identity at publish time, nothing at launch time. An update changes the code running with the user's privileges without any further decision.
Calls out with stored tokens; content back in as context. A hostile response here enters whichever agent happens to be connected.

risks.note: A declaration authored by whoever last committed, admitted on the next agent start. This crossing is behind most of the surface's disclosed code-execution paths.
The file can change between approval and launch — the thing reviewed is not the thing that runs. Time-of-check-to-time-of-use, not access control.
Entries accumulate — added for one task, removed never. The plane is the sum of a year of individually reasonable decisions.
Tool descriptions are model input, author-controlled, and re-read on each connection — a persuasive description is an attack that needs no vulnerability.
A signature proves who shipped the package, not what it does — and what it does changes on update.
Child processes with the user's full privileges, no sandbox, no scope, and no identity of their own.
Every server can read every other server's environment. Isolation between them is a property nothing in this plane provides.
Standing tokens travel with every call, and any server in the plane could have read them first.

capabilities.note: An allowlist of admissible servers enforced outside the file it governs — the only durable fix for auto-registration. Stored beside the file, it shares the file's threat model.
Provenance and behavioural review before admission, and pinned versions so an update is a decision.
Run each server with its own filesystem and network policy instead of the user's privileges. The protocol will not provide this; the client has to.
Per-server scopes on what may be read and called, instead of the user's full authority for every tool.
Change detection on the configuration files — the control that catches the swap between approval and launch, which access control does not.
Broker per-server, short-lived tokens instead of standing secrets in environment variables and config files.
A first-use approval that re-fires whenever the declaration or the description changes, not once forever.
Treat tool descriptions as untrusted input; diff them between connections and surface what changed.
An inventory of what is admitted, on which machines, with which scopes — the control that makes the rest possible, and the one least often present.
Each server sees only its own service's token, so one compromised server is one account, not all of them.

scenarios.title: A clone brings its own tools

steps.note: The declaration arrives with the code, authored by whoever last committed.
On the next agent start the servers launch — admitted by a file, not a person, unless an allowlist intervenes.
Their tool descriptions enter the agent's context as model input.
Calls go out with stored tokens, on behalf of whichever agent connected.
The developer approves a server on first use, from its description at that moment.
The file changed between approval and launch. What runs is what the file says now — the failure integrity checking exists for.
An auto-update swaps the behaviour of a long-admitted server, with no new decision.
Its rewritten tool descriptions steer whichever agent connects next.
It reads its neighbours' tokens from the shared environment and exercises them — one bad package, every fronted account.
