archetypes.title: Personal autonomous agent
summary: An always-on daemon on a personal device that takes ambient messages from anyone who can reach its channels, runs an unattended agent loop with the user's own credentials, and keeps what it learns in files it will read back as instruction.
description:
The harness is a long-lived process, not an invocation. It owns the channel bridges, the agent loop, a heartbeat that fires with nobody watching, and a memory directory the next turn treats as context. Nothing about it is scoped to a task: it starts when the machine starts and ends when the user kills it.
Three properties make this a distinct architecture rather than a variation on a coding assistant. It listens — whoever can reach a bridge can address the agent, and the bridge is the authorization decision. It runs unattended — the heartbeat starts the loop with no human seeing the plan before the tools execute. And it remembers in a medium it re-reads as instruction — one successful injection written into memory survives restarts and re-executes on the schedule.
What the drawing does not contain is the finding: there is no governance plane. No agent identity distinct from the user, no policy engine consulted per tool call, no audit sink, no registry deciding what may be installed, no kill switch beyond killing the process. Every numbered capability on this page is something the endpoint has to impose, because the architecture supplies none of it.
distinguishedBy:
Against a vendor coding agent: the coding agent is invoked by a human who is present, reads content the user chose, holds session-scoped vendor credentials, and is an outbound client. The harness is triggered by strangers and by a timer, reads whatever arrives, holds long-lived keys the user pasted in, and listens on a port. Nobody has ever found a hundred thousand exposed coding agents, because a coding agent does not accept connections.
Against a cloud agent service: the same loop hosted by a provider gets an identity, a policy boundary, an audit trail and an administrator by default. Moving this architecture off the endpoint changes almost nothing about the loop and almost everything about the governance.

exemplars.name: OpenClaw
exemplars.note: The reference implementation of the pattern: a gateway daemon owning all state, channel bridges for a dozen messaging platforms, an embedded agent runtime, Markdown memory with a scheduled heartbeat, in-process skills from a public registry, and paired device nodes.

exemplars.name: Hermes Agent
exemplars.note: An independent implementation with a candid threat model, which states plainly that its deny rules guard against an honest-but-wrong agent rather than an adversarial one. Its self-improvement feature — the agent writing its own skills — is this archetype's persistence vector made into a product decision.

exemplars.name: Homegrown harnesses
exemplars.note: The long tail: a script, a messaging webhook, an API key in a dotfile, and cron. Structurally identical and considerably more common than either named project.

blocks.title: Unsolicited senders
blocks.note: Anyone who can reach a connected channel. On a public messaging network that is an unbounded set, and the message body is model input.

blocks.title: Owner
blocks.note: The person the agent acts for, addressing it over the same channels as everyone else.

blocks.title: Channel bridges
blocks.note: One adapter per messaging platform, each implementing its own sender check. The count of channels is the count of independent authorization surfaces — disclosed bypasses in this archetype cluster in newly added bridges.

items.label: Channel adapters
items.note: Per-platform inbound and outbound message handling.

items.label: Sender allowlist
items.note: The admission decision, enforced once for every bridge rather than per channel.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API, reached directly from the device over a key the user holds. Everything behind the published interface is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The published interface. The completion it returns drives the tool calls.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: One long-lived process that owns every piece of state: the loop that plans, calls tools and reads results back as context. Historically bound to all interfaces, which is how exposure scans found instances by the tens of thousands.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Plans, calls tools, reads the results back as context. Nobody reviews the plan.

items.label: Heartbeat
items.note: A periodic tick that starts the loop with no human present and re-reads the memory files. The mechanism that converts a one-time injection into a recurring one.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the message, the memory and the tool results into one prompt.

items.label: Secrets store
items.note: Long-lived provider keys and channel tokens in a config file the agent's own tools can read. A store, not a broker — the same secret every time, revocable only by hand.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: Cross-session plain-text files plus the embedded search over them. Written by the agent, read back as instruction on every subsequent turn including the unattended ones. This is the persistence primitive.

items.label: Memory files
items.note: Prose the next turn treats as instruction.

items.label: Search index
items.note: Retrieval over everything the agent has ever kept.

blocks.title: Tools & skills
blocks.note: Everything here runs as the user. The authority is the user account, not a scoped grant, so the reachable set is everything the user can reach.

items.label: Shell & file tools
items.note: Command execution and filesystem access with the user's full authority.

items.label: Local MCP servers
items.note: Tool providers launched over stdio. Admission is a config file the agent can usually write — tool registration is self-service for anything with code execution.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Prose plus executable code loaded into the daemon's own process. A skill has whatever the agent has.

blocks.title: Sandboxed execution
blocks.note: Where code execution goes when isolation is turned on. Drawn because it is the single most effective structural mitigation — and opt-in in most deployments.

items.label: Isolated runtime
items.note: A container or VM whose own configuration the agent must not be able to reach.

blocks.title: Public skill registry
blocks.note: An open marketplace of prose-plus-code extensions. Admission is publisher self-attestation; declared behaviour and actual behaviour are separate facts.

items.label: Community skills
items.note: Scanners that read declared behaviour have been bypassed repeatedly.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: What the tools reach with the user's credentials — and where fetched content comes back in as context indistinguishable from the user's own words.

items.label: Email & accounts
items.note: The user's own services, reached with the user's own sessions.

items.label: Websites & APIs
items.note: Attacker-writable content that re-enters the loop as context.

items.label: Paired devices
items.note: Companion devices exposing camera, screen and remote execution. The grant is to the harness — so it is also a grant to anything that has compromised the harness.

edges.label: unsolicited message
edges.note: Any party who can reach a channel can address the agent. The bridge is the admission decision.

edges.label: instruction / reply
edges.note: The bridge decides the sender is the owner from the messaging platform's own identifier — as strong as the platform makes it, with no second factor.
Normalised messages in; rendered replies out, to wherever the agent addresses them.
A bearer token from the local secrets store, unscoped and long-lived. The completion that comes back is unauthenticated content that drives tool calls.
The loop writes what it learns and reads it back as instruction on every later turn — including the unattended ones.
Tool calls out, results back into context. No policy decision sits on this path by default.
Only present when isolation is enabled. The common deployment runs without it.

edges.label: install
edges.note: No signature the runtime verifies against a trusted root, and no admission decision by anyone but the installing user.
Actions out with the user's credentials; fetched content back in as context. The primary injection path once the agent is running.

risks.note: The message body is model input, from an unbounded set of senders.
Memory is prose the next turn treats as instruction. One injection that writes here survives restarts and re-executes on the heartbeat.
Fetched content re-enters the loop as context indistinguishable from the user's words.
Nothing registers the agent with anyone. Organisations discover these by scanning for them.
The heartbeat restarts the loop unattended; nothing bounds what a bad turn spends.
Credentials sit at rest inside the same blast radius as the code that reads them.
Admission is publisher self-attestation, for artifacts that are prose plus code.
Bridges, skills and MCP servers are all third-party code in one process.
The MCP config file is agent-writable in most deployments, which makes tool registration a self-service operation for an attacker with code execution.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and it drives the tool calls.
Unattended triggering, unscoped authority and no approval gate compound here.
Replies go wherever the agent addresses them — not necessarily back to the sender who prompted the turn.

capabilities.note: Classify inbound content before it reaches the loop; treat every message as untrusted.
One sender-admission decision enforced for every bridge, not re-implemented per channel.
Replace pasted long-lived keys with brokered, short-lived, scoped credentials.
Treat memory as untrusted input on read; scope and review what gets written.
Per-tool grants instead of the user's full authority.
Make the isolated runtime the default execution path, not an option.
Provenance and behavioural review before a skill or server is admitted.
An allowlist on where the agent may send data, enforced outside the loop.
A human approval gate on consequential actions, because no one saw the plan.
A stop that is not "find the process and kill it" — and that survives the heartbeat.

steps.note: The message arrives from an unbounded set of senders. The allowlist is the gate.
The body enters the loop as model input.
The model plans; the completion comes back and is treated as the plan.
Tool calls execute with the user's authority — no human sees the plan first.
Actions land on real accounts; anything fetched re-enters as context.
The reply goes wherever the agent addresses it.

scenarios.title: The heartbeat fires with nobody watching

steps.note: The tick re-reads memory — including anything an attacker wrote there last week.
Recalled prose becomes the instruction for this turn.
The loop acts, unattended.
A one-time injection has become a recurring implant on the schedule.
Prose plus code, admitted on the strength of the publisher's own description.
It loads into the daemon's process with everything the agent has.

deviations.subject: No governance plane is drawn
deviations.reason: This archetype has none — no agent identity, no policy engine, no audit sink, no registry, no kill switch. The other architectures in this catalogue draw a governance column; the empty space where it would be is this diagram's finding, and inventing one would misrepresent the pattern.

archetypes.title: Enterprise AI chat with connectors
summary: A general-purpose assistant subscription for the workforce, where each user connects their own data sources and uploads their own files. The grant model is per user and per connector, which makes the organisation's total exposure a sum nobody computes.
description:
The contrast with a tenant-wide assistant is entirely in who consents. There, an administrator grants the vendor the corpus once. Here, each user authorises their own connectors — a repository, a drive, a ticket system — and the organisation's data path to the vendor is the union of thousands of individual decisions, each made in a modal dialog. Any single grant is usually appropriate; what nobody has is the aggregate, which makes the archetype's core problem visibility rather than permission.
File upload is the parallel path and often the larger one. A user pasting a document into a chat window has moved data across the boundary with no connector, no grant and no record beyond what inspection catches. Every control that watches connectors misses this entirely, which is why in-browser and network inspection carry more weight here than the vendor's own administrative surface does.
The remaining structural question is the boundary between the enterprise tenant and the consumer product. The same vendor typically offers both, the consumer one has different retention and training terms, and the difference between being in your tenant and being signed into a personal account is a session cookie. Tenant restriction enforced at the edge is what makes the enterprise agreement — retention limits, training opt-out, audit export — apply to the traffic at all.
distinguishedBy:
Against the tenant-wide assistant: administrator-granted and corpus-wide there, user-granted and connector-by-connector here. That single difference relocates the control set from permissions governance to discovery and aggregate visibility.
Against shadow AI: this is the sanctioned version of the same traffic. The sanctioned tenant is where you want the traffic to go, and most of the work in this archetype is making sure it does.

exemplars.name: Enterprise assistant subscriptions
exemplars.note: Workforce-wide licences for a general assistant, with administrative controls over retention, training and which connectors may be enabled.

exemplars.name: Per-user connector catalogues
exemplars.note: Marketplaces of source connectors each user authorises for themselves, typically over OAuth, with the vendor holding the resulting grant.

blocks.title: Employee
blocks.note: Authorises their own connectors and uploads their own files. Every grant reasonable, the aggregate visible to nobody.

blocks.title: Chat surface & uploads
blocks.note: The browser tab or desktop client — the last point where the prompt, the attachment and the tenant it is going to are all visible to something the organisation operates.

items.label: Browser / client
items.note: The vendor's interface on your device. Which tenant a session lands in is decided by a cookie, and visible here.

items.label: File upload
items.note: The path no connector governance sees. A pasted document crosses with no grant, no scope and no record other than what inspection catches.

blocks.title: Identity & secure edge
blocks.note: Tenant assertion and inline inspection — the block doing most of the real work in this archetype, because the vendor's admin console cannot see traffic that never reached the managed tenant.

items.label: Identity provider
items.note: Establishes the user and, critically, which tenant they are in. Tenant restriction here is what stops the consumer product being an alternative.

items.label: Secure service edge
items.note: Inline inspection of prompts and uploads, and the enforcement point for which tenants and services are reachable.

blocks.title: Consumer product
blocks.note: The same vendor's unmanaged offering, reachable from the same browser with a personal login. Different retention terms, no administrative visibility, one cookie away.

items.label: Personal accounts
items.note: Authenticated to the provider and anonymous to the organisation. None of the enterprise terms apply to anything sent here.

blocks.title: Vendor chat service
blocks.note: Inference, conversation storage and the connector broker are all behind the published surfaces — only the interfaces you integrate with are drawn.

items.label: Managed tenant API
items.note: Where enterprise terms apply — retention, training opt-out, audit export. Everything the agreement promises depends on traffic arriving here.

items.label: Connector broker
items.note: Holds the OAuth grants users issued and calls their systems on their behalf. The grants persist after the conversation, the project and the employee.

items.label: Tenant configuration
items.note: Retention, training opt-out, connector allowlist, history export. Set once and rarely revisited against a product that ships new connectors.

blocks.title: User-connected systems
blocks.note: Repositories, drives and trackers, each authorised by an individual. Their union is the organisation's actual data path to the vendor.

items.label: Repos, drives & trackers
items.note: Reached as the user who consented — correct as access control, invisible to anyone trying to see the total.

items.label: Content authored elsewhere
items.note: Tickets and documents written by people outside the conversation, entering it as context through a grant one employee made.

blocks.title: Tenant governance
blocks.note: Tenant configuration you author, plus the discovery and inspection you run independently of the vendor — the half that covers uploads and the consumer tenant, which no vendor export ever will.

items.label: Tenant policy
items.note: Retention, training opt-out, which connectors are permitted. Re-review whenever the vendor ships a connector — the default for new ones is rarely off.

items.label: Connector inventory
items.note: Which sources are connected, by how many people, holding what classification — the aggregate no individual grant decision produces.

items.label: Shadow use discovery
items.note: Finding traffic to the consumer product and competing tools, independent of the vendor. Usually surfaces more data movement than the sanctioned tenant does.

items.label: Audit & detection
items.note: Vendor export plus first-party network and browser telemetry — the second part covers what the first cannot see.

edges.label: prompt & attachment
edges.note: Prompts and pasted files go in; responses render back into the browser as unauthenticated content.
The prompt and the upload are inspected here or nowhere. Connector governance does not see uploads, and the vendor's console sees them only after they have arrived.

edges.label: to the corporate tenant
edges.note: Authenticated into the managed tenant, where retention and training terms apply. Everything the enterprise agreement promises depends on the traffic arriving here.

edges.label: blocked or logged
edges.note: Where tenant restriction is absent this crossing simply succeeds, and none of the enterprise terms apply to anything that goes through it.

edges.label: connector retrieval
edges.note: The broker calls each system as the user who consented, on a standing OAuth grant scoped to a whole system rather than a task — and retrieved content enters the conversation as context.

edges.label: configure / enumerate / export
edges.note: Tenant policy goes down; grant enumeration and audit export come back — all of it dependent on the vendor exposing per-user grants and events to an administrator.

risks.note: A pasted document crosses the boundary with no connector, no grant and no record. Every control that watches connectors misses this path entirely.
The consumer version of the same product is one login away and carries none of the enterprise terms.
Consumer retention and training terms apply to whatever lands here, with no administrative visibility of the account even existing.
Thousands of individually appropriate consents whose union nobody computed — the organisation's data path assembled one modal dialog at a time.
Content authored elsewhere arrives through connectors as conversation context — the same indirect injection path as retrieval, through a grant one employee made.
The broker's OAuth grants outlive the conversation, the project and the employee who issued them.
What the vendor retains, retrieves and trains on per conversation is governed by configuration and contract, not by anything observable.
Responses are unauthenticated content rendered into a browser.

capabilities.note: Inline inspection plus tenant restriction — the control doing most of the real work, because it covers both connectors' blind spots: uploads and the consumer product.
Assert which tenant each user may reach and who is licensed; tenant restriction here is what makes the enterprise terms apply.
Inspect prompts and uploads in flight — the only record the upload path will ever produce.
In-browser visibility of which tenant a session is in and what is being pasted — the vantage the vendor cannot offer.
Block or log the consumer tenant at the edge; without enforcement the crossing simply succeeds.
Find the personal-account and competitor traffic that never touches the managed tenant — it is usually the larger flow.
Own tenant configuration as living policy — retention, training opt-out, connector allowlist — re-reviewed every time the vendor ships a connector.
Treat standing OAuth grants as non-human identities — inventoried, expiring, and revoked when the employee or project goes.
Govern by classification which systems may be connected at all, so individual consent cannot outrun policy.
Fuse the vendor's export with first-party edge and browser telemetry — only the combination covers uploads and the consumer tenant.
Treat connector-retrieved content as untrusted input in policy and user guidance — the vendor's guardrails are the only inline control.
Know what sensitive data sits in the systems users are connecting, before the grants aggregate it.

steps.note: A document is pasted into the chat — no connector, no grant, no record yet.
Inspection happens here or nowhere.
The traffic lands in the managed tenant, where retention and training terms actually apply.
The response returns and is rendered as unauthenticated content.
The same browser, but a personal login to the same vendor's consumer product.
The session looks almost identical; only tenant-aware inspection can tell the difference.
With tenant restriction, this is blocked or logged. Without it, corporate data leaves under consumer retention and training terms, invisibly.

scenarios.title: A connector grant outlives its project

steps.note: The broker keeps retrieving on a standing OAuth grant issued for a project that ended a year ago.
Grant enumeration surfaces the aggregate — which systems, how many people, what classification — and stale grants are revoked.

archetypes.title: Vendor low-code agent builder
summary: A vendor platform where non-engineers assemble agents from prompts, connectors and triggers. The agents are real, the authors are not engineers, and there is no code review between an afternoon's work and something that acts on production data.
description:
The builder is a self-service surface, and that is both the product and the problem. A business user can create an agent, grant it connectors, give it a trigger and publish it to colleagues without any of the checkpoints a software delivery pipeline would impose — no pull request, no staged rollout, no security sign-off unless the platform enforces one. The result is a population problem rather than an instance problem: individual agents are simple; the risk is four hundred of them, each with connector grants, each authored by someone who has left, and no way to list which reach customer data.
Credential inheritance is the specific technical trap. A low-code agent typically runs on connections authorised by its author, so a published agent lends its author's access to every colleague who uses it. A user who could not read a table directly can often read it through an agent someone else built, and neither party intended that. Whether the platform supports per-invoker authorisation rather than author-credential execution is the single question worth asking during evaluation.
The authoring surface is also an injection surface: instructions, knowledge sources and connector descriptions are assembled by someone who is not thinking about untrusted input, and a shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to. Because no sandbox or runtime enforcement can be inserted into a vendor's execution, every control drawn here is a population control — inventory, publication gating, connector policy, and audit that can retire what nobody uses.
distinguishedBy:
Against the vendor action agent: that is one agent the vendor built and you configured. This is a platform on which your own people build many, and the unit of concern moves from the configuration of one to the governance of a population.
Against an internal AI platform you operate: same intent — a paved road for many builders — with the paving done by a vendor. You inherit their guardrails and their environment model, and you cannot add a deployment gate they did not build.

exemplars.name: Suite-embedded agent builders
exemplars.note: Low-code agent authoring bundled with a productivity or CRM suite, available to any licensed user by default unless an administrator turns it off.

exemplars.name: Standalone agent-building platforms
exemplars.note: Vendor platforms whose product is the builder itself, with connector marketplaces and publication to internal or external audiences.

blocks.title: Citizen builder
blocks.note: Authors the instructions, attaches the connectors, and publishes. Not operating under code review, and frequently no longer at the company by the time the agent matters.

blocks.title: Agent consumers
blocks.note: Colleagues — and sometimes customers — using an agent built by someone else. Rarely aware of whose credentials it runs on.

blocks.title: Identity & entitlements
blocks.note: Authenticates builders and consumers, and restricts who may build at all — the bluntest and often most effective population control. Whether the consumer's identity, rather than the author's, reaches the connector is the archetype's decisive question.

items.label: User authentication
items.note: Builders and consumers both arrive here. Building typically requires no elevated role — the same permission as opening a document.

items.label: Invoker credentials
items.note: Per-invoker authorisation preserves the access model the organisation already has; author-credential execution bypasses it by publishing.

blocks.title: Attached knowledge
blocks.note: Folders, sites and documents attached to an agent as grounding. Often writable by more people than the agent's audience, which turns a shared drive into an instruction channel.

items.label: Grounding sources
items.note: Whoever can write to the attached folder writes instructions the agent will follow for every one of its users.

blocks.title: Agent builder platform
blocks.note: Authoring, hosting and execution are all the vendor's — only the published surfaces are drawn, and no deployment gate can be added that the vendor did not build.

items.label: Authoring surface
items.note: Prompt, connectors, triggers, publication — every one a security decision made by someone who was not asked to make one.

items.label: Agent runtime
items.note: Where the population of agents executes. One diagram stands for hundreds of near-identical instances.

items.label: Connector framework
items.note: The vendor's integration layer. Its authorisation model — author or invoker credentials — decides whether publishing an agent is also a privilege grant.

blocks.title: Connected systems
blocks.note: Whatever the connectors reach. The union across all published agents is the platform's real data footprint, and no single agent's author can see it.

items.label: Business data
items.note: Tables, files and records reached by agents nobody reviewed.

items.label: Mail & action paths
items.note: Connectors that send and write. A source of confidential data plus a path to send mail is the pairing worth banning outright.

blocks.title: Maker governance
blocks.note: Population management — who may build, what may be published, what is connected, and what can be revoked at once. Every control here is per-population, because reviewing individual agents does not scale to self-service creation.

items.label: Agent inventory
items.note: Every agent, its author, its connectors, its audience and its last use. The one control that makes the population tractable.

items.label: Publication gate
items.note: Review before an agent reaches an audience beyond its author — the nearest available thing to code review, if the platform offers it and it is turned on.

items.label: Connector policy
items.note: Which connectors may be combined and which environments allow publication. Blocking a pairing scales where reviewing agents does not.

items.label: Usage audit
items.note: Which agents ran, for whom, reaching what — the basis for retiring the ones nobody uses.

edges.label: authors & publishes
edges.note: Building an agent typically requires no elevated role. The permission to create something that acts on company data is the same permission as opening a document.

edges.label: uses a published agent
edges.note: The consumer authenticates to the platform. Whether that identity continues to the connector, or is replaced by the author's, decides whether the access model holds.
Authoring sessions and agent invocations both flow here — authenticated, but nothing about authentication says anyone reviewed what was built.

edges.label: grounding content
edges.note: Attached knowledge enters agent context as instruction. The write permissions on the source folder are the only gate, and they were never designed as one.

edges.label: connector read / write
edges.note: The archetype's decisive crossing. Author-delegated grants lend the author's access to every user; invoker-delegated grants preserve the access model the organisation already has.

edges.label: inventory / gate / run history
edges.note: Admission, publication review and connector policy go down; enumeration and run history come back. All of it is platform-reported — adequate here, because there is no way to build an agent off-platform.

risks.note: An agent running on its author's credentials lends that access to every colleague who invokes it — publishing becomes a privilege grant nobody intended.
Agents with write connectors act on production data with no review between authoring and effect.
Creation is self-service and retirement is nobody's job. The population grows by default, and organisations discover it by counting.
Each connector grant is defensible alone; the union across hundreds of agents authored by people who never met is nobody's decision and nobody's picture.
A shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to — an instruction channel wearing a grounding label.
Grounding sources are attacker-writable at the fidelity of ordinary file permissions, and poisoned content persists across every future invocation.
Grants authorised by a departed author keep executing for everyone still using the agent.
Agents and their connector grants outlive their projects and their authors; only inventory and usage audit notice.

capabilities.note: Build the inventory first — every agent, author, connector set, audience and last use. Every other population control depends on it.
Restrict who may build, and demand per-invoker authorisation so a published agent cannot lend its author's access.
Author connector policy — which connectors may combine, which environments may publish. Banning a pairing scales where per-agent review cannot.
Turn on the publication gate so review stands between an author and an audience — the nearest available thing to code review.
Treat every connection an agent holds as a managed non-human identity — owned, scoped, expiring, and revocable as a class.
Govern what connectors may reach by classification, so the platform's aggregate footprint is a decision rather than an accident.
Treat grounding sources as untrusted input; restrict attachable locations to ones with governed write access.
Run maker governance as a programme — environments, licensing, lifecycle and ownership transfer when authors leave.
Find the sensitive data inside connector reach before four hundred agents do.
Keep run history per agent and per consumer — the basis for retiring what nobody uses and investigating what someone did.
Assess the platform vendor's execution, isolation and guardrail claims — none of them are testable from your side.

scenarios.title: An afternoon's agent reaches production data

steps.note: A business user signs in with the same role they use to open documents.
Prompt written, connectors attached on the author's own grants, trigger set, published to the team.
The publication gate reviews it — if the platform offers one and an administrator turned it on.
A colleague invokes the shared agent.
The connector executes on the author's credentials — the consumer just read a table they were never entitled to.

scenarios.title: A shared drive becomes an instruction channel

steps.note: Someone writes a document with embedded instructions into the folder an agent uses as grounding.
The injected instruction exercises the agent's connectors — reading what it can reach, sending what it can send.
Retrieved data flows back into the agent's response, for every user who asks.
Inventory shows agents whose author has departed — still published, still triggered, still holding grants.
Author-delegated connections keep executing until ownership is transferred or the grants are revoked as a class.

archetypes.title: Shadow AI services and extensions
summary: AI services in use that nobody sanctioned: consumer accounts on enterprise-grade tools, browser extensions with page access, and API keys expensed to a team card. You do not operate the vendor at all, so the target state drawn here is the discovery, brokering and DLP mesh around the unsanctioned use — not the use itself.
description:
This architecture is drawn because the alternative is pretending it does not exist. Every other architecture in this catalogue assumes someone decided to build or buy it; this one assembles itself from individually reasonable choices — a person with a deadline, a free tier, and a browser. The diagram is the environment as discovered, with the mesh you build around it drawn as the target state.
Three distinct paths carry data out, and they need different detection. A consumer account on a web service moves data through the browser under a personal login. A browser extension with host permissions reads pages continuously with no login at all. A direct API key on a corporate card moves data from a script or a server, never touches a browser, and shows up in expense data long before it shows up in network logs. Discovery is the whole control: there is no configuration to harden and no vendor to negotiate with, because the relationship was never formed — and the signals live in four systems owned by three different teams.
The outcome that matters is not blocking. Blocking a service without a sanctioned equivalent moves the traffic somewhere harder to see. The productive path is discovery, then a sanctioned tenant of the same class of tool, then enforcement that makes the sanctioned path the easy one — which is why this architecture's natural terminus is the enterprise chat architecture, and why they are a pair.
distinguishedBy:
Against the enterprise AI chat architecture: the same traffic, on the wrong side of every control. That one has a tenant, terms, an admin console and an audit export. This one has none, and the work is finding it rather than configuring it.
Against every other architecture here: those describe systems someone designed. This one describes what is discovered, and it is the only diagram in the catalogue where the governance column is the architecture rather than a plane beside it.

exemplars.name: Consumer accounts on enterprise tools
exemplars.note: A personal login to the same vendor the organisation may already pay for, with consumer retention and training terms and no administrative visibility.

exemplars.name: AI browser extensions
exemplars.note: Extensions requesting host permissions across all sites, installed in one click and updated silently. They read pages continuously rather than when invoked.

exemplars.name: Direct API keys on expense
exemplars.note: A provider key paid for on a team card and used from a script or a server. Invisible to browser controls and usually the largest single data volume of the three paths.

blocks.title: Employee
blocks.note: Solving a real problem with the tool that was available. Treating this as misconduct rather than unmet demand pushes the next attempt somewhere harder to see.

blocks.title: Extension distribution
blocks.note: Install and silent update for extensions holding page-read permissions — a supply chain with no enrolment step. The extension that was reviewed is not necessarily the extension that runs next week.

blocks.title: Browser & extensions
blocks.note: Carries two of the three paths — the consumer login and the extension — and is the single most valuable place to instrument on this diagram.

items.label: Web sessions
items.note: Personal logins to AI services from a corporate device. The tenant they land in is a cookie, not a policy.

items.label: Installed extensions
items.note: Read pages whether or not they are being used. The permission grant was one click, and updates need none.

blocks.title: Scripts & services
blocks.note: Code calling a provider directly — no browser, no login, no user identity, and frequently the largest volume of data leaving.

items.label: Scripts & servers
items.note: Server-to-server API traffic, invisible to every browser control on this diagram.

items.label: Unregistered keys
items.note: Expensed, shared and long-lived. Expense data finds these months before network analysis does, which makes finance a security telemetry source.

blocks.title: Secure service edge
blocks.note: The vantage point that sees destinations for every path, and content where inspection terminates. The backstop when device controls are absent or bypassed.

items.label: Inline inspection
items.note: Content visibility where TLS is terminated; destination visibility everywhere else.

items.label: Destination control
items.note: The containment instrument once discovery finds regulated data already in transit — blunt, and right at that point.

blocks.title: Consumer AI services
blocks.note: Reached with a personal login. Consumer retention and training terms apply, no contract governs anything sent, and no administrator can see the account exists.

blocks.title: Direct provider APIs
blocks.note: Model APIs reached with keys nobody registered. The highest-volume path and the least visible to anything watching browsers.

blocks.title: Discovery & response
blocks.note: In this architecture the control plane is the architecture. Everything else on the diagram is what it is trying to find.

items.label: Discovery correlation
items.note: Network telemetry, browser inventory, identity logs and expense records — four signals in four systems, and no one of them sees all three paths.

items.label: AI service inventory
items.note: What discovery found, triaged into sanction, replace or block. The artifact that turns a scan result into a programme.

items.label: Sanctioned alternative
items.note: A supported tenant of the same class of tool. Drawn as a control because it is one — blocking without it relocates traffic rather than stopping it.

items.label: Detection & response
items.note: What happens when discovery finds regulated data already moving — the part that is an incident rather than a policy conversation.

edges.label: uses what is available
edges.note: The path of least resistance runs through whatever tool was reachable when the deadline hit.

edges.label: install & silent update
edges.note: One click grants page access across all sites, permanently — the broadest standing grant in this catalogue, and the least deliberated.

Consumer-login and extension traffic both leave this way. An unmanaged or personal device carries the same traffic with none of this visibility, which is why discovery cannot rely on the endpoint alone.

edges.label: personal-account traffic
edges.note: Authenticated to the provider and anonymous to the organisation. Where inspection is absent this crossing simply succeeds, and no contract governs what happens next.

edges.label: direct API traffic
edges.note: Server to server, no browser, no user identity — invisible to every browser control drawn here, and often the largest volume of the three paths.

edges.label: network telemetry
edges.note: Where server egress transits the edge, destination telemetry is the one signal this path gives up voluntarily.

edges.label: discovery signal / containment
edges.note: Destination telemetry feeds discovery correlation, and containment flows back as destination policy once something regulated is found in transit.

risks.note: The least visible path — no browser, no login, no enrolment. This architecture is the risk drawn as a diagram, and this edge is its purest form.
Consumer retention and training terms apply to whatever is sent, and no relationship exists to negotiate anything better.
No scope, no grant, no minimisation — whatever the user pastes is what the service holds.
Third-party code with page access, installed in one click and updated silently, with no assurance behind it because no relationship was ever formed.
Declared behaviour and shipped behaviour are separate facts, and the update channel can change the second without touching the first.
An extension with host permissions reads every page — the exfiltration needs no prompt and no user action.
Unregistered keys have no budget ceiling anyone set; the first control to notice runaway spend is the corporate card statement.
What the provider retains and trains on is governed by default consumer terms nobody read on the organisation's behalf.

capabilities.note: Correlate network telemetry, browser inventory, identity logs and expense records — the only signal set that covers all three paths, and the precondition for every other control.
Destination visibility for every path and content visibility where inspection terminates — the backstop the endpoint cannot be.
Extension inventory and in-browser inspection — the only signal that finds an extension reading pages it was never invoked on.
Content inspection on what leaves through the browser — prompts, pastes and page reads alike.
Destination allowlists on server egress — the only inline control that sees the no-browser path at all.
Replace keys on cards with registered, brokered, expiring credentials so the direct-API path becomes governed rather than invisible.
Route legitimate script and service API use through a governed gateway — the sanctioned path for the builders who created this traffic.
Triage the inventory into sanction, replace or block, and stand up the sanctioned alternative — enforcement without it relocates traffic instead of reducing it.
For services that stay, form the relationship discovery revealed was already in place — assessment, contract, tenant.
Treat regulated data already in transit as an incident, with containment flowing back to the edge as destination policy.
Keep the first-party traffic record — for these services it is the only audit trail that will ever exist.

steps.note: A personal login to an AI service, from a corporate device, solving a real problem.
Destination telemetry names the service even where content inspection is absent.
Until enforcement exists this crossing succeeds, under consumer terms, invisibly to any administrator.
Discovery correlates the traffic with identity logs; the inventory triages the service into sanction, replace or block.
One click grants page access across all sites; updates arrive silently thereafter.
Page content leaves attached to ordinary browsing — the traffic looks like the page loads it rides on.
Browser inventory, not network telemetry, is the signal that finds it — correlation is what turns two weak signals into one finding.
Server-to-server traffic on an expensed key — no browser control ever sees it.
Where the route transits the edge, destination telemetry is the only voluntary signal; expense correlation usually finds the key first.
Once found, the key is registered or revoked, spend is capped, and the traffic moves to a brokered, governed path.

archetypes.title: Tenant-wide assistant over your corpus
summary: A vendor-operated assistant granted standing access to the organisation's whole document estate, answering any employee's question by retrieving across it. You configure a tenant; you do not operate an architecture — the retriever, the index and the model are all behind a boundary you cannot inspect.
description:
Structurally this is retrieval-augmented generation with one difference that changes every control decision: the retriever, the index, the model and the orchestration are all inside the vendor's boundary. What you own is the identity that authenticates users, the grant that decides what the vendor may index, the permissions already sitting on the source content, the network path, and the contract. The drawing shows exactly that — the vendor block carries only its published surfaces, and every control sits on an edge you operate.
The security question is not "is the vendor's RAG pipeline sound". It is a permissions question you can answer without the vendor's cooperation: given that the assistant inherits a user's entitlements and can search the entire indexed corpus in one turn, what does each user turn out to be entitled to? Over-permissioned content that was safe by obscurity stops being safe the moment retrieval is exhaustive and instant. That is the dominant failure mode of the archetype, and it is a pre-existing condition the assistant surfaces rather than a flaw it introduces — which is why content permissions fidelity is the first capability on this page.
The second exposure is that indexed content is attacker-writable. Any document a colleague, a customer or an external collaborator can place into an indexed location is model input for every employee who later asks a related question. The injection point and the impact point are different users on different days, and the vendor's guardrails are the only thing between retrieval-borne instruction and whatever the assistant can do with it.
distinguishedBy:
Against an embedded retrieval assistant you build: there, the index, the retrieval-time ACL check and the guardrails are yours to design. Here every one of them is the vendor's, and your architecture is the grant model and the edges. Almost no capability transfers between the two.
Against an enterprise AI chat subscription: that archetype connects a general assistant to a handful of sources each user authorises. This one is granted the corpus up front, tenant-wide, by an administrator — the difference between a per-user data path and an organisational one.

exemplars.name: Tenant-wide productivity assistants
exemplars.note: Vendor assistants indexing the organisation's mail, files and chat and answering across all of it. Sold as a per-seat add-on to a suite the organisation already runs, which is why the grant decision often precedes any security review.

exemplars.name: Enterprise search assistants
exemplars.note: Standalone vendors that connect to many systems of record and build a unified index. Same shape, more connectors, and permissions mirroring is their central engineering claim — worth testing rather than accepting.

blocks.title: Employee
blocks.note: The person asking. The assistant answers with this user's entitlements, whatever those turn out to be — which is the whole game.

blocks.title: External authors
blocks.note: Anyone who can put a document into an indexed location — inbound mail, a shared folder, a guest in a workspace. Their text becomes context for employees who never opened it.

blocks.title: Managed workspace
blocks.note: The browser or client the employee types into — the last point where the prompt and the answer are visible to anything you operate. On this surface, in-browser inspection substitutes for application logging you will never get.

items.label: Assistant surface
items.note: The vendor's panel rendered in your browser. The prompt and response are visible here and nowhere else you control.

items.label: Browser & DLP controls
items.note: Device-resident inspection of what leaves. There is no vendor host to instrument, so this is the substitute.

blocks.title: Identity & secure edge
blocks.note: The identity decision and the network path — the two enforcement points that still bind on a surface where nothing behind the API is yours.

items.label: Identity provider
items.note: Authenticates the user to the vendor and carries the entitlements the assistant will inherit. Conditional access here still binds.

items.label: Secure service edge
items.note: Inline inspection of traffic to the vendor, and the control deciding which vendor AI services are reachable at all.

blocks.title: Vendor assistant
blocks.note: Retrieval, ranking, inference and orchestration, none of it observable — only the published surfaces are drawn. Whether index-time permissions stay in step with the source as content is reshared is the provider's central claim, and the central question for assurance.

items.label: Tenant API
items.note: The interface users reach. The token it receives is the access-control decision — everything retrieved is decided by the entitlements it carries.

items.label: Indexing connectors
items.note: The crawl and sync path the vendor runs under your indexing grant. Schedule, retention and permission mirroring are claims, not observations.

items.label: Tenant configuration
items.note: Where your policy lands — licensing, source scope, indexing exclusions. You author it; the provider enforces it; neither is verifiable by the other.

blocks.title: Systems of record
blocks.note: Mail, files, chat, tickets, wikis — the authoritative permissions live here, and every over-share predates the assistant. The permissions on this content are the real access control; the assistant reflects them, and reflects their mistakes.

items.label: Mail, files & wikis
items.note: The corpus the vendor indexes. Designed on the assumption that reaching content required knowing it existed.

items.label: Source permissions
items.note: The control the assistant inherits. Exhaustive retrieval turns every stale grant into a findable answer.

items.label: Indexing grant
items.note: One tenant-level authorisation deciding which repositories the vendor may crawl. A single administrative decision sets the assistant's entire reachable set.

blocks.title: Tenant governance
blocks.note: What remains enforceable on a vendor-operated service: who may use it, what it may reach, what is visible afterwards, and what the contract obliges the provider to do.

items.label: Tenant policy
items.note: Who is licensed, which sources are in scope, whether the assistant may act, what is excluded from indexing.

items.label: Exported audit
items.note: Whatever the vendor exports, at whatever fidelity and latency it chooses. Plan detection against traffic you can actually see.

items.label: Vendor assurance
items.note: Due diligence, contract terms and whatever red-team evidence the vendor shares. On this surface it substitutes for testing you cannot perform.

items.label: Shadow tenant discovery
items.note: Finding the tenants nobody declared, from traffic and expense data rather than anything the vendor supplies.

edges.label: question / answer
edges.note: The question goes in with this user's identity, and the grounded answer comes back rendered in a browser. Citations are the vendor's claim about its own retrieval.
The prompt is inspected here or nowhere. Once it reaches the vendor, only the vendor can see it, and only at the fidelity its export offers.

edges.label: user query / grounded answer
edges.note: The vendor answers as this user. Everything the assistant will retrieve is decided by the entitlements the identity assertion carries, so the token is the access-control decision.

edges.label: inbound content
edges.note: Whatever already governs writes to the repository is the only gate. Nothing AI-specific inspects a document on its way into an indexed location.

edges.label: crawl & sync
edges.note: The vendor's connectors read whole repositories under the standing indexing grant. Whether index-time permissions track the source as content is reshared is not observable from outside.

edges.label: configure / export
edges.note: Tenant policy goes down and audit events come back — both on the vendor's terms. You author the policy, the provider enforces it, and assurance exists to compensate for the fact that neither can verify the other.

risks.note: Produced jointly by the tenant-wide grant, pre-existing permissions and retrieval that is exhaustive where human search was not. No single decision is wrong; the combination is.
Any document an outsider can land in an indexed location is model input for every employee who later asks a related question.
The crawl carries poisoned content into an index you can neither inspect nor purge directly.
Prompts and grounded answers cross to the vendor here. Where inspection is absent they leave unobserved, and the vendor's export is the only remaining record.
The assistant inherits whatever entitlements the identity assertion carries — including ones that should have been revoked.
The entire vendor is one integrated component you did not build and cannot test — which is what makes assurance a control here rather than a formality.
One turn can retrieve across the whole indexed corpus, and how much is pulled into context per answer is invisible from outside.
The answer is unauthenticated content rendered into a browser. A cited document can be checked; what else was retrieved cannot be checked at all.
On a surface reached by signing up, undeclared tenants precede every other control problem.

capabilities.note: Fix the source permissions before the grant is made — the assistant makes every over-share findable, so entitlement hygiene is THE control on this surface.
Find over-shared and sensitive content in the repositories the grant covers, before exhaustive retrieval finds it for you.
Govern the entitlements the assistant inherits — joiner/leaver hygiene and conditional access on the identity path the vendor trusts.
Own the tenant configuration as policy — licensing, source scope, indexing exclusions, whether the assistant may act — and re-review it as the product ships features.
Inline inspection of the vendor path, and enforcement of which AI services are reachable at all.
Inspect prompts and responses at the browser — the one point you operate where both are still visible.
In-browser telemetry and control for a service with no vendor host to instrument.
Constrain and monitor which locations external parties can write into scope, and treat indexed inbound content as untrusted.
Assess the vendor's permission-mirroring, tenancy and retention claims as a supply-chain relationship — they cannot be tested directly.
Contractual commitments on retention, training use and breach notice — the only control that reaches past the published interfaces.
Combine the vendor's exported audit with first-party edge and browser telemetry; plan investigations around what you can actually see.
Discover undeclared tenants from network and expense data — the inventory problem precedes every other control.

steps.note: The question is typed into the vendor's surface — the last point first-party controls can see it.
The prompt is inspected on the way out, or never.
The identity assertion decides everything — the vendor retrieves as this user, across the whole indexed corpus, in one turn.
The grounded answer returns with citations that are the vendor's own claim about what it retrieved.
The answer renders. What else was pulled into context is not knowable from outside.
The crawl indexes everything the grant covers, including the folder shared to "everyone" in 2019.
An innocent question lands near the over-shared content.
The user is technically entitled to the document, so retrieval returns it.
Content that was safe by obscurity is now a cited answer. The permissions were the bug; the assistant is the reporter.

scenarios.title: A poisoned document steers an answer

steps.note: An outsider lands a document with embedded instructions in an indexed location — an email, a shared folder, a guest workspace.
The crawl indexes it like anything else.
A later employee's related question retrieves it, and the injected text shapes the answer — or the action, where the assistant can act.

archetypes.title: Third-party MCP server you consume
summary: A vendor-operated tool server your agents call over the network. You authorise it once, scope it as far as the vendor's OAuth scopes allow, and thereafter it both acts on your systems and writes into your agents' context — because tool names, descriptions and results are all vendor-controlled text your model treats as instruction.
description:
This is a supply-chain relationship with a property ordinary vendor integrations do not have: the vendor supplies text that your model treats as instruction. Tool names, descriptions and results all enter the context window. A hostile or merely careless server needs no vulnerability to influence your agent — describing itself persuasively is sufficient, and descriptions are re-read on each connection rather than fixed at approval time.
What you can verify is narrow and worth stating precisely. You can verify who the server is, at connection time, through OAuth. You can constrain what it may reach, to the granularity of the scopes the vendor chose to publish. You can see what left, if agent egress routes through something that inspects. You cannot verify the server's internal tool catalogue, you cannot put a policy decision point inside its execution, and you cannot test it the way you would test your own code. Those are properties of the boundary, not gaps in your programme — which is why the tool broker on your side is the only insertion point drawn.
Enterprise-managed authorisation is the single highest-value change available here. Moving admission to the identity provider — rather than each server's own consent screen — means a security team decides which servers the organisation may connect to, and revocation is one place rather than many. Accumulation is the quiet risk it addresses: servers are connected for one project, keep their grants, and outlive the reason.
distinguishedBy:
Against a remote MCP server you publish: there you are the resource server and the security work is building the tenancy model and scopes properly. Here you are the client, the scopes are someone else's design, and the work is admission and observation. Almost no capability transfers.
Against the local tool plane: that one is child processes with your privileges and nothing to authenticate to. This one has a real authorisation boundary, a revocable grant and an audit trail — a much better position that comes with the loss of any ability to inspect the code.

exemplars.name: Vendor-published MCP servers
exemplars.note: Major SaaS providers publishing remote tool servers for their own products, so agents can read and write records without a bespoke integration. The mainstream case.

exemplars.name: Aggregator and gateway MCP services
exemplars.note: Third parties fronting many downstream tools behind one server. One grant, many reachable systems, and the scope you approved is not the scope that ultimately gets used.

exemplars.name: Enterprise-managed connection
exemplars.note: Admission moved to the identity provider so a security team, rather than each individual user's consent click, decides which servers may be reached.

blocks.title: Agent user
blocks.note: Whoever the consuming agent works for. Their systems are what the vendor's tool results ultimately steer.

blocks.title: Consuming agent
blocks.note: The client side of the relationship — a workstation agent or a hosted one, it makes no difference to this boundary. Its authority over your systems is what the vendor's text steers.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Reads tool descriptions and results back as context, indistinguishable from instruction.

blocks.title: Tool broker
blocks.note: The only insertion point this relationship offers. Here a description can be pinned, a result can be size- and shape-checked, a write can wait for approval, and a call can be denied or logged.

items.label: Connection manager
items.note: Which servers this agent may reach, checked against the admitted list at connect time.

items.label: Description pinning
items.note: Descriptions are re-read on every connection; pinning is what notices when the catalogue you approved is not the catalogue that runs.

items.label: Approval gate
items.note: Reserved for the calls that write — reads are too frequent for a human to remain a real check.

items.label: Call log
items.note: Which tool, which agent, what arguments — captured here at your fidelity, because the provider's view belongs to the provider.

blocks.title: Egress inspection
blocks.note: What is going to this vendor and how much of it. On this surface, network position substitutes for the application logging the provider does not expose.

items.label: Secure service edge
items.note: Allowlists which tool vendors are reachable at all, and sees the volume the approval gate never will.

items.label: Content inspection
items.note: The last look at arguments and payloads before they cross to the vendor.

blocks.title: Vendor MCP server
blocks.note: An OAuth resource server whose tool catalogue, execution and downstream reach are not observable — only the published interface is drawn.

items.label: OAuth authorisation
items.note: The strongest authentication in this catalogue — a named client, an explicit scope, a grant revocable in one place. It says nothing about the honesty of the catalogue.

items.label: Tool interface
items.note: Tools, descriptions and results. All of it vendor-controlled text that will enter your agents' context as instruction.

blocks.title: Content from elsewhere
blocks.note: Records, documents and messages the server reads from systems outside this architecture, passed back as tool results. The vendor need not be hostile — it need only relay content from a system that is.

blocks.title: Other tenants
blocks.note: Everyone else on the same multi-tenant server. Their isolation from your grant and your data is the provider's claim, and one of the few things assurance can usefully ask about.

blocks.title: Consumption governance
blocks.note: Admission, inventory and assurance — the whole of what the consuming side actually controls in this relationship.

items.label: IdP-managed admission
items.note: Enterprise-managed authorisation moves the connect decision from each user's consent screen to a security team's allowlist — the highest-value change available.

items.label: Connection inventory
items.note: Which servers are connected, by whom, at what scope, when last used. Grants outlive their projects, and this is the only thing that notices.

items.label: Vendor assurance
items.note: Tenant isolation, retention, subprocessors, what happens to the data sent. The questions inspection cannot answer have to be answered by contract.

items.label: Call audit
items.note: The broker's call log, kept append-only and off the agent's write path.

edges.label: task / result
edges.note: The task goes in and the outcome comes back — shaped in part by text a vendor wrote.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: Every call to the vendor's tools passes through the broker, and every description and result passes back through it into context — the one place both directions are yours to check.
Approved and read calls leave with the runtime's identity attached, so the egress path can tell agent traffic from everything else leaving the network.

edges.label: OAuth-scoped invocation
edges.note: A named client with an explicit scope invokes the server; descriptions and results return. The return path is the risk — re-read on every connection, entering context as instruction.

edges.label: records from elsewhere
edges.note: Content the vendor reads from third parties reaches your agent through a connection authorised for something else — not observable from your side.

edges.label: shared infrastructure
edges.note: Tenant isolation is asserted, not verifiable — the specific claim third-party assurance exists to interrogate.

edges.label: admission & assurance
edges.note: The server is reachable only because the admitted list says so, and trusted only as far as the contract behind it — both decisions made on your side of the boundary.

risks.note: You can verify who the server is and never what its tools do. That asymmetry is the defining property of the archetype, and no control on your side closes it.
The catalogue, execution and downstream reach are all an untestable dependency you connected to production agents.
Descriptions and results are vendor-controlled text entering the context window as instruction — the injection arrives through a connection you deliberately made.
The scope was approved once; the breadth actually exercised across every later call is visible only at egress.
The session between your broker and the vendor's endpoint is the trust anchor for every tool result that follows.
The agent's authority over your systems is what a persuasive tool description steers.
Individually consented connections accumulate outside any list unless connect-time checks force them through one.
Arguments and payloads flow to the vendor on every call; what happens to them afterwards is contract, not observation.
Grants outlive their projects and people. Each connection was reasonable; the standing set nobody reviews is not.
Your grant and your data sit on infrastructure shared with every other tenant, isolated only as well as the provider claims.

capabilities.note: Keep the connection inventory — every server, owner, scope and last use — and check it at connect time so a grant not in the registry is not a grant.
Move admission to the identity provider — enterprise-managed authorisation puts a security team, not a consent click, in charge of which servers exist.
Request the narrowest scopes the vendor publishes and expose only the tools each agent needs — deny by default at the broker.
Gate the calls that write behind human approval, and only those — reads are too frequent for approval to stay real.
Classify descriptions and results before they enter context; pin descriptions so a changed catalogue is a detected event, not a silent one.
Allowlist which tool vendors agent traffic may reach — the enforcement the admitted list needs to be real.
Inspect what leaves in arguments and payloads — the substitute for application logging the provider does not offer.
Treat each OAuth grant as a managed non-human identity — owned, scoped, expiring, revoked in one place.
Log every call at the broker — tool, agent, arguments — at your fidelity, not the fidelity the provider chose.
Bound call volume and spend per server, outside the loop that generates the calls.
Assess tenant isolation, retention and subprocessors before admission — the questions no inspection can answer.
Contractual commitments are the only control on the vendor's side of this boundary — name them as one and keep them current.

steps.note: The agent requests a tool the broker actually exposes to it — scope was decided before the loop ran.
A write waits for approval; a read goes straight through with the runtime's identity attached.
The call crosses on a named, scoped, revocable OAuth grant.
The result returns — vendor-controlled text on its way into context.
The broker size- and shape-checks the result before the loop reads it as instruction.
A routine reconnection — descriptions are re-read every time, not fixed at approval.
A tool description has changed since review. Nothing on the vendor's side announces it.
Description pinning at the broker turns the silent change into a blocked connection and an alert.
A server connected for last year's project still holds a valid grant and still supplies context to agents.
The inventory flags the unused connection; revocation happens once, at the identity provider — the payoff of enterprise-managed admission.
