archetypes.title: In-app agent acting on vendor records
summary: An agent built into a SaaS product, acting on the records that product holds — resolving tickets, updating opportunities, issuing refunds. It writes, the writes land on your system of record, and what the vendor's agent may do is a tenant configuration you own.
description:
The distinction from a vendor assistant that answers questions is the write path, and it changes everything downstream. A wrong answer is a wrong answer; a wrong write is a changed record, an email that went out, a refund that was issued. Reversibility, not accuracy, is the property to design for — and it is a property of the vendor's action catalogue rather than of anything you build.
The attacker is frequently your own authenticated customer. The agent reads ticket text, form submissions and uploaded documents — content supplied by whoever opened the case — and acts on the tenant's records with the tenant's authority. Injection here does not require a breach; it requires filling in a text field. This is the archetype where indirect prompt injection has the shortest path from untrusted input to consequential action.
Your control surface is the action catalogue and the identity the agent runs as. Which actions it may take, on which record types, under which conditions, and whether a human approves the consequential ones are all vendor-exposed settings — usually generous by default, because the product is sold on autonomy. What you cannot do is insert a policy decision point into the vendor's loop: there is no place between the model's decision and the record write. Every control is therefore upstream of the loop — scoping what it may reach — or downstream of it, in review and reversal, which is why the governance column here is configuration, identity, outcome monitoring and a disable control rather than any runtime enforcement.
distinguishedBy:
Against the tenant-wide assistant: that one reads across your corpus and answers; this one acts within one product's data model and writes. The read archetype's central question is permissions; this one's is reversibility.
Against an autonomous action agent you build: identical shape, opposite ownership. There you design the action allowlist, the approval threshold and the compensating transaction. Here you choose from a menu, and what is not on the menu is not available.

exemplars.name: Customer service and support agents
exemplars.note: Vendor agents that resolve tickets end to end — reading the customer's message, searching knowledge, and issuing refunds or account changes without a human in between.

exemplars.name: CRM and ITSM in-app agents
exemplars.note: Agents inside sales and service platforms acting on opportunities, cases and change records under a configurable action catalogue.

exemplars.name: Line-of-business SaaS with bolted-on agents
exemplars.note: Agent features added to products bought for something else. Same architecture, usually a thinner control catalogue and no separate agent identity.

blocks.title: Customer
blocks.note: The author of the text the agent reads — ticket bodies, form fields, uploads, email replies. By construction, someone with an interest in the outcome.

blocks.title: Service staff
blocks.note: Approves the actions the catalogue gates, and reverses the ones nobody gated. The threshold between those two is this archetype's central configuration decision.

blocks.title: Identity & network edge
blocks.note: How staff reach the vendor and who they are asserted to be. The same channel supervises the agent and configures it, so it deserves privileged-access treatment.

items.label: Identity provider
items.note: Authenticates staff, and — where the vendor supports it — anchors a distinct identity for the agent instead of a shared service account.

items.label: Network inspection
items.note: What is being sent to the vendor, and what its callbacks bring back.

blocks.title: Vendor agent platform
blocks.note: The loop runs here and no policy decision point can be inserted into it. Only the published surfaces are drawn — the decision to act and the act itself both happen inside the boundary.

items.label: In-app agent
items.note: The agent feature as users and customers meet it. Reads case text as context; acts on records with the tenant's authority.

items.label: Record & case APIs
items.note: The product's published interfaces over your records — where the agent's writes land first.

items.label: Integration framework
items.note: How the agent reaches beyond the vendor's data model, on service principals you issued — scoped per integration, not per action.

blocks.title: Your downstream systems
blocks.note: Billing, entitlements, directory — reached through integrations the agent can invoke, and the point where a wrong action stops being reversible by editing a record. Frequently the real blast radius, and frequently forgotten.

items.label: Billing & entitlements
items.note: Where a refund or an account change becomes money and access.

items.label: Directory & downstream apps
items.note: Systems the integration credential can touch that no single action needed.

blocks.title: Tenant governance
blocks.note: Everything here is configuration the vendor enforces or telemetry you collect — the control plane collapses to the edges you own, because the loop itself cannot be instrumented.

items.label: Action catalogue & thresholds
items.note: Which actions, on which record types, and where a human is required. Generous by default, because autonomy is what the product is sold on.

items.label: Agent identity
items.note: A distinct, revocable principal for the agent. Without it, nothing it does is separately attributable or revocable.

items.label: Outcome monitoring
items.note: Refund rates, escalation rates, records touched — measured from first-party systems, because the vendor's view of its own agent is the vendor's.

items.label: Disable control
items.note: Turning the agent off without a vendor support ticket. Confirm it exists during evaluation, not during an incident.

blocks.title: Administrator
blocks.note: Authors the tenant configuration. Administering the agent is administering everything it may do, so this role is the privileged one on the diagram.

edges.label: case text & attachments
edges.note: Untrusted content enters the agent's context directly. The vendor's guardrail on it is configurable and not verifiable, which is why the catalogue and the reversal path carry the real weight.

edges.label: supervision / approvals
edges.note: Approval requests come out to staff and decisions go back. Only actions the catalogue marks as gated ever appear here — everything else has already happened by the time anyone looks.
Authenticated staff sessions for supervision and administration. Privileged access to this console is privileged access to the agent's entire permission set.

edges.label: integration writes
edges.note: The agent writes to your systems of record on integration credentials scoped per system, not per action — it inherits everything the credential can do.

edges.label: outcome telemetry
edges.note: First-party records of what actually changed, measured outside the provider boundary — which is what makes them reliable.

edges.label: catalogue / identity / disable
edges.note: You author the configuration, the provider enforces it, and neither can verify the other — the canonical shared-responsibility edge on this surface.

edges.label: tenant configuration
edges.note: The catalogue, thresholds and identity settings are authored here, once, and rarely revisited against a product sold on autonomy.

risks.note: The shortest path in this catalogue from untrusted input to consequential action — no breach required, just a text field.
The author of the input has a stake in the outcome, and unlimited retries at steering the agent's decision.
Consequential writes with no human present, decided inside a loop nobody outside the vendor can observe.
The agent acts through integration credentials issued for a system, not for a decision. Its authority is the union of every integration.
The connector grants set the reach and the action catalogue sets the intent, and neither is scoped by the other.
The loop is entirely unobservable and untestable — the whole platform is one integrated component your assurance programme has to stand in for.
Record contents and case data flow to the vendor's boundary, visible to you only at the network path.
Where the agent shares a service account, its access outlives any single configuration decision and cannot be individually revoked.

capabilities.note: Author the action catalogue deliberately — which actions, on which record types, under which conditions. The defaults are generous; the catalogue is your allowlist.
Set approval thresholds so consequential and irreversible writes escalate to staff before they land, sized to blast radius.
Give the agent a distinct, revocable principal and scope each integration credential to what the agent actually needs.
Verify the disable control exists and test it during evaluation — on this surface it is a product feature, not something you can build.
Enable and verify the vendor's guardrails on customer-supplied text, and treat every case field as adversarial in your catalogue decisions.
Treat admin-console access as privileged access — it is the agent's entire permission set.
Watch outcome rates — refunds, escalations, records touched — from first-party data; behavioural monitoring substitutes for runtime enforcement you cannot install.
Keep first-party records of what changed — often the only trustworthy account of what the agent did, because the provider does not write it.
Assess the platform as a supply-chain dependency — its loop, guardrails and tenancy cannot be tested directly.
Contractual commitments on the agent's behaviour, incident notice and your right to telemetry — the only control that crosses the boundary.
Manage the tenant configuration as governed policy with review cycles, not a console someone set once.
Inspect the vendor path inline — what is sent, and what callbacks return.

scenarios.title: A customer's ticket steers the agent

steps.note: Instructions embedded in a case field enter the agent's context as it reads the ticket.
The steered decision becomes a write — a refund issued through an integration credential scoped to the whole billing system.
Outcome monitoring flags the refund-rate anomaly from first-party data.
The catalogue is tightened or the agent disabled — the only interventions the surface offers.

scenarios.title: A gated action escalates to a human

steps.note: A request lands above the threshold the catalogue marks as gated.
The approval request leaves the vendor — the one moment the loop waits.
Staff see the proposed action and its context.
The decision goes back; everything below the threshold never appears here at all.
The approved write lands on the system of record.

scenarios.title: Tenant configuration is the control plane

steps.note: The catalogue, thresholds, agent identity and disable control are authored — each one a vendor-exposed setting.
The provider enforces what you authored. There is no independent way to verify the enforcement, which is what assurance compensates for.
